chapters.title: Chapter 1151. Rewriting the Reality of the Corridor With Every Heartbeat
paragraphs: In the heart of that swirling hellscape of gold and violet light, Apollo heard it.

The sound pierced through the ringing in his ears and the wet rasp of his own labored breathing. For a fraction of a second, a heartbeat so brief it would have been invisible to any observer, he allowed his focus to slip.
He glanced sideways.
Through a haze of sweat and blood, he saw him.
Rex.
Standing at the precipice of the circle, his face contorted in what looked like raw, unadulterated terror, his hand raised as if to ward off the inevitable.
A strange, painful tightness constricted Apollo’s chest. It wasn’t just physical pain; it was a surge of something dangerously close to admiration.
’Of course,’ Apollo thought, his mind fragmenting under the strain of the duel, ’of course Rex would try to intervene.’
’Of course he would rush into the furnace.’
’He has stepped into every goddamn crisis this city has endured for the past year without blinking.’
’That is who he is... That is the man I trust.’

The bitter irony of the moment that Apollo was standing between two identical masks of heroism, reading genuine loyalty in the eyes of a predator, was completely lost on him. He was too far gone, too buried in the primal need to survive.
"NO!" Apollo screamed.
The word tore from his throat, raw and ragged, shaking with the impossible effort of maintaining his defensive stance while shouting across the chaos. "STAY BACK, REX!"
"DON’T YOU DARE!"
The masked figure sensed the momentary lapse. The stranger didn’t hesitate; he exploited it.

With a flick of his wrist that looked almost casual, he unleashed a telekinetic volley. Three jagged chunks of broken stone, each the size of a human skull, screamed through the air from three different angles.
WHIP CRACK!
Apollo twisted his body with desperate agility, but he wasn’t fast enough. The middle projectile clipped his left shoulder with the force of a sledgehammer.
SHLICK.
The stone tore through fabric and flesh alike, gouging a furrow across his deltoid. Blood sprayed across the stone floor in a crimson arc, hot and steaming in the cool air.
Apollo grunted through clenched teeth, the pain igniting a fresh spike of adrenaline that burned like acid in his veins.
"This is mine!" Apollo roared back at Rex, his eyes blazing with a desperate pride. "I have to finish this myself!"
"Don’t you interfere!
At the edge of the circle, Rex Rexilion froze.
The hesitation that crossed his features was nothing short of a theatrical masterpiece. For one and a half agonizing seconds, he allowed his face to transform into a battlefield of its own.

He showed the world the internal agony of a man torn between respecting a friend’s dying wish and the instinct to save them from certain slaughter. His jaw tightened until the muscles corded like rope; his brow furrowed in anguish; his forward foot remained planted, poised for a charge that would never come.
Finally, he offered a slow, reluctant nod, the gesture of a man conceding defeat to fate itself. He stepped backward, retreating into the safety of the Aethelgard ranks.
"Get him some space," Rex commanded, his voice rough and strained, as if the effort of holding back his ’concern’ was physically taxing.
He turned to the soldiers crowding around him, his eyes hard and commanding. "If the tide turns or if he falls, we go in together."
"All of us at once. No heroics, no suicidal charges."
"We hit him like a hammer."
The soldiers nearest him nodded eagerly, their faces pale with relieved gratitude. To them, Rex wasn’t just a comrade; he was the anchor holding their courage together.
They saw a leader who was disciplined enough to hold back even when his heart was breaking.
Nobody looked at him twice. Nobody questioned the sincerity of his grief.
Behind the mask, Rex’s eyes remained fixed on Apollo’s bleeding shoulder, cold and hungry.
’Almost there,’ he thought. ’Just a little more pressure.’
’Just a few more broken bones, and then you’re mine.’
Xerollion, the man behind the mask saw the shift in Apollo’s posture and made a cold, clinical decision. The moment Apollo refused Rex’s help, the game changed from a test to an execution.

It was a simple, ruthless calculation. An Apollo who refused assistance was an Apollo who would push himself past the breaking point, past the threshold where survival instincts should force a retreat.

And an Apollo who fought past that point would finally reveal the true, unguarded mechanics of what the Apostle of Life could actually achieve. Rex had been starving for that data for months; now, he intended to feast on it.
’Time to peel back the layers,’ Xerollion thought behind his mask, his breathing steady while Apollo’s came in ragged gasps. ’Let’s see what makes your divinity tick.’
He began the layering process with terrifying precision.

First came telekinesis. With a violent twist of his fingers, CRUNCH SHATTER the accumulated debris of the corridor; shattered armor plating and broken spear shafts were yanked into orbit around the duel.
This wasn’t the chaotic storm of a novice; this was a coordinated system of death. The fragments moved in synchronized, deadly arcs, each piece tracking Apollo’s heat signature independently.
They swarmed him like angry hornets, forcing his guard to split between the blade in front of him and the shrapnel screaming at his flanks.
Then, he layered on the Elemental Mastery.
Waves of supernatural fire began to roll across the stone floor in low, undulating sheets. This wasn’t normal combustion; it was a hunting flame.
When one wave surged upward, catching Apollo across the ribs with the force of a molten sledgehammer, the Apostle cried out in genuine, shocked agony.
"GAHH!" Apollo’s voice broke as he stumbled back, clutching his side.
His divine barrier, the instinctual shield that should have absorbed elemental heat automatically, had failed to engage.

The energy signature Xerollion was wielding was so alien, so fundamentally ’wrong’ to the world’s natural laws, that Apollo’s magic didn’t even recognize it as a threat category until it was already searing through his flesh.
But the most terrifying part was the martial choreography. Xerollion fought the close-quarters combat like a conductor leading a symphony of slaughter.

Every thrust of his weapon was positioned to force Apollo to dodge into the path of a telekinetic stone; every defensive parry was a calculated setup for three subsequent attacks that would land exactly two seconds later.
’Left hook to force the retreat now, the stone spike from below now, the fire sweep yes, dance for me, little god.’

Apollo, bleeding from a dozen shallow cuts and panting through the smoke, realized he could no longer play defense. He could feel his ribs grinding against each other with every breath, the metallic tang of blood filling his mouth.
If he didn’t escalate, he would be dismantled piece by piece.
"Fine," Apollo growled through gritted teeth, blood spattering his chin. "You want to see what I can do?! THEN LOOK!"
Apollo opened up.
The golden light erupting from his body didn’t just glow; it detonated.

The intensity climbed to a level that turned the entire corridor into a bleached white furnace, throwing the shadows of the thousands of watching soldiers up the walls in enormous, distorted shapes that danced like demons.
The very air began to hum with the frequency of creation itself.
With this escalation, the quality of his strikes underwent a terrifying metamorphosis. His power was no longer just blunt force; it was reversed entropy, the power to undo time itself.
CLANG!

A chunk of floating debris caught a glancing blow from Apollo’s fist. Instead of breaking into fragments, it instantly crumbled into fine, ancient sand, the state it would have become after eight thousand years of wind and rain.
The effect was instantaneous and absolute.
CRACK BOOM!
The stone beneath Apollo’s feet couldn’t withstand the pressure of his stance; radial fractures spread outward like spiderwebs with every step he took, each crack glowing with residual gold.

The air itself seemed to warp around his movements, leaving behind a faint, shimmering golden haze that lingered in his wake like the ghost of a star. He wasn’t just fighting anymore; he was rewriting the reality of the corridor with every heartbeat.

chapters.title: Chapter 1152. The Struggle Makes the Eventual Breaking So Much Sweeter
paragraphs: At exactly the four-minute mark of this escalating nightmare, the impossible happened. Apollo found his opening.

It wasn’t a lucky strike; it was a masterpiece of desperate calculation. For three excruciating exchanges, Apollo had been feeding Xerollion false data, deliberately overcommitting to his left side, telegraphing a clumsy stumble, and building a feint that felt like weakness.
He baited the trap. He saw the masked figure’s guard drop by a mere four inches, a micro adjustment in anticipation of a failed lunge.
’NOW!’ Apollo’s mind screamed.
He planted his lead foot, feeling the stone crack beneath his divine weight, and unleashed an uppercut that carried every ounce of momentum from his legs, his core, and his raw fury.
CRACK THUD!
The sound was sickening—the wet, splintering noise of bone meeting unstoppable force. The blow caught Xerollion square along the jaw.
The masked figure’s head snapped sideways with such violent velocity that his neck vertebrae audibly popped. For one enormous, roaring second, the Aethelgard side of the corridor erupted.
A primal, terrified shriek rose from the soldiers, a sound of hope so loud it shook dust from the ancient ceiling.
"HE GOT HIM!" someone screamed. "APOLLO DID IT!"
But the triumph lasted less than a heartbeat.

The head snapped back to center within half a second, moving with an unnatural, mechanical precision. Before the pain could even register in Xerollion’s nerves, his Infinite Regeneration had already knitted the fractured mandible back together.
The bone fused with terrifying speed; the cartilage reasserted itself before the blood could even trickle from his lips.
Xerollion simply rolled his neck in a casual, almost bored gesture, and the world turned upside down.
WHOOSH.

In a blur of motion too fast for the human eye to track, Xerollion closed the distance. His gauntleted hand shot forward like a striking viper, fingers locking around Apollo’s throat with the crushing finality of a steel trap.
CHOKE.
"Nnngh!" Apollo’s protest died in his throat as his windpipe collapsed under the pressure.

The lift that followed was not merely a feat of strength; it was a violation of physics. Xerollion’s Peak Superhuman Physique provided the raw, terrifying power, while his telekinesis amplified the grip to a molecular level.

Apollo was wrenched off his feet, his boots kicking uselessly three feet above the stone. Both of Apollo’s hands clawed frantically at the wrist holding him, his fingernails scraping against the armor, but the grip did not shift by a single millimeter.
It was as if he were trying to pry apart two mountain ranges.
Xerollion held him there suspended in midair for two full seconds. In the deadly theater of this duel, those two seconds weren’t a tactical pause; they were a statement of absolute dominance.
A message to Apollo and to everyone watching: ’You cannot hurt me.’ You cannot even touch me.’
Then, with a grunt of contempt, Xerollion hurled him.
BOOM!
Apollo became a golden streak of broken momentum. He hurtled across the corridor twenty meters in the blink of an eye.

When he hit the far wall, it wasn’t a collision; it was an explosion. He punched through the outer layer of reinforced stone like it was wet parchment, vanishing into a catastrophic cloud of pulverized rock, mortar, and choking dust.
The silence that followed was absolute. It wasn’t just quiet; it was a vacuum.
The Aethelgard soldiers stood frozen, their breath trapped in their lungs, the sudden absence of the magical cacophony feeling like a physical blow to their eardrums.
’Did he die?’ The question hung unspoken in the air. ’Is that all the Apostle of Life has left?’
Four seconds passed.
Four seconds of agonizing, suffocating stillness.
Then, the rubble began to shift.
The silence of the corridor was shattered not by a scream, but by the grinding of stone.
From the heart of the pulverized wall, a silhouette emerged. Apollo didn’t stagger out of the rubble like a broken man; he stepped out like a vengeful god emerging from a tomb.

Blood ran in thick, crimson rivulets down the left side of his face from a jagged gash above his eyebrow, matting his hair and stinging his eye. His ornate chestplate was spiderwebbed with deep fractures, the metal twisted inward from the impact.
For one horrifying heartbeat, his left arm hung at an impossible, nauseating angle; the elbow joint clearly shattered before a surge of brilliant gold pulsed through the limb.
CRACK SNAP.
The sound of bones knitting back together was wet and violent. The life affinity forced the joint back into its socket with brutal efficiency, overriding the pain with raw cellular reconstruction.
He didn’t limp. He walked.
The golden radiance surrounding him hadn’t dimmed from the impact; if anything, it had become more pressurized, more dangerous.
"You’re strong," Apollo said.

His voice was hoarse, the words catching on the blood pooling in his throat. His breathing was ragged, with each inhale sounding like a wet rasp that indicated his punctured lungs were struggling to find air.
"Stronger than anything I have ever faced..."
"Anything I have ever heard of." He paused, tilting his head back to spit a glob of copper-tasting blood onto the pristine stone.
He wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist in one defiant motion. "But I’m not going to stop... I can’t stop."
"I know." Xerollion’s voice drifted through the haze of dust.
There was no mockery in it, only something far more unsettling: genuine, predatory pleasure. "That’s exactly what makes this enjoyable, Apollo."
"The struggle makes the eventual breaking so much sweeter."
Apollo’s eyes locked onto the mask. "Then let’s see you break."
"ACTIVATE."
The word wasn’t shouted; it was commanded.
For two centuries, Academy texts had attempted to codify the Full Activation of an Apostle of Life. They spoke of ’temporal manipulation’ and ’biological restoration,’ but they were pathetic lies.
They couldn’t capture the terror of it. Those standing in the northern corridor who had never witnessed such divinity understood within one terrifying second that reality itself was being rewritten.

The golden light didn’t just brighten; it transformed. It ceased to be mere photons and became a physical presence, a crushing weight of existence that expanded outward from Apollo in a perfect, terrifying sphere.
It swallowed forty meters of the corridor in every direction, and inside that golden radius, the arrow of time began to spin backward.
WHOOSH SHHH.
The sound was like a thousand reversed whispers. The cracks in the walls groaned as they sealed themselves shut.

The dust suspended in the air didn’t just settle; it condensed, flowing backward like reverse snowfall, reassembling into fragments that knitted themselves back into the stone surfaces they had been torn from.

The furrows Apollo’s own boots had ground into the floor smoothed themselves flat, as if the violence had never occurred. At the very edge of the radius, wounded soldiers felt their wounds seal and their exhaustion vanish in a rush of supernatural vitality.
Several men collapsed to their knees, weeping openly, overwhelmed by a sudden, inexplicable euphoria they couldn’t comprehend.
"GLORY TO THE APOSTLE! "A roar went up from the Aethelgard side, thousands of voices joining in a thunderous hymn of desperate hope.
But inside the golden sphere, Xerollion felt something alien.

It was a disorienting, nauseating sensation. He examined it with the detached, clinical interest he applied to all novel stimuli, noting the way his own cells seemed to be receiving urgent, divine instructions to revert to an earlier configuration.
His body wasn’t being treated as flesh and bone but as a mathematical equation being solved in reverse. For one agonizing second and a half, the effect took hold.
His wounds from earlier closed; his muscles relaxed into a state of pre-combat readiness; his very timeline began to unravel.
Then, the countermeasure triggered.
THUM THUM.
Full Potential Adaptation completed its analysis in a microsecond. Inside Xerollion’s mind, the mechanism resolved itself as a clean structural map.
Target: Entropy Reversal.
Method: Cellular register manipulation via divine authority channel.
Countermeasure: Static Temporal Anchor.
The adaptation engaged with the cold finality of a guillotine. The sensation of being pulled backward simply... stopped.

His body slammed back into its present state, anchoring itself to the current moment with absolute stubbornness. When the golden wave of Apollo’s power washed over him again, it passed through him like wind through smoke, leaving him completely untouched.
The Apostle was pouring everything he was into the universe, and the masked man simply stood there, unchanged.
Behind the ruined, blood-flecked mask, Rex’s lips curled upward. A slow, hungry smile spread across his face.
"My turn."

Inside Xerollion’s mind, the mechanism resolved itself as a clean structural map.
Target: Entropy Reversal.
Method: Cellular register manipulation via divine authority channel.
Countermeasure: Static Temporal Anchor.
The adaptation engaged with the cold finality of a guillotine.
The sensation of being pulled backward simply... stopped.
His body slammed back into its present state, anchoring itself to the current moment with absolute stubbornness.
When the golden wave of Apollo’s power washed over him again, it passed through him like wind through smoke, leaving him completely untouched.
The Apostle was pouring everything he was into the universe, and the masked man simply stood there, unchanged.
Behind the ruined, blood-flecked mask, Rex’s lips curled upward.
A slow, hungry smile spread across his face.
"My turn."

chapters.title: Chapter 1153. Watch How Fast the Darkness Returns When the Candle Burns to the Wick
paragraphs: The golden sphere pressed against Xerollion like a physical tide, a tsunami of divine authority attempting to drown his very existence.
For three excruciating seconds, he had actually felt it—the terrifying, beautiful pull of entropy reversing, the sensation of his own heartbeat stuttering as time tried to unmake him.
It was the first time since his confrontation with Kaeleth that anything had made contact with him in a way that required genuine cognitive processing.
Three seconds of real, tangible effect. That wasn’t a failure; it was a data point of immense value. Most gods would have been unmade in the first millisecond.
’Impressive,’ Rex thought, his mind working with cold, inhuman speed even as the golden pressure roared around him. ’The output is magnificent... The scale is unprecedented...’
He filed the sensation away with genuine appreciation, a predator cataloging a new kind of venom. He reflected, not for the first time, on the grim mathematics of his own ascension.

His power, his godhood, and his terrifying adaptability—all of it had been purchased with the broken bodies and shattered souls of those who had dared to show him their ’best work.’ He didn’t hate them for it; he thanked them. Their corpses were the currency of his evolution.
Across the shimmering circle of golden light, the reaction of the two armies split with perfect, devastating clarity along the line of comprehension.
On the Aethelgard side, the atmosphere was one of religious ecstasy. The soldiers screamed themselves hoarse, their voices cracking as they roared encouragement.

To them, the sheer, overwhelming scale of the activation was proof enough of divine intervention. They had spent the last hour watching their sacred formations get systematically dismantled, watching their brothers die in the mud.
Now, seeing their Apostle bathe the world in a radiance that could heal wounds and reverse time, they believed salvation had finally arrived.
"HE’S REWRITING THE WORLD!" a young soldier screamed, tears streaming down his face as he raised his sword to the golden sky. "THE GOD IS HERE! WE CAN’T LOSE!"
They saw a sunrise. They saw the end of the nightmare.

A few dozen meters away, Cassandra stood like a statue carved from obsidian. She folded her arms across her chest, her eyes narrowed, watching the way the golden light licked at the edges of Xerollion’s static field.
Her expression was not one of awe but of profound, weary pity.
Gorvasha stepped up beside her, his breath hitching as the heat from Apollo’s aura washed over them. "Cassandra... look at it."
"The Apostle has unleashed everything... The tide has turned."
Cassandra didn’t blink. Her gaze remained fixed on the masked figure who stood unmoving in the center of the storm.
"They think that’s a victory," she said, her voice flat and devoid of emotion.
"What do you mean?" Gorvasha asked, glancing nervously at the screaming soldiers behind them. "Look at the scale of it!"
"Nothing has ever been this bright, this powerful."
"They think it’s a victory because it’s the largest thing they have ever seen," Cassandra interrupted, her words cutting through the noise like a blade. "But scale is not strength."
"Power without endurance is just a firework."
She watched as the golden light began to flicker at its most intense points, the strain of maintaining such a reality warping field showing in the minute tremors of Apollo’s stance.
"Watch what happens when those four minutes run out," she whispered, a dark warning hanging in the air. "Watch how fast the darkness returns when the candle burns itself to the wick."
Apollo crossed the threshold into the third minute of his divine activation, and the cost of godhood began to extract its toll.

The exhaustion wasn’t just fatigue; it was a parasitic drain that felt as though his very marrow was being siphoned out through his pores. Around the two and a half minute mark, the ’payment’ for reversing entropy became clear.

His guard dropped a fraction of an inch between exchanges, a fatal vulnerability against any other opponent. His breathing, once a steady rhythm of power, had become a wet, labored rasp that fought to be heard over the cacophony of clashing steel and magical discharge.

Sweat cut clean, pale lines through the drying blood on his face, stinging his eyes as he fought to maintain focus. His hands had begun to betray him; they shook between strikes, a fine tremor that forced him to reset his grip on his weapon each time, his knuckles white with the effort of containing the quaking muscle.
’Don’t falter... Not now.’
’Not when they’re watching.’
But he attacked anyway. And God help anyone standing in his way; he attacked with the precision of a surgeon and the fury of a dying star.
The opening combination of the third minute was a revelation—the most sustained, flawless offense he had produced since the duel began. Eleven strikes delivered in under four seconds.

Each blow was not just physical; each one carried the crushing, consecrated weight of his life affinity. The air screamed as his weapon cut through it, each swing leaving behind a trail of golden afterimages.
This wasn’t just divine technique; it was a confession. Every strike was fueled by an anger that had been compounding like pressurized steam since the moment he realized what Xerollion truly was.
’Veylor.’ Apollo’s teeth ground together so hard his jaw ached.
He could see Veylor’s face, the man who had been three weeks away from proposing to Iris, a man who believed in honor.
’Calivara.’ The woman who had stood beside him since his first day of training.
’Eryndra.’ Who had laughed at his terrible jokes when the rest of the world stayed silent?
’And the others...’
And beneath them all, the shattered remains of his own faith. He had extended his trust to a world that had seemed, for one brief, beautiful moment, like it might be fundamentally decent.
Now, he was standing in a corridor of corpses, fighting a monster that ate hope for breakfast.
CRACK SHINK! CRACK SHINK!
Xerollion moved like liquid mercury. He blocked nine of the eleven strikes with effortless, inhuman economy.
But the other two, the two that bypassed his guard, he took them deliberately.

Apollo had noticed this pattern halfway through the second minute, but his pride had refused to let him acknowledge the terrifying truth. The masked figure wasn’t failing to defend; he was choosing when to be hit.

Every so often, a strike that should have been intercepted would be allowed through at a slightly reduced angle. Xerollion would shift his weight just enough to absorb the impact rather than avoid it, letting the divine energy sear through his armor and bite into his flesh.
’Why?’ Apollo’s mind screamed. ’Why would you let me hit you?’
The answer arrived in the way Xerollion’s shoulders relaxed when the blow landed. The truth was worse than any tactical error: his opponent was enjoying the sensation.
Xerollion was treating Apollo’s desperate, righteous fury as nothing more than a series of exquisite stimuli. He was tasting the pain, savoring the divine burn against his skin.
Then, the atmosphere shifted. The air grew heavy, charged with enough static to make the hair on every soldier’s neck stand up.
What came next was the most punishing ninety seconds of the entire duel: a ninety-second descent into a hell of grinding bone, shattered magic, and raw, unadulterated violence.

It was a massacre of endurance that would punish both men in ways that transcended the physical. For Apollo, it was the slow, agonizing death of his spirit; for Xerollion, it was the exquisite torment of a predator being pushed to his absolute limit.

chapters.title: Chapter 1154. A Predator Who Had Been Hunting Him With Foreknowledge
paragraphs: Somewhere in the meat of that ninety-second hellscape, Apollo abandoned technique entirely. The disciplined structure, the flawless forms taught by the High Masters of Aethelgard, the measured breathing, and the calculated parries—it all burned away in the furnace of his desperation.
He stopped being a trained Apostle and became something primal, something ancient and starving.
He stopped fighting like a soldier and started fighting like an animal trapped in a cage with a god.
CRUNCH.
His elbow smashed into Xerollion’s jaw with enough force to shatter granite, but the masked man merely tilted his head, absorbing the impact with a sickening wet sound. Apollo didn’t stop.
He threw knees into ribs, headbutts that sent sprays of blood flying from his own nose, and desperate, ragged strikes that lacked any semblance of elegance.

For one heartbeat, Apollo managed to close the distance, wrapping his arms around Xerollion’s torso in a desperate grappling attempt. His fingers dug into the gaps of the armor, his muscles screaming as he tried to leverage the monster to the ground.
For one and a half seconds, it worked. The momentum shifted.
Then reality reasserted itself with brutal cruelty.
SHRAK.

Xerollion didn’t fight the grapple; he exploited it. With a terrifyingly precise twist of his hips and a sudden reversal of leverage that felt less like strength and more like physics bending to his will, Xerollion wrenched Apollo’s center of gravity away.
Apollo was hurled backward as if thrown by an invisible giant. His spine slammed into the stone floor with a bone-deep THUD that echoed through the corridor.
Apollo scrambled up immediately, his vision swimming in red haze. His lungs burned like they were filled with molten lead.
He lunged forward again, throwing a desperate overhand right that missed by a hair’s breadth, the sheer force of his swing cracking the stone floor where Xerollion had stood.
FWOOSH.
Xerollion met the onslaught with a quality of movement that defied human comprehension. To the soldiers watching, paralyzed by terror, he seemed to exist in the spaces between seconds.
There was never any hurry in him.
No wasted motion. No panic.
He moved through Apollo’s hurricane of violence like a ghost walking through rain.

A strike that would have severed a man’s head whistled past his throat, the wind of it ruffling his hair, but Xerollion was already rotating into the counter move before the first blow had even finished its arc.
THWIP TAP.
A two-knuckle strike landed with surgical precision against the inside of Apollo’s elbow. Apollo’s arm went instantly numb, the nerves misfiring in a cascade of useless electricity.

Before he could compensate, Xerollion’s palm connected with his hip, a short, sharp impact that killed Apollo’s balance mid-commitment. Then came the most insulting blow: an open-handed slap across Apollo’s temple, delivered with the casual nonchalance of someone brushing away a fly.
Apollo’s world tilted. His equilibrium shattered.
For three agonizing seconds, his brain couldn’t decide which way was up, giving Xerollion the opening to drive three consecutive strikes into Apollo’s left ribcage.
CRACK. CRACK. CRACK.
The sound of ribs snapping was like dry kindling breaking underfoot. Apollo gasped, a spray of crimson mist escaping his lips as his chest cavity buckled.

But the Life affinity roared to life. Gold light flooded the damaged tissue, the broken bone fragments grinding against each other before being forcibly fused back together. In under two seconds, the pain was replaced by a searing, artificial vitality.
Apollo kept coming.
"Why..." Apollo gasped, the words tearing through a throat raw from screaming.
Blood flecked his teeth as he steadied himself between exchanges. "Why are you drawing this out?"
His anger had mutated; beneath the rage was something raw, something terrifying and profoundly lonely. "You could have killed me ten minutes ago."
"I know you could have... Why let this continue?"

Xerollion caught Apollo’s rising knee on his forearm, the impact sending a shockwave up his arm that he welcomed. He allowed the force to push him back half a step—a deliberate gift, a tactical concession that both men recognized instantly.
"Probably closer to twenty minutes," Xerollion said, his voice unnervingly calm beneath the mask. "But then I’d never have seen what you actually are."
He stepped forward, the golden light of Apollo’s aura reflecting off the dark surface of his mask. "Nobody has ever pushed you far enough to find your floor, Apollo."
"Your enemies have all been beneath you, cowering in the shadow of your divinity."
"Your allies have all been careful with you, treating you like something precious that might break."
Xerollion’s head tilted slightly, almost inquisitively. "I’m the first person in your life who has ever been genuinely curious about where the bottom is."
"I want to see what’s left of you when the god dies and only the man remains."
"That’s what this is to you," Apollo spat, blood dripping from his chin. "Curiosity... A game."
"That’s what everything is to me."

Apollo launched into a desperate, spinning backfist, a technique so violent it carried enough centrifugal force to decapitate a lesser man. The air whistled as his fist cut through the space where Xerollion’s temple should have been.
WHOOSH CLANG!
Xerollion didn’t just dodge; he flowed. He ducked beneath the arc of the strike with the eerie grace of something that wasn’t entirely human, his expression remaining as impassive as stone.
In the same fluid motion, he surged upward, driving his shoulder directly into Apollo’s sternum.
CRUNCH.
The impact sounded like a sledgehammer hitting a sack of wet gravel. Apollo’s ribs groaned under the pressure, and the force was enough to lift his entire muscular frame off the ground.
He was launched backward, his boots skidding helplessly against the stone as he slid eight meters across the corridor floor, leaving bloody streaks where his armor scraped against the masonry.
A collective sound rose from the Aethelgard soldiers, a strangled, horrified noise like a wounded animal sensing its pack leader had been broken.
Apollo’s vision swam in crimson. His lungs felt flattened, his diaphragm spasming as he fought to pull air into a chest that felt like it had been collapsed by a siege engine.
Gritting his teeth until they threatened to shatter, he pushed himself up onto one unsteady knee. His muscles screamed in protest, each fiber twitching with exhaustion.
Finally, he forced himself to his feet, but the golden radiance that had once been an all-consuming sun had noticeably dimmed. It was guttering now, flickering like a candle caught in a hurricane.
’Two minutes and fifty seconds.’
The number burned in his mind like acid. He could feel the ceiling coming—not the physical stone above him, but the invisible, absolute limit of his power approaching from within.
It was a specific, cold dread, the feeling of a man watching his own executioner approach from the inside of his own ribs.
"You’re running out of time," Xerollion observed.

His voice was horrifyingly level. He sounded like someone commenting on the weather, despite the fact that Apollo had just driven a fist into his sternum with enough force to crack the reinforced plate armor beneath his robes.
Beneath the metal, Apollo could see the faint glow of divine energy as Xerollion’s internal organs knit themselves back together in the microscopic space between one word and the next.
"Four minutes," Xerollion continued, stepping forward with measured, predatory strides. "That’s your ceiling, isn’t it?"
"I’ve been curious for quite some time about what actually happens to you when the clock runs out."
"What happens when the light fails?"
Apollo’s pupils dilated. His heart hammered against his damaged ribs like a trapped bird.
It was a small moment, a fractional lapse in his combat focus, but in a duel fought at this lethal velocity, it was an eternity. And Xerollion saw it.
He saw the way Apollo’s entire posture shifted from defiance to genuine, bone-deep terror.
The four-minute limitation was not public knowledge. It wasn’t written in any Academy text, nor was it whispered in the halls of Aethelgard.

Apollo had discussed it precisely four times in his entire adult life: once in confidence with Kaelira, once with his mother, once during a classified strategic briefing with Valentina, and once most devastatingly during an exhaustive, hour-long tactical session with Rex Rexilion in a private training yard six months ago.
They had been planning for exactly this scenario.
The suspicion didn’t just enter Apollo’s mind; it crystallized. He watched the horrific realization surface with the clarity of a blade cutting through fog.
The implications were catastrophic. If Xerollion knew about the four-minute limit, he wasn’t just an opponent; he was a predator who had been hunting Apollo with foreknowledge.
He had been waiting for this exact moment of vulnerability.
For a heartbeat, Apollo stood frozen, his mind caught between the terror of the betrayal and the immediate need to survive.
Then, the sheer weight of the injustice broke him. Rage, hot and corrosive, rolled over the realization like a tidal wave, burying the question beneath a mountain of fury.
He didn’t have the cognitive capacity to process a betrayal of this magnitude while simultaneously trying to prevent his own death.
"SHUT UP! "Apollo roared, the sound less human than divine. "SHUT YOUR GODDAMN MOUTH AND FIGHT ME!"

The four-minute limitation was not public knowledge.
It wasn’t written in any Academy text, nor was it whispered in the halls of Aethelgard.

Apollo had discussed it precisely four times in his entire adult life: once in confidence with Kaelira, once with his mother, once during a classified strategic briefing with Valentina, and once most devastatingly during an exhaustive, hour-long tactical session with Rex Rexilion in a private training yard six months ago.
They had been planning for exactly this scenario.
The suspicion didn’t just enter Apollo’s mind; it crystallized.
He watched the horrific realization surface with the clarity of a blade cutting through fog.
The implications were catastrophic.
If Xerollion knew about the four-minute limit, he wasn’t just an opponent; he was a predator who had been hunting Apollo with foreknowledge.
He had been waiting for this exact moment of vulnerability.
For a heartbeat, Apollo stood frozen, his mind caught between the terror of the betrayal and the immediate need to survive.
Then, the sheer weight of the injustice broke him.
Rage, hot and corrosive, rolled over the realization like a tidal wave, burying the question beneath a mountain of fury.
He didn’t have the cognitive capacity to process a betrayal of this magnitude while simultaneously trying to prevent his own death.
"SHUT UP!
"Apollo roared, the sound less human than divine.
"SHUT YOUR GODDAMN MOUTH AND FIGHT ME!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1155. His Godhood Had Been Caught Like a Child’s Tantrum
paragraphs: The roar that tore from Apollo’s throat wasn’t just a sound; it was a release of every ounce of grief, betrayal, and exhaustion he had accumulated since the first drop of blood hit the floor.
He didn’t just throw a punch. He threw his entire existence.

Every remaining reserve of his divine activation, every spark of the Life affinity that refused to die, was violently compressed. He channeled it through his shoulder, down his arm, and into the knuckles of his right fist.

The energy became so dense it defied physics; the air in front of his fist didn’t just move, it ignited. A corona of searing golden flame erupted before his knuckles had even traveled two feet, a localized supernova that screamed with the sound of tearing reality.
FWOOOOOM!
The sheer displaced air pressure hit the Aethelgard formation like a physical shockwave. Soldiers sixty meters back stumbled, their armor rattling as the invisible wall of force rolled over them.
This wasn’t a strike; it was a cataclysm. A strike that could have leveled a fortified citadel.
A strike that could have cracked the foundation of the world.
Apollo’s vision was nothing but white light and the burning agony of his own muscles tearing under the strain of containing that much power. He expected to see Xerollion vaporized.
He expected to see the corridor collapse into rubble. He expected to see the monster shattered.
Instead, reality simply... stopped.
CLACK.
The sound was small.
Pathetic.
Almost mundane. But in that moment, it sounded louder than the explosion.
Xerollion had caught it. With one hand.
There was no flashy magical barrier to absorb the impact. No telekinetic field to deflect the force.
No elemental counter surge to dissipate the golden fire. Xerollion simply reached into the heart of the supernova, raised his right hand, and closed his fingers around Apollo’s fist.

He stopped the strongest attack an Apostle of Life had ever produced with nothing but the raw, terrifying physical output of a body that had been elevated past every theoretical human ceiling months ago.
The golden flames licked against Xerollion’s palm, searing his glove, but he didn’t flinch. He didn’t even blink.
He just held it. He held the apocalypse in his grip.
Then came the silence.
It wasn’t just a quiet moment; it was a vacuum. Every voice in the northern corridor died instantly.
Ten thousand soldiers, spectators, and nobles stopped breathing in unison, as if the very concept of sound had been forbidden by divine decree.
The only thing that existed was the low, hungry hum of the golden activation still burning across the walls, casting grotesquely long shadows.

In the center of that golden hellscape, two figures stood locked together. Apollo’s fist was buried in Xerollion’s open palm, the divine energy grinding against his skin like molten glass, yet there was no forward momentum.
There was no recoil. There was absolutely nothing happening.
Apollo’s breathing had stopped. His eyes, wide and bloodshot, stared fixedly at the point of contact.
Rex watched him from across the space, and in that moment, Rex knew he would remember this expression for as long as he drew breath.
It wasn’t fear. Fear was a reaction to a threat.

What Apollo was experiencing was something far more devastating. It was the psychological vertigo that comes when a load-bearing assumption of reality gives way to the sickening, hollow sensation of discovering that the ground you have trusted beneath your feet for years was never actually there.
His entire understanding of power, of divinity, of the hierarchy of the world, had just been dismantled by a single gesture.
His godhood had been caught like a child’s tantrum.
Xerollion didn’t move.
He didn’t taunt, and he didn’t smile. He simply held the position, a monument of unshakable, terrifying certainty, waiting for the broken man to realize that his world was gone.
Xerollion held the grip. He didn’t just maintain contact; he maintained dominance.
He held Apollo’s fist for three agonizing seconds longer than any tactician would deem necessary. Those three seconds were not wasted; they were a performance.

Every second that passed without Apollo breaking Xerollion’s stance was a second that carved a new scar into the collective psyche of Aethelgard. Ten thousand witnesses—generals, nobles, and hardened soldiers—were watching, and they were all learning a lesson in humiliation.

They saw the golden fury of an Apostle fail to budge a single finger. They saw the impossible happen, and in that silence, the corridor’s understanding of power restructured itself in real time, bending to accommodate a new, terrifying truth.
’I am not the one who needs to fear the end,’ Apollo thought, his mind fracturing. ’I am the one who has already reached it.’
Then, Xerollion pushed.
It wasn’t a shove; it was a statement of absolute physical superiority.
SHRAK THUD!

Apollo was hurled backward. His boots screamed against the stone as he skidded six full steps, his entire body recoiling from the release of force. His arm felt as though it had been wrenched from its socket, the tendons straining at the limit of their elasticity.
And at the exact moment his heel caught the stone and his momentum died, the universe seemed to break.
The golden light around Apollo didn’t just fade. It died.
VROOOOM SHHHH.

The enormous radius of reversed entropy, the divine field that had been holding the very stones of the corridor together, collapsed inward with a sound like a dying star. The magical stitches holding the reality of the room together snapped.

Cracks that had been fused shut by Apollo’s Life affinity suddenly tore open across the walls with wet, grinding sounds. Dust that had been suspended in the golden glow resumed its slow, mournful fall from the ceiling.
And Apollo Brightsoul fell.
He didn’t fall gracefully. He crashed to one knee with a bone-jarring impact that echoed fifty meters away.
CRUNCH.

The price of divinity came due all at once. The accumulated exhaustion of four minutes of sustained, apocalyptic output slammed into a body that had already endured twenty minutes of systematic, brutal destruction.

His nervous system screamed in protest, each nerve ending firing off warnings of total shutdown. He collapsed forward, bracing both hands against the cold stone floor just to keep from faceplanting into his own blood.

Sweat and crimson droplets fell steadily from his chin, pitter pattering against the floor like rain. His chest heaved in ragged, desperate gulps, each breath feeling like he was inhaling broken glass.
’I am empty,’ Apollo thought, his vision tunneling into blackness. ’There is nothing left... Not even the spark.’
Xerollion stepped forward. His boots made soft, measured clicks on the stone as he approached the kneeling god.
He stood over Apollo, framed by the wreckage of the corridor, looking as though he had simply finished a light morning stroll. His armor was pristine.
His breathing was steady, calm, measured, and utterly devoid of the exertion that should have accompanied such a feat.
The contrast was more violent than any punch thrown during the fight.
"There it is," Xerollion said. His voice carried effortlessly through the stunned silence, dripping with a satisfaction that was absolutely, cruelly unconcealed. "Four minutes."
He looked down at the broken Apostle, his eyes cold and analytical beneath the mask. "I wanted to see it. I wanted to witness the exact moment the light gutters out."
"And now... now I have."

chapters.title: Chapter 1156. Trying to Pour an Ocean Into a Teacup
paragraphs: The silence that filled the northern corridor afterward was not empty; it had a physical texture, thick and suffocating like smoke. It pressed against the eardrums of every soul present, a heavy, velvet weight that made the air itself feel difficult to inhale.

Thousands of Aethelgard soldiers stood frozen, pressed against the perimeter of the battle circle. Their eyes were wide, fixed with horrified fascination on their greatest living hero, the sun incarnate, the Apostle of Life, now reduced to a broken, bloodied figure kneeling in the dirt before a man who hadn’t even broken his stride.

The thunderous chanting that had shaken dust from the vaulted ceilings three minutes earlier had vanished, replaced by a low, poisonous murmur. It was the sound of collapsing hope: thousands of voices whispering questions they didn’t want the answers to.
’What happens now?’
’How do we survive this? Who protects us when the light fails?’
Somewhere in the middle ranks, a young soldier began to sob, a raw, hiccuping sound of pure terror, and the veterans beside him didn’t even flinch.
They couldn’t.
They were too busy watching the death of an era.
On the opposite side, the atmosphere shifted from tense dread to something far more sinister. The Underlayer’s formation began to smile.
It wasn’t a cheer. There was no need for the vulgarity of shouting.
Demons, orcs, shadeveil creatures, and voidkin exchanged glances with the calm, satisfied expressions of gamblers watching a long shot bet finally come in.
They weren’t surprised; they were vindicated. Behind the front ranks, protected by layers of monstrous flesh and steel, Mordecai Vrael let out a long, shuddering breath.

His hands, which had been clenched so tight his knuckles were white, finally relaxed. For the first time since the siege began, he allowed himself to believe that the darkness would not be extinguished.
The realm would survive.
’Gods help us,’ Apollo thought, his forehead nearly touching the blood-slicked stone. ’I am empty... I am nothing but ash.’
Then, the sky broke.
A column of light descended through the ceiling. It was gold, but it was not the gold of Apollo’s affinity that fierce, burning, aggressive radiance that demanded worship.
This was different. This was something cleaner, more ancient, and infinitely more terrifying in its purity.
The light tore through three hundred meters of solid granite as though the stone were merely a suggestion, as though the mountain itself had stepped aside to make way for a sovereign.
SHHHHHHHHHHHH...

The sound was like silk tearing across the universe. The light spilled into the corridor in a wide, soft column of impossible brilliance, making every torch, every magical lantern, and every enchanted blade in the room look like cheap, mechanical toys.
It settled around the kneeling Apollo Brightsoul like water finding its level, pooling around his battered frame.
And then, the miracles began.
FZZZT CRACK.
The wounds didn’t just heal; they were erased. This wasn’t the desperate, straining regeneration of Apollo’s own exhausted power.
This was absolute restoration. The jagged gash above his eyebrow sealed instantly, leaving skin as smooth as marble.
The wet, grinding sound of his cracked ribs resetting echoed through the silent hall as they snapped back into perfect alignment.
The bone-deep, soul-crushing exhaustion, the kind of fatigue that kills men in their sleep, was violently lifted from his body as if pulled away by unseen hands.
Apollo gasped, his lungs suddenly expanding without pain, his heart finding a rhythm that felt stronger than it had before the fight began. His muscles filled with a terrifying, borrowed vitality.
He didn’t choose to rise; he was commanded to. The light itself acted as a physical force, lifting his broken body off the bloodied stones and forcing him back onto his feet.
He stood tall, bathed in that alien radiance, his eyes reflecting a power that was no longer entirely his own.
"My child."
The voice did not travel through the air; it manifested within the marrow of their bones. It came from everywhere in the corridor at once and from no particular direction.

It was warm, enormous, and carried an authority so absolute that the word gentle felt like a pathetic, inadequate lie—a thin veneer stretched over something that could have unmade reality with a single syllable.
"You have fought alone long enough," the voice resonated, vibrating through the stone floor and up through the soles of every boot present. "Let me help you now."
The reaction that rolled through both armies was not a sound but a physical wave, a collective recoil of souls.
In the Aethelgard formation, four of the six surviving Apostles collapsed to one knee. It wasn’t a conscious choice; it was a biological imperative.

Their very designations, the divine sparks that defined their existence, were screaming, responding to a presence that was several orders of magnitude above the entities that had granted them their power.

Valentina, a woman who had not knelt to any king, god, or demon in fifty years, felt her neck buckle. Her head bowed before her mind could even register the command, her muscles betraying her to the sheer weight of the sanctity flooding the room.
On the opposite side, the primal terror of the Underlayer took hold. The demons, the orcs, and the voidkin creatures that feared nothing mortal backed up two full steps in perfect, terrified unison.
It was an instinctive, ancestral retreat, the desperate flinch of prey encountering something their entire species had spent eight hundred years learning to avoid at all costs.
Elliot stood frozen, his mouth hanging open, his throat working convulsively but producing no sound. His mind was a static storm of terror and awe.

Evelyn took three stumbling steps backward, her legs moving before her consciousness could even process the threat, her hands clawing at the air as if trying to find purchase in a world that had suddenly become unfamiliar.
And standing among the Aethelgard front ranks, Rex Rexilion wore an expression of awed reverence. His lips were parted, his eyes wide and glassy with tears he didn’t know he was shedding.
One hand was half raised instinctively, not to shield himself from pain, for the light was not painful, but to shield himself from the terrifying purity of it.
Twenty meters away, Valentina had gone entirely white. Her skin looked like bleached bone under the golden downpour.
She had felt divine presences before. Every apostle in the network had been forged in their presence.
She had stood before two different pantheon members during her sixty years of service, and she had survived those encounters because they had been arrangements.

Those gods had deliberately compressed their essence, folding their power down into a scale a mortal nervous system could accommodate without hemorrhaging. Those encounters had been polite introductions between equals.
This? This was not an introduction.
This was an intrusion.
Whatever had reached into the corridor had not bothered to consider what its arrival would feel like to the fragile creatures standing beneath it. It was like trying to pour an ocean into a teacup.

Valentina felt her own designation hum in her chest like a struck bell, vibrating so violently she feared her ribs might crack from the internal resonance. Her vision blurred as her brain struggled to process the sheer magnitude of the energy saturating the air.
’It’s too much,’ she thought, her heart hammering against her sternum like a trapped bird. ’There is too much of it...’
’We aren’t meant to see this...’
"Headmaster," a young soldier beside her gasped.
His voice was a thin, breaking thread, shaking so badly it was almost unrecognizable. "What... what is that?"
"Is it an attack?"

Valentina reached out, her fingers spasming as she gripped the armored arm of the nearest soldier just to keep from collapsing. She had to force herself to draw air into her lungs; each breath felt heavy, as though she were inhaling liquid gold.
"That," Valentina said, her voice cracking before she steadied it with sheer force of will, "is the reason the Apostles of Life have always been the most numerous designation in the world."
She looked up into the blinding, impossible column of light, her eyes watering from the sheer intensity of the presence.
"Because," she whispered, "we are not the source."
"We are merely the echoes."

chapters.title: Chapter 1157. A Man Who Had Seen the Face of God and Found It Insufficiently Impressive
paragraphs: Beside Valentina, Morwenna Nightwing, a woman whose reputation was built on a foundation of unshakable composure and icy defiance, had collapsed.

She had lowered herself onto one knee with the mechanical inevitability of a marionette whose strings had been yanked by an unseen hand. When her conscious mind finally caught up to her body’s treasonous movement, she didn’t fight it.

She didn’t reach for her sword or attempt to reclaim her dignity. She simply remained there, frozen, because her instincts had made a far more accurate assessment of the situation than her pride ever could.
Her body knew what her mind refused to acknowledge: they were not standing in the presence of a guest; they were standing in the presence of the Host.
’This isn’t power,’ Morwenna thought, her knuckles white where they pressed against the stone. ’This is... inevitability.’

Twenty meters away, hidden behind the unreadable porcelain surface of his mask, the real Rex was experiencing something far more terrifying than awe. He was experiencing the complete and total failure of his own god-tier perception.
Since the first blow had been struck in the duel, Rex’s Divine Perception had been running at full capacity, a continuous stream of data flooding his consciousness.

It had been handling Apollo’s designation with the practiced ease of a master surgeon parsing the intricate lattice of the Life affinity, mapping the flowing channels of golden energy, and cataloguing the exact source of Apollo’s authority.
To Rex, Apollo had been a problem to be solved, a finite equation.
Then the light descended.
The instrument of his mind did not report a larger number. It did not report a spike in power.
It reported something that shouldn’t exist: an absence of edges.
’What... what am I looking at?’ Rex’s inner voice was a scream muffled by layers of analytical detachment.
He tried to find the boundary of the presence, the perimeter where the divine ended and the mortal began, and he found nothing.

He tried to map its structure, to dissect it into components he could understand, but every attempt returned the same impossible sensation: it was like trying to measure the volume of a raging ocean by dipping a single fingertip into the water.
He remembered Kaeleth. Kaeleth had been enormous, yes.
Kaeleth had been a force of nature that commanded terror. But Kaeleth had been finite.

Kaeleth had possessed a domain, a throne, and an anchor structure, a metaphysical tether that could be found, grasped, and shattered. Rex had located those vulnerabilities within minutes of entering Kaeleth’s domain and had systematically torn them apart.
This thing? This had no shape.
This had no vulnerability.
This was not a being standing somewhere else and extending its attention into this corridor. This was not a projection or an avatar.
This was simply present. It was in the stone beneath his boots; it was in the air filling his lungs; it was woven into the very atoms of the blood coursing through his veins.

The column of light pouring from the ceiling was not the entity itself; it was merely the fraction of itself that had chosen to become visible, a pinprick of light that was so obviously a mere fragment that Rex’s mind physically refused to construct an estimate of what the whole might look like.
A cold, visceral realization settled in his gut, more brutal than any blade.

The Goddess of Life had not descended to join the fight. She had simply pressed one finger against the fabric of the world, and that single finger alone was more massive, more terrifying, and more absolute than everything Rex Rexilion had ever fought combined.
Behind the mask, his face remained a perfect, terrifying statue of calm. But beneath the porcelain, his pulse betrayed him.
His heart rate rose by exactly eleven beats per minute, the only outward sign of a man realizing he was standing in the shadow of something that could erase him without even noticing it was there.

Rex kept his posture exactly as it had been: rigid, unyielding, a statue carved from shadow and defiance. To every terrified soldier in the Aethelgard ranks and every snarling demon in the Underlayer, he appeared as a masked figure standing in perfect, unnatural stillness.
He looked like a man who had seen the face of God and found it insufficiently impressive. That impression that mask of absolute, unflinching control was worth maintaining at almost any cost.
If he flinched now, if he showed even a tremor of recognition for the power pouring through the ceiling, the psychological collapse of both armies would be instantaneous.

But beneath the porcelain stillness, Rex’s mind had descended into a state of hyperaccelerated calculation. His thoughts were no longer human; they were cold, mechanical, and running through millions of variables with the speed of a supercomputer under stress.

’This is a catastrophic anomaly,’ he thought, the words echoing in the sterile space of his mind. This is no longer a duel against an Apostle. ’This is a fight adjacent to the upper framework of existence itself.’
’Ten thousand witnesses.’
’No retreat possible.’
’My surface identity is forty meters deep in the enemy’s killing zone.’
’If I move, I expose the lie...’
’If I stay, I am cornered by a deity...’
Lustia’s warning crawled up his spine like frost, each word carrying an uncomfortable, razor-sharp clarity: ’Don’t let your name get loud in the wrong circles.’
’Fuck,’ Rex thought grimly. ’My name hasn’t just gotten loud.’
’I just set off every alarm bell in the universe.’
Twenty meters away, Apollo Brightsoul began to rise. His movement was not the clumsy struggle of a wounded man but something fluid and terrifyingly graceful.

He ascended into the column of light with his eyes closed, his face upturned as if drinking from a fountain of liquid stars. When his eyelids finally fluttered open, the sound that escaped his throat was not a gasp but a low hum of harmonic resonance.
His eyes had changed.
The familiar gold of his affinity had been consumed.
Now, they burned with a light that had transcended color to a white-hot, pulsing brilliance that seemed to contain its own internal weather patterns.
A secondary register of light, whiter and more ancient than anything mortal could conceive, pulsed beneath the gold like the heartbeat of a star.

The aura surrounding his body had split: there was still the familiar, comforting warmth of his own power, but it was now encased in a second, purer sheath. This new layer clung to his flesh like divine mercury, rippling and snapping with every micro movement of his muscles.
CRACK THOOM.
The sound of his power stabilizing was like a thunderclap contained within a vacuum.
Apollo rolled his shoulders once. The sound of his joints popping was audible even over the divine hum, each click and pop echoing with supernatural clarity.

He felt the power coursing through him, not as an external gift, but as an intrinsic part of his biology. His muscles felt denser, his reflexes sharper than the speed of thought, his very soul feeling as though it had been forged anew in a furnace of pure concept.
Everything worked. Everything worked better than it had ever worked.
The pain that had moments ago been a screaming agony in his ribs and skull had been replaced by a terrifying, exhilarating emptiness.
"You won’t touch me again," Apollo said.

His voice did not merely carry across the distance; it struck. It came out doubled, his own heroic tenor layered beneath a deeper, resonant divine timbre that made the stone walls of the corridor vibrate in sympathetic agony.
The words landed physically against the soldiers’ armor, a shockwave of vocal authority that made several men stagger.
"Not with what I’ve just been given."

chapters.title: Chapter 1158. Trapped Between the Need to Survive and the Need to Remain Hidden
paragraphs: The air didn’t just move; it shattered.
Apollo didn’t run; he detonated. One moment he was a figure of radiant stillness twenty meters away, and the next, he was a streak of white gold lightning tearing through the space between them.
He crossed the distance faster than any mortal eye could track, his movement bypassing the concept of velocity entirely.

Xerollion, the man beneath the mask, the predator who had dominated this duel with terrifying precision, felt something he hadn’t experienced since his first day of combat: the sickening lurch of being surprised.
For approximately one and a half seconds, his mind had been divided, pulled between the immediate threat of Apollo and the incomprehensible reality of the Goddess’s presence.
That hesitation was a death sentence. For the first time all day, his reaction was half a beat behind his instinct.
His defensive posture formed, but it was a ghost of a shield, already crumbling before it could solidify.
The punch got through.
BOOM.

Apollo’s fist, armored in two overlapping layers of divine light that hummed with the frequency of a dying star, connected with Xerollion’s sternum. The sound was wet, metallic, and bone-deep, a sound like a sledgehammer striking a slab of marble wrapped in raw meat.
The impact didn’t just push Xerollion; it launched him. He was driven backward four meters across the unforgiving stone floor.

His boots screamed against the masonry, carving twin grooves into the solid rock as he struggled to find purchase, but the momentum was absolute. His spine buckled under the sheer kinetic force, and the sound of his ribs cracking sharp, staccato pops like dry kindling snapping echoed through the corridor.
Rex, deep within the analytical fortress of his mind, noted the impact. He didn’t feel alarm; alarm was too primitive, but he felt something dangerously close to it.
The data was undeniable: ’The strike registered.’
The divine sheath hadn’t just enhanced Apollo’s speed; it had added physical mass to his very concept. The force behind that fist was no longer measured in Newtons but in inevitability.

The silence of the divine presence was instantly obliterated as the Aethelgard formation exploded into a cacophony of panicked noise. Steel scraped against scabbards, boots scrambled for position, and shouts of terror and confusion rose like smoke.
"Move! Protect the flanks!" someone screamed.
Cassandra’s arms, previously folded in a display of controlled tension, snapped open. Her entire body coiled like a spring, her eyes blazing with the need to intervene.

Beside her, the massive Gorvasha’s grip shifted on her war hammer, the leather wrappings creaking under her tightening fist. The demon blooded warrior took one thunderous step forward, her muscles bunching to charge into the chaos.
Before she could launch, Cassandra’s hand shot out, catching Gorvasha’s shoulder with bruising force. The grip was iron.
"Not yet," Cassandra hissed.
Her voice was tight, strained through clenched teeth as she fought to maintain her own composure.
"He was pushed back, Commander!" Gorvasha growled, her breath coming in ragged bursts. "He’s vulnerable! If we strike now,
"I know he was pushed back, you fool!" Cassandra snapped back, her eyes never once wavering from the center of the storm where the two combatants stood. "Look at the ground! Look at the air!"
"He hasn’t given the signal yet."
"If we charge in there now, we won’t be fighting the enemy; we’ll be dying in the crossfire of gods."
"We will be collateral damage in a war we cannot comprehend."
She squeezed Gorvasha’s shoulder harder, forcing the warrior to remain rooted.
"He is still in control," Cassandra whispered, though her own heart was hammering against her ribs. "Trust him... Trust Lord Xerollion."
Apollo did not merely press the advantage; he unleashed a cascade of divine violence.

The rhythm of the duel shattered. Previously, their exchange had been a predictable dance of feints and counters, but now Apollo moved with a terrifying, multilayered complexity that defied the very laws of combat.
The strikes came faster than the human eye could process a blur of white gold motion that turned the corridor into a pressure cooker of kinetic energy.

Rex’s mind screamed warnings as his Full Potential Adaptation labored at its absolute limit. His ability was designed to solve problems, but it was being asked to solve an equation that changed its variables mid-calculation.
The first component of Apollo’s attack was familiar: the warm, golden torrent of his own life affinity. Rex had already mapped its cadence; he knew its weight and its reach.
But the second component, the divine sheath, was an unpredictable nightmare.
SHING CRACK THUD.
The second layer shifted its nature with every impact. One moment, it was a pure disruption of matter, turning Rex’s reinforced armor into brittle glass that shattered under the slightest pressure.

The next, it wasn’t even touching his body physically but was instead a crushing pressure on his soul register, making his consciousness waver as if his very essence were being squeezed by a titan’s fist.

Occasionally, it manifested as something more insidious: a metaphysical poison that forced Rex’s own regeneration to hesitate, causing wounds that should have healed instantly to linger like festering injuries.
’Adaptation failing to sync... recalculating... recalculating...’ Rex’s inner monologue was a frantic stream of data.
His ability kept falling exactly one contact behind. To adapt to a mechanism, one had to encounter it cleanly, to understand its fundamental pattern.
But the divine layer refused to hold still. It was a liquid godhood, shifting its properties faster than his mind could catalog them.
The cost was written in blood.
SPLAT.
A clawing strike from Apollo’s palm tore through Rex’s forearm. Normally, the wound would have vanished before the blood could even bead.

Now, the gash stayed open for three agonizing seconds, crimson arterial spray painting the stone floor. A deeper slash across his shoulder left a jagged crater in his flesh that took nearly five seconds to knit back together.

It was a marginal degradation—the difference between instantaneous and almost instantaneous—but in a fight where Apollo was landing three divine enhanced strikes every second, that margin was a death sentence. The damage was accumulating and the blood was pooling.
Rex began to give ground.

He retreated in measured, deliberate steps, his boots skidding through his own blood. He wasn’t retreating in defeat; he was retreating with the calculated precision of a master duelist trading space for time.

Each step back bought his analysis another millisecond of exposure, another chance to glimpse the pattern behind the chaos. Behind the porcelain mask, his brain was burning through glucose at an impossible rate, his neurons firing with enough intensity to cook his own flesh.
’I can end this,’ Rex thought, the cold pragmatism of a killer overriding the strain of survival. ’I can end this right now.’
The options laid themselves out before him like weapons on a rack:
First: Gravity Manipulation.
At full output, he could increase the gravitational constant within three hundred meters to catastrophic levels.
He would flatten Apollo into a crimson smear against the floor, crushing everything in the corridor, including himself, regardless of whatever divine reinforcement Apollo carried.
Fundamental physical force wasn’t concerned about divine layering; gravity was the universe’s ultimate truth.
Second: Sovereign Necromancy.

With a single word, he could rip the dormant souls from the thousands of corpses scattered across the battlefield and funnel them into this corridor. A tide of undead fury would overwhelm Apollo in seconds.
Third: Temporal Authority.
He could reach into the clockwork of reality and simply stop time. The engagement would freeze between one heartbeat and the next, allowing him to dissect Apollo while he stood like a statue.
But each solution was a poisoned chalice.
’Tactical victory, strategic annihilation,’ Rex mused bitterly.

If he used any of them, he would reveal everything. Ten thousand witnesses would see the true monster behind the mask. A goddess was watching through the channel she had opened, her divine attention focused directly on him.
And worst of all, forty meters away stood the Aethelgard front rank. There, wearing his own face, stood the version of himself that had to remain an unsuspected ally.
If Rex unleashed his true nature here, he would destroy the very foundation of the deception that kept his army alive.
The corridor groaned as Apollo lunged again, the air screaming as the divine light tore through it.
Rex braced himself, his ribs aching, his blood warm on his skin, trapped between the need to survive and the need to remain hidden.

It was the way a mountain declines to be moved by an argument.
Rex knew he had to change the variables, and he did so with desperate precision.
In ninety seconds, he shifted his approach three times. First, he applied Gravity Manipulation at moderate output.

For four seconds, Apollo’s movements became sluggish, his divine footsteps heavy as if wading through mercury. But then, the white layer began to compensate, pulsing with a countergravitational rhythm that pushed back against the curse.
Next, he pivoted to energy manipulation.
This was a surgical strike, aimed not at Apollo’s body but at the microscopic seam where his natural life affinity met the foreign divine reinforcement.
The result was spectacular. A genuine stagger, Apollo’s head snapped back, and for one glorious microsecond, the white sheath flickered like a dying candle.
Rex filed that data away with the hunger of a starving man: ’There is a seam... There is a weakness.’
Finally, he considered Sovereign Necromancy. His fingers twitched with the urge to summon the dead, to flood the corridor with the rotting hands of the fallen, and to drag Apollo down into the earth.
But he held back. He could not risk raising a corpse in front of an Apostle of Life while a goddess’s gaze burned through the divine channel.
The risk of exposure was too absolute.
"You keep changing methods," Apollo taunted, his voice echoing with that terrifying, doubled resonance.
He moved in a blur, a combination of strikes that ended in a devastating spinning heel kick that caught Rex across the temple. "That’s what a man does when nothing he has is working!
Rex stumbled, blood streaming from beneath his mask, but his eyes remained sharp, focused, and deadly.
"That’s what a man does when he’s collecting data," Xerollion spat.
He threw up his crossed forearms to catch Apollo’s follow-up strike, a hammer fist aimed at his skull.
CRACK.
The sound was sickening, the unmistakable noise of radius and ulna splintering under divine pressure. Pain exploded through Rex’s arms, white hot and nauseating, but he didn’t break his stance.
"Though I admit," Rex growled through gritted teeth as he felt the bones grinding beneath his skin, "the distinction is getting academic."
Apollo didn’t just strike; he unleashed a three-hit execution designed to dismantle Rex’s very sense of space.
THUD CRACK BOOM.
A lightning-fast jab to the solar plexus to stagger, a hooked elbow that shattered Rex’s left cheekbone, and then the finisher.

Apollo pivoted, his entire body coiled like a loaded spring, and brought both fists down in a devastating downward hammer blow. The force wasn’t just kinetic; it carried the crushing weight of divine judgment.
The impact was apocalyptic. Rex was launched backward, not just sliding, but punching through the corridor wall like a cannonball through parchment.

The sound was a thunderclap of masonry exploding, followed by the wet, grinding noise of flesh meeting solid stone. When the dust began to settle, Rex was embedded a full meter deep into the solid rock.
A crater yawned open around him, with radial fractures spiderwebbing three meters in every direction, the stone groaning as it settled around his broken form.
For the first time in the entire engagement, the underlayer side of the corridor fell into a deathly, suffocating silence.
Ten thousand soldiers, ten thousand witnesses, held their breath in unison. The only sound was the settling of dust and the distant, fading echo of Apollo’s divine radiance.
Then, movement.
Rex began to peel himself out of the ruined masonry. Every movement was slow and deliberate, a conscious decision to not let the pain overwhelm his motor functions.
He shrugged loose chunks of granite off his shoulders, the stone clattering to the blood-slicked floor. He straightened his spine with an audible pop crack that made several nearby soldiers flinch.
Behind the mask, his mind was running a brutal inventory.
’Four major lacerations closing.’
’Rib three: cracked, mended, cracked again under the impact.’
’Left radius: hairline fracture, stabilizing.’
’Internal bleeding: minimal, compensated by regeneration.’
None of it mattered. None of it would matter in sixty seconds.
All of it was real, painfully, viscerally real in a way nothing had been since the apocalyptic slaughter in the throne room outside of time.
But beneath the ruined edge of his mask, Rex’s expression was not one of frustration.
It wasn’t anger, and it wasn’t even pain.
But it was delightful. A genuine, unguarded, terrifying delight.
’Finally,’ he thought, a dark smile tugging at the corners of his mouth. ’Someone who can actually make me bleed.’

This was only the second time in his entire existence that anything had forced him to exert this level of effort. The first time had ended with a god lying broken on the floor of his own domain, missing a vital piece of his divinity.
There was an enormous, almost intoxicating pleasure in this—the specific, predatory joy of a man who has spent months drowning in boredom finally being asked to actually try.
Underneath that pleasure, however, his strategic mind was already cold and calculating, assembling the only viable answer.
’I cannot fight this here,’ he reasoned, watching Apollo’s silhouette through the haze of dust. ’Not with this audience watching.’
’Not with a goddess using this very moment as a window into my soul.’
’And not with my other body standing forty meters away as a hostage to my reputation.’
Every problem he had enumerated—the audience, the Goddess, the strategic exposure—had the same fundamental shape: they were all problems of location.

Then, as if hearing his unspoken calculus, Lustia’s voice drifted from the golden chamber. It didn’t sound like a distant echo; it sounded as though she were standing directly beside him, her words carrying perfect, crystalline clarity:
"A personal domain, Rex..."
"A space you author entirely, where your own rules supersede the world’s default physics."
"A place where you can retreat, where you can plan, and where no one—not even a goddess—can interrupt you."
The words ignited something in his mind.
A solution.
A sanctuary.
A killing field where he could finally drop the mask entirely.
The system notification flickered into his peripheral vision the instant he reached for the concept in his mind.
[Domain Creation: 15,000 pts.] Confirm purchase?]
Rex didn’t pause. He didn’t weigh the cost.
He didn’t calculate the risk. He simply slammed his mental fist into the confirmation.
[Purchase Confirmed. Initiating Domain Genesis...]
