chapters.title: Chapter 1160. Congratulations to Me, I Now Own a Doorway to Nowhere
paragraphs: The energy didn’t merely leave him; it hemorrhaged.

Fifteen thousand points a fortune built on the bones of fallen armies, the ashes of a conquered god, and the excruciating strain of nineteen maximum bonds surged out of Rex in a violent, invisible torrent.
It felt like his very marrow was being vacuumed out through his pores. For a heartbeat, there was a terrifying emptiness, a void where his power used to be, leaving him feeling exposed and fragile.
Then, something else flowed back in.
It wasn’t the familiar weight of a new skill settling into his muscle memory or the sharp clarity of a passive ability slotting into his consciousness. This was something fundamentally alien.
It didn’t settle into him; it unfolded around him. It was an expansion of his very existence, a sense of available volume where there had previously been only air and stone.

It was a giddy, vertigo-inducing awareness, the terrifying realization that he was no longer just a man standing in a corridor, but a man carrying a door. And behind that door lay a canvas of infinite potential, a private reality that would bend to his every whim, his every cruelty, his every law.
[Domain Creation (Initial Tier) integrated.]
[Warning: Anchoring principle not yet defined.]
[Reality stability compromised.]
[Structural integrity limited until anchor is established.]
Rex read the system warning with cold indifference. The warning flickered red in his peripheral vision, casting a bloody glow across the cracked surface of his mask.
’Stability?’ he thought, a dark, predatory amusement bubbling up through the pain in his ribs. ’I don’t need stability.’
’I need an arena.’
He dismissed the notification with a mental flick. The concept of ’stability’ was for those who feared the consequences of their own power.
Rex was done fearing consequences. He was ready to author them.
"Now this," Xerollion murmured, his voice a gravelly whisper that barely stirred the dust settling around him. "This is interesting."
The words were private, swallowed by the debris, but they carried the weight of a promise. The game had changed.
The rules were about to be rewritten.

Across the twisted wreckage of the corridor, Apollo Brightsoul remained unchanged. He stood amidst the rubble like a statue of wrath, bathed in a double sheath of gold and white light that burned so brightly it cast long, dancing shadows against the cracked walls.
His fists were still raised, knuckles glowing with divine heat, his chest heaving in a slow, controlled rhythm. His eyes, those burning crucibles of celestial intent, never left Rex.
Apollo wasn’t waiting for Rex to heal. He wasn’t waiting for the dust to clear.

He was waiting for the next opportunity to destroy, his entire being coiled in a state of absolute, unyielding readiness. He was a predator who had tasted blood and found he liked the hunt too much to let the prey escape.

The air between them hummed with lethal tension, charged with the static of Apollo’s divine aura and the gathering storm of Rex’s newly awakened domain. The corridor was no longer just a passage; it had become a threshold.

Rex planted his feet in the blood-soaked stone, feeling the raw, unanchored power of his domain pulsing like a second heartbeat. He looked at Apollo through the fractured lens of his mask and felt the hunger return.
"Come then, Apostle," Rex whispered, the words carrying a lethal edge. "Let’s see what happens when the world stops telling us what’s possible."
Xerollion raised both arms wide, his fingers splayed like claws as if he were physically tearing the fabric of reality apart.
The energy that erupted from him was not light; it was something far more sinister. A torrent of violet-black radiance bled from his pores, but it didn’t shine; it pulsed.
Each wave of color hit the air with a slow, heavy thrum, sounding less like magic and more like a massive, wet heartbeat echoing from somewhere deep beneath the stone floor.
Thump thump. Thump thump.
The sound resonated in the teeth and bones of every soldier present.
The atmosphere itself began to fail. Dust motes and shattered masonry rose from the ground, suspended in midair by some impossible new law of physics.
Then, the vibration sharpened into something agonizing.
Crrr ack.
Spiderweb fractures appeared in the empty space between Rex and Apollo. These weren’t cracks in the walls or the floor; they were cracks in the air itself.
Thin, jagged lines of nothingness spreading across the void, exactly like the dimensional hemorrhages Rex had witnessed while dismantling Kaeleth’s domain.
But there was a terrifying difference: this time, Rex wasn’t watching the destruction. He was the architect and he was the one writing the apocalypse.
"What are you—" Apollo started, his divine voice cracking as he saw the void opening before him.
The question died in his throat because the floor beneath them simply ceased to exist.
There was no thunderous explosion. There was no gust of wind.

There was only a sudden, terrifying absence—a hole in the world where solid rock had been a heartbeat before. From that abyss, a spiraling vortex of violet-black energy roared upward, hungry and absolute.

It surged like a leviathan’s maw, swallowing both Rex and Apollo whole in a single, silent gulp. The spiral collapsed inward on itself, sealing the wound in reality in under a second, leaving nothing behind but a faint, acrid smell of burnt ozone and dead space.
The corridor erupted into chaos.
The roar that tore from ten thousand throats was not the controlled chanting of battle; it was a primal scream of confusion and terror. The disciplined lines shattered.

Soldiers surged forward in panic, colliding with their own comrades in a desperate, blind scramble. Commanders screamed orders that were instantly drowned out by the cacophony of steel clashing against steel and the wet sounds of panicked men breaking ranks.
Elliot broke free from the formation, his boots skidding on blood-slicked stone as he sprinted toward the center of the carnage.
"APOLLO!" he screamed, his voice raw, tearing out of his lungs. "APOLLO, ANSWER ME!"

He launched himself at the spot where the vortex had been, but he didn’t hit stone. He slammed into an invisible wall of condensed energy with enough force to send him sprawling backward onto the hard ground.
THUD.
Gritting his teeth against the pain in his shoulder, Elliot scrambled up and threw himself at the barrier again. "APOLLO!"
WHAM.

Each strike against the emptiness produced nothing but a flat, violet ripple that shivered across a surface that had no visible form. It wasn’t a shield; it was a boundary between two different universes.
"Elliot, stop!" Evelyn’s voice pierced through his desperation.
She lunged forward, wrapping both arms around his chest in a desperate tackle, physically hauling him backward. "Stop it! Let it go!"
"He’s in there alone!" Elliot roared, fighting her grip, his eyes bloodshot and wild. "He’s trapped in whatever that hellscape is!"
"I know." Evelyn’s voice cracked, her composure fracturing like the air had moments before.
Her hands trembled as she held him, her gaze locked on the empty space where two titans had stood seconds earlier. "I know he is."
Behind them, the Underlayer continued to burn, but for those watching the void, the world had already ended.

chapters.title: Chapter 1161. Coughing Up Blood in a Universe I Bought With Loyalty Points, No Regrets
paragraphs: On the Underlayer’s side of the carnage, the chaos seemed to momentarily freeze around two figures. Cassandra and Gorvasha stood rigid, their eyes locked on the impossible vacancy where the corridor’s center had simply vanished.
For the first time since either of them had knelt before Lord Xerollion, the iron discipline that defined them cracked. They shared a single, harrowing look—an expression of raw, unvarnished unease.
"Did you know he could do that?" Gorvasha asked.
His voice was flat, stripped of its usual gravelly confidence, less a question and more a desperate attempt to ground himself in reality.
"No." Cassandra’s jaw tightened so hard it looked as though her teeth might shatter. "And I have been in his confidence longer than anyone here."
"I have seen him unmake armies, Gorvasha, but I have never seen him unmake existence."

Meanwhile, in the heart of the Aethelgard formation, the performance of a lifetime was unfolding. Rex Rexilion tore himself away from the chaos, his face contorting into a mask of perfect, devastating panic.
"APOLLO! NO!" he shrieked, the sound tearing from his throat with such convincing agony that nearby soldiers instinctively recoiled.
He lunged toward the invisible barrier, muscles straining, veins bulging in his neck as three armored soldiers threw their full weight against him to hold him back.
To every horrified witness, he looked exactly like what he was pretending to be: a man watching the only thing that mattered disappear into an incomprehensible nightmare.
’Let them believe it,’ Rex thought behind the wall of his false terror. ’Let them think I am helpless.’
’Let them think the monster has won.’
But inside the domain, the world had gone utterly, terrifyingly quiet.
The violent spiral had spat them out into a realm that defied every law of perception. There was no sky, no horizon, and no distant walls to give a sense of scale.

It was an endless, yawning expanse of nothingness that refused to resolve into distance. Beneath their feet, there was no stone, no dirt, only a surface of slow pulsing, violet-black light that felt unnervingly like walking on firm flesh.
When they stepped, the surface gave slightly, a sickeningly organic recoil that sent vibrations up through their boots.
The silence was absolute. The screams of ten thousand soldiers, the clash of steel, the thunder of magic—all of it had been severed as cleanly as a limb.
There was only the wet, rhythmic sound of two sets of breathing in a space that had been conjured from nothingness mere seconds before.
Apollo turned in a slow, deliberate circle, his golden armor casting a faint, lonely glow against the encroaching dark.
When he spoke, his voice didn’t travel through air; it seemed to vibrate directly into the space around them, echoing off surfaces that didn’t exist.
"Where is this?" Apollo demanded, his hand instinctively moving to the hilt of his blade.
His divine aura flickered, struggling to find purchase in a world where physics had been revoked.
"Somewhere we can finish this without being interrupted."
Xerollion’s voice was transformed. It was deeper now, layered with a thousand harmonics that made it sound as though several entities were speaking in unison.

It carried the same unsettling register as Lustia’s chamber, a sound that felt like it was being whispered directly into the brain rather than heard by the ears. "No witnesses... No distractions... Just you and me now."

Rex felt the power of the domain thrumming through his veins, the violet light beneath them responding to his very heartbeat. He could feel the ’rules’ of this place waiting for his command, waiting to be written in blood.
Apollo didn’t flinch. There was no tremor of fear in his stance, no hesitation in his eyes.
Instead, there was only a hard, focused wariness, the cold, lethal expression of a predator who had realized he was no longer in a hunting ground but in a cage.
His eyes burned with celestial fire, promising one thing and one thing only: whatever rules Rex wrote here, Apollo intended to break them with sheer, unrelenting force.
Then, Apollo moved.
He didn’t just attack; he detonated. A streak of gold light tore through the violet void, a lance of celestial fury aimed directly at Rex’s sternum.
The fight that followed was not merely a duel; it was a cataclysm. Both men knew, in the primal, instinctive core of their beings, that they were experiencing something beyond mortal comprehension.
This was the pinnacle, the absolute apex of their respective existences.

Without the constricting walls of the corridor to cage them, the battle exploded into three-dimensional chaos. They became twin comets of gold and violet, launching off the pulsing floor into the yawning volume of the domain.
Rex would kick off the surface, feeling the organic recoil beneath his boots, propelling himself upward to meet Apollo midair.
CRACK BOOM!
They collided twenty meters above the floor, the impact producing a miniature supernova. Gold sparks hemorrhaged from Apollo’s fists while violet tendrils lashed out from Rex’s defensive barriers.

Each point of contact produced a concussive detonation that sent shockwaves rippling through the domain. The violet-black floor responded to every strike, rolling outward in slow, concentric waves like the surface of an enormous, patient liquid, absorbing the displaced energy of their god-tier violence.
Apollo held the rhythm. That was the terrifying truth that Rex had to confront between every bone-jarring exchange.
’Damn it,’ Rex thought, his mind racing through calculations even as blood spattered across his vision. ’It’s not just strength... It’s the variance...’

The residual touch of the goddess had done more than amplify Apollo’s power; it had made him fundamentally unpredictable. Every time Rex attempted to model Apollo’s attack patterns, the divine component shifted.
One strike would carry the weight of molten sunfire; the next, the piercing precision of a lightning bolt; the third, a crushing pressure that felt like gravity itself had gone mad.
Rex would adjust his guard for one expression of divine wrath, only for the next blow to arrive with a different harmonic signature, bypassing his defenses entirely.
And Rex was paying for it in blood.
Snap.
A sickening crack echoed through the void as Apollo’s elbow connected with Rex’s right forearm. The bone splintered audibly, sending a white-hot spike of agony through Rex’s nervous system.
He didn’t have time to scream; he barely had time to breathe before Apollo was on him again.
Squelch.
A blade of pure light grazed Rex’s side, opening a gash that wept crimson onto the violet floor. The blood didn’t pool; it sizzled against the domain’s surface.

A deep, mottled bruise spread across his ribs faster than his enhanced regeneration could knit the tissue back together. His left cheekbone cracked under a glancing blow, the mask’s edge tearing skin and sending a warm trickle down his jaw.
For the first time since he had watched a god kneel in a collapsing throne room, Rex Rexilion found himself on the back foot. He was not orchestrating this dance; he was struggling to survive it.

The part of his psyche that had defined itself as the apex predator, the man who walked into any room knowing he was the most dangerous thing in it, was reeling. His instincts were screaming at him, confused by a threat that refused to be solved.
But beneath the tactical assessment, beneath the pain and the mounting exhaustion, something darker and more exhilarating was stirring.
’This is it,’ Rex thought, a feral grin splitting his lips even as he coughed up blood. ’This is what I live for.’
’This beautiful, murderous chaos.’
He was, in the most twisted sense of the word, having the time of his life.
They broke apart for a fraction of a second, hovering in the weightless void. Apollo’s breathing was ragged now, his chest heaving beneath his gleaming armor.
A steady stream of blood leaked from his nose, where Rex had landed a devastating counterstrike several exchanges prior. His golden radiance flickered like a dying candle in a storm.
"You’re slowing down," Apollo spat, the words punctuated by a wet wheeze.
His eyes remained fixed on Rex with deadly intensity, refusing to acknowledge his own deteriorating condition.

Rex wiped a smear of crimson from his mouth with the back of his hand, the violet light of the domain reflecting off the fresh blood. His broken arm throbbed in time with the domain’s heartbeat, but his gaze was sharper than it had been at the start.
"I’m learning, Apollo," Xerollion answered, his voice carrying that terrifying, layered resonance. "There’s a difference."

chapters.title: Chapter 1162. Turns Out Gravity Is Just a Suggestion, and So Is My Dignity
paragraphs: The middle stretch of that hellish engagement stretched on for nearly six minutes of unrelenting, bone-crushing contact. It didn’t feel like a fight anymore; it felt like two fundamental forces of nature trying to annihilate one another.
The battle moved through phases, shifting from tactical probing to raw, unbridled slaughter, the way a conversation might shift from polite inquiry to screaming accusations.
It began as a test of physics. Both men sought to understand what this new, impossible space would permit, and the domain Rex’s own creation was terrifyingly accommodating.
Within the first thirty seconds, Rex discovered that he didn’t need to work to manipulate the local gravity; he simply had to will it.

The violet-black floor would rise like a liquid wave to meet his feet if he needed leverage; the very air would thicken into a solid mass if he needed something to brace against. The environment wasn’t just a stage; it was an extension of his own nervous system.
He put that power to immediate, lethal use.
WHOOSH.
Rex dropped the local gravity to a quarter of its normal strength. Apollo, committed to a devastating forward lunge, overextended.
His momentum carried him forty meters past Rex in the sudden weightlessness. Rex didn’t hesitate; he snapped his fingers, restoring gravity to full force at the exact apex of Apollo’s flight.
CRUNCH.
The sudden return of weight sent Apollo plummeting, his body struggling to reorient as he fell through the void. But Apollo was not a man who obeyed the laws of physics; he commanded them.
The second time the gravity shifted, Rex felt a spike of genuine surprise. Apollo didn’t tumble helplessly.

Mid-fall, Apollo twisted his body with inhuman grace, his golden aura flaring like a gyroscope. He slammed into the underside of a floating formation of violet light as though it had always been solid ground.
With a grunt of exertion, he pushed off, propelling himself back at Xerollion from a vertical angle that Rex’s gravitational manipulation had been specifically designed to make impossible.
"Too slow," Apollo growled, his voice carrying through the void like grinding stone.
What followed was eleven seconds of pure, claustrophobic brutality. There was no footwork, no tactical retreat, no measured distance.
They entered each other’s guard and stayed there, two titans locked in a death embrace, trading strikes that neither could fully block.
CLANG. THUD. CRACK.

Gold and violet light hemorrhaged from every point of impact, flaring like miniature suns. The domain rippled outward from their collision in violent, concentric waves that screamed across the empty expanse, each impact sending shockwaves that would have liquified a normal human’s organs.
Rex took the brunt of it. A devastating hook to the ribs produced a wet, splintering sound as two bones snapped clean through.

Worse still, the blow struck a hairline fracture in the divine layer protecting his core, preventing his regeneration from sealing the wounds for four agonizing seconds. Blood sprayed from Rex’s mouth, tasting of copper and burnt energy.
’Not today,’ Rex snarled internally. ’Not like this.’
He seized the moment of Apollo’s close proximity. Using a precise telekinetic tether, he yanked at Apollo’s front foot, sending the divine warrior stumbling.
In the same fluid motion, Rex drove his elbow upward with everything he had.
SHATTER.
The elbow connected directly with Apollo’s collarbone. The sound was like a sledgehammer hitting a marble pillar.
Apollo’s shoulder collapsed inward, the bone grinding into fragments. But before Rex could savor the victory, he watched in grim fascination as the goddess’s residual light flooded Apollo’s system.
The shattered bone knit itself back together in less than half the time Rex’s own body took to repair itself.

Rex skidded back three meters, his boots carving grooves into the pulsing violet surface as he fought to regain his equilibrium. His breathing was ragged, each inhale a battle against the pain in his ribs.
"That’s the part I find genuinely unfair," Xerollion said, wiping crimson from his chin.
His voice was calm, but there was an edge of something new beneath it—recognition. "You’re healing faster than I am now."
"Do you understand how rare that is? The power imbalance is shifting."

Apollo straightened his shoulder, the golden glow around his neck fading as the bone fused perfectly back into place. His eyes were twin furnaces of celestial wrath, burning brighter than the domain itself. He didn’t look tired; he looked consecrated.
"Good," Apollo said, his voice dropping to a lethal whisper. "Then I’ll just have to break you faster."
And he came again.

The battle shifted gears with the deadly precision of a predator changing its hunting style. The raw, unbridled violence of the previous minutes crystallized into something far more dangerous: a cold, calculating war of attrition. The phase turned technical.
Rex stopped simply reacting; he began actively hunting the divine mechanism at the core of Apollo’s power. He started playing a lethal game of baiting.
He would deliberately overextend a guard or leave a rib exposed, not out of carelessness, but to provoke a specific expression of Apollo’s divine energy.

He needed to see how the goddess’s residual light reacted to different pressures, how it flowed when Apollo struck with anger versus when he struck with calm resolve. He was feeding data into his adaptation ability, trying to force a clean read on the unpredictable variable.

But Apollo was not some mindless brute or a god playing at being a warrior. He was a graduate of the Academy’s most elite tactical programs, a man who had spent six years mastering the art of reading opponents before he ever received his divine designation.
By the fourth repetition of Rex’s pattern, Apollo recognized the trap. He saw the deliberate openings. He saw the way Rex was trying to map his soul.

In response, Apollo began varying his commitment patterns. He would initiate a strike with maximum force, then abruptly cut the power mid-swing, or he would feign a lunge only to pivot into a defensive posture that denied Rex the very data he craved.
’Fuck,’ Rex thought, his teeth grinding together as his enhanced senses screamed at him. ’He’s reading me.’
’He’s not just fighting me; he’s fighting my ability to learn.’
For the first time in Rex’s entire second life, he faced someone who understood his process well enough to weaponize it against him.

Then, something unexpected happened. A sound tore through the oppressive silence of the domain, a sound so foreign to the terrifying, masked figure of Xerollion that it seemed to violate the very air.
Rex laughed.
It wasn’t a cruel chuckle or a villainous cackle. It was a genuine, startled laugh, the sound of a man who had just stumbled upon something magnificent in the middle of a massacre.
It was raw, unfiltered surprise that broke through his controlled persona.
HA !
The sound echoed off the nonexistent walls, disorienting and alien. For Apollo, that laugh was a glitch in the matrix.
His concentration wavered. His divine aura flickered as he searched for the meaning behind that sudden outburst of humanity.
That quarter-second of hesitation was everything.
NOW.
Rex didn’t waste a heartbeat. He slammed his fist into the floor, triggering a localized gravity spike.
"Stay down," he snarled.
BOOM.
The gravity around Apollo instantly surged to nine times his own body weight. Apollo was slammed into the violet surface with the force of a falling star.

The impact produced a wet THUD as the air was punched out of his lungs. Rex didn’t stop there; he lunged forward, driving his armored heel into Apollo’s chest with enough force to crater the pulsing floor beneath them.
CRACK CRUNCH.

The surface beneath Apollo shattered like obsidian, sending spiderweb fractures racing through the violet light. Rex could almost feel the ribs beneath Apollo’s armor buckling under the concentrated pressure.

But Apollo was a creature of divine resilience. His white sheath flared with blinding intensity, the holy energy absorbing the brunt of the crushing force and redistributing the kinetic energy across his entire frame.
Apollo roared through the pain, his eyes blazing gold as he exploded upward from the crater.
WHAM.
Before Rex could recover his stance, Apollo’s fist connected with Rex’s jaw. The force was catastrophic.

Rex’s head snapped sideways with enough torque to send his entire body spinning ninety degrees through the air. His vision blurred into a kaleidoscope of violet and gold as his teeth clattered together, blood spraying from his split lip like crimson confetti.

The two men separated, panting, blood dripping onto the floor where it sizzled and burned. The tension between them was no longer just physical; it was psychological, a coiled spring wound to the point of snapping.
They stood there for a heartbeat, two gods measuring each other’s remaining life force, knowing that the next move would not be a probe or a test.
The end of it came four exchanges later.

A jagged, spiderweb crack tore across the violet-lit surface in a single microsecond, splitting the mask from temple to jaw. Then, with a sound like breaking glass amplified a thousand times, the entire helm disintegrated.
Fragments of reinforced material and dissolving energy sprayed outward like shrapnel, glittering deadly in the dim light.
The impact didn’t just knock Rex back; it launched him. He became a human projectile, hurtling thirty meters across the domain.

His body slammed into one of the slow-rotating light formations near the floor with a wet, meaty THUD. He tumbled through the construct, sparks of violet energy licking at his torn clothes, before finally coming to a stop on his side.
He lay motionless among the scattered shards of his mask and the fading embers of his power.
The mask was gone. His face was bare.
Apollo landed twenty meters away, his boots skidding across the pulsing floor as he fought to maintain his balance. His chest heaved in ragged, desperate gasps.
Blood dripped from his own split knuckles, his golden aura flickering dangerously low. His vision was swimming, his muscles screaming for release, but adrenaline forced his head up.
He raised his eyes, bracing for the counterattack, ready to see the monster he had just unmasked.
And then, the world stopped.
Apollo froze. His heart stuttered. The oxygen seemed to vanish from his lungs.

For a long, agonizing moment, his mind refused to function. The human psyche has safeguards and barriers designed to protect itself from truths too devastating to process, and his mind was slamming them shut.
He saw dark hair, matted with blood and sweat. He saw a jawline he had sat across from at a hundred meals, sharing quiet words and stolen glances.

His eyes traced the profile of the man who had pulled him from the rubble of a burning plaza when his own ribs had been shattered. He saw the man who had sat beside him in the dirt of a training yard during his darkest nights, offering words of wisdom that had saved his sanity.
He saw the man who had stood like an immovable pillar at his shoulder in the council chambers, defying the entire Apostle network to defend Apollo’s honor.
The monster wasn’t a monster. The enemy wasn’t an enemy.
The man he had been trying to kill was the only reason he was still alive.
"Rex."
The name escaped Apollo’s lips like a broken prayer. It lacked conviction; there was no anger in it, no triumph, no accusation.

It was merely the hollow, confused sound of a man reading a foreign word, a sound that carried the terrifying weight of recognition without understanding. His voice cracked, the syllables dissolving into the charged air of the domain.
But Rex did not hear him.

Rex lay sprawled on the pulsing violet floor of a domain he had authored less than twelve minutes ago, a space that, in his own subjective perception, had felt like an eternity of bloodshed and bone-deep exhaustion.
His ears rang with the aftershocks of the impact, his vision swimming in crimson droplets from the gash above his eye, but he was deaf to Apollo’s plea.
Rex was no longer engaged in the fight. He was no longer present in the moment.
His gaze was locked on something else entirely.
He wasn’t looking at Apollo’s devastated face. He wasn’t looking at his own reflection in the slick, violet surface beneath him, a reflection that showed a man broken, bleeding, and unmasked.
His eyes were fixed on something far beyond the reach of Apollo’s golden light, staring into the impossible emptiness of the domain’s far horizon.
He was looking at a point where there should have been nothing but the endless, swirling void. A point he had personally designed to be vacant. A point he had sworn was empty.
Someone was standing there.
The figure was a violation of every law Rex had written for this space. It wore the same dark clothing.
It held the same unnerving, motionless posture. And it wore the same plain, featureless mask, but unlike Rex’s shattered helm, this mask was perfect... uncracked... whole... and impeccable.

Beneath the eye slits, there was no human iris, no divine glow; there were only two burning pits of violet black energy, a darkness so dense, so ancient, that it seemed to drink the very light Rex had spent his life cultivating.
It didn’t breathe. It didn’t shift its weight, but it simply existed.
It was a foreign object inserted into Rex’s reality, standing with the terrifying, patient stillness of something that had been waiting behind the door long before the door was even built.
’No,’ Rex thought, his mind suddenly screaming. ’That’s impossible... I built this.’
’I am the architect... I control the parameters...’
’There is nothing there... There is—’

With a wet groan of pain, Rex pushed himself up onto one elbow, his muscles twitching involuntarily. Every contingency Rex had spent over a year constructing—every fallback position, every tactical deception, every calculated risk—vanished.

His brilliant, analytical mind, which had just danced circles around a divine warrior, suddenly went completely silent. For the first time in his second life, Rex felt something he had forgotten existed: genuine, primal dread.
Twenty meters away, Apollo took an uncertain step forward. His fists were still raised in a combat stance, knuckles raw and bleeding, but his posture was collapsing.
His face was a mask of agony, still trying to force the name he had spoken to carry meaning, to bridge the impossible chasm that had just opened between them.
"Rex!" Apollo called out again, louder this time, his voice cracking with desperation. "Rex, look at me!"
"What is this? What are you doing?"
Rex didn’t answer. He didn’t even flinch at the sound of his friend’s voice.
He couldn’t. His entire existence had narrowed down to that single point in the distance.
His pupils dilated, tracking the impossible.
Because the figure had finally begun to move.
It didn’t run. It didn’t charge.
It simply began to walk. Each step was silent, measured, and inevitable, cutting through the violet haze like a blade through silk.
Thump.
Rex felt it in his teeth. Not a sound, but a vibration.
A heartbeat that wasn’t his own.
Thump.
The figure was coming. And Rex knew, with the cold certainty of a dying man, that whatever was walking toward them wasn’t a guest in his domain.
It was the owner.

chapters.title: Chapter 1164. Turns Out ’God of My Own Domain’ Has an Asterisk I Wasn’t Told About
paragraphs: The figure in the distance was gone.
One moment, the impossible silhouette had been cutting through the violet haze with the steady, inexorable rhythm of a death march; the next, there was only... nothing.
Rex blinked once. Then twice.

His eyelashes felt heavy with dried blood and sweat as he stared at the empty horizon where the intruder had stood. The far reach of the domain held absolutely nothing—no residual energy trails, no displaced air, no fading footsteps.
There was only the same slow, nauseating violet pulse rolling outward toward a horizon that simply did not exist, a seamless repetition of a void he had engineered with surgical precision.
’Where did it go?’ His mind screamed. ’There was no displacement.’
’No teleportation signature... No dimensional fold...’
His Divine Perception, a constant, humming subroutine in the back of his consciousness that monitored every molecule of his domain, remained stubbornly silent. It reported the space as empty.

In fact, as Rex dug deeper into the data streams, a cold shiver that had nothing to do with the ambient temperature raced down his spine: his perception had been reporting that space as empty the entire time.
The figure hadn’t appeared; it had simply been there, invisible to every sensor Rex possessed, a ghost in his own machine.
That realization was more terrifying than any blade.
’Focus,’ he commanded himself, forcing the panic down into a dark corner of his mind. ’Panic is a luxury of the dying.’
’You are not dying yet.’
He filed it. That was all he could do.

Rex was a man built on the architecture of information; he was a master of categorizing chaos. A problem with no available action was a problem for later, and at this exact microsecond, ’later’ was a concept he couldn’t afford to indulge.
His immediate reality was still bleeding, still broken, and still standing in the middle of a battlefield.
But the implications burned in his mind like acid. He had built this domain himself, four minutes ago, out of raw willpower and conceptual mathematics.
He had authored every cubic meter of this reality. He had decided the density of the air, the frequency of the violet light, and the exact texture of the floor beneath his shattered body.
There had been nothing in this space except two people, himself and Apollo, and the floor he had willed into existence.
And yet, something had been standing there. Something wearing his own face’s covering.
Something that had looked at him with eyes that burned with a violet-black intensity deeper and more ancient than any power he had ever touched.

His mind, functioning like a supercooled quantum processor, immediately began running the probabilities. He ran all three logical conclusions in under a second, the data cascading through his neurons with ruthless efficiency:
Option One: It was a parasitic manifestation.
Something that had been attached to his own soul—a shadow, a remnant, a hitchhiker that had only become visible when his own protective barrier, the mask, had been stripped away.
Option Two: It was an environmental anomaly.

Something that existed in the fundamental substrate of reality, the ’dark matter’ of the universe that his Domain Creation had accidentally carved space around, revealing something native to the void itself.
Option Three: The worst possibility.
An intrusion. A third party capable of breaching an authored domain uninvited, bypassing all safeguards, all locks, and all divine protections.
Rex’s jaw tightened as his thoughts landed on the third option. Lustia’s teachings echoed in his mind like a funeral dirge: ’The absolute value of a domain is its isolation.’
’Inside your own creation, you are God.’
’Nothing can reach you unless you allow it.’
If someone could walk into his domain without permission, then his entire concept of safety and his entire identity as an untouchable architect was a lie.
He took the three terrifying possibilities, compartmentalized them, and slammed the mental folder shut. He couldn’t fight a ghost that didn’t exist, and he couldn’t fight a concept.
For now, he had to deal with the breathing, bleeding man twenty meters away who was still calling his name.
He filed the horror away and waited for the next attack.
In front of him, Apollo Brightsoul had stopped moving entirely.

The world around them continued its violent, supernatural decay; the shards of Rex’s shattered mask were still dissolving into loose, glittering motes of violet light where he had landed, swirling like radioactive snow, but Apollo was frozen.

He stood twenty meters away, caught in a grotesque stasis, staring at the face they had both spent months, years, and a lifetime hiding from each other. His expression was a horrifying blank slate, a psychological paralysis where shock had overridden every other human emotion.

His fists were still raised in defensive fists, his knuckles raw and weeping crimson; his shoulders still carried the coiled, explosive tension of a man mid-combination, ready to unleash another devastating blow.
Every muscle in his body was still locked in the choreography of war, but his mind had abandoned the battlefield entirely.
"No.
The word was a strangled exhale, barely audible over the low hum of the domain’s energy.
Apollo’s foot dragged backward. It wasn’t a tactical retreat; there was no shift in his center of gravity, no readiness to counter, and no defensive posture.
His body was simply recoiling instinctively, a primal rejection of the reality his eyes were reporting. He was physically attempting to flee from the truth.
"No, this is not... this is not possible." Apollo’s voice rose in pitch, cracking with a desperate, hysterical edge. "This isn’t you..."
"The mask... the energy... signature everything said—" His hands began to shake, the golden light flickering around his palms like a dying candle. "Rex...? Say something!"
"Fight me! Hate me! Just say something!"
Rex did not answer.
Instead, he began to get up.

He did it with a terrifying, methodical slowness that was more unsettling than any display of rage could ever be. He pushed himself up from the pulsing violet floor, his movements deliberate and measured.

His joints protested with wet, grinding sounds—the sound of cartilage protesting under the strain of impact. He rolled his left shoulder once, wincing almost imperceptibly as the bone settled back into its socket with a sickening click pop, testing the damage from Apollo’s overhand strike.
Then, with the unhurried, almost mundane irritation of a man brushing lint off a tailored suit, he reached down and swept the loose glitter of dissolving mask fragments off his sleeve.
The fragments burned faintly against his skin, but he ignored them. He made no attempt to turn away from the divine warrior who had just tried to kill him.
He made no attempt to hide. He didn’t even reach for his shapeshifting abilities, a power that could have reconfigured his features into someone else’s in less than a heartbeat.
He simply stood there, exposed, bleeding, and utterly vulnerable, letting Apollo drink in the devastating reality of his face.

The silence that followed was not empty; it was heavy, pressurized, like the air before a catastrophic storm. It stretched between them, thick with the copper tang of blood and the ozone of spent magic.
Rex let it stretch. He knew the cruel mathematics of revelation.
There was a specific, devastating art in letting a person assemble a terrible picture for themselves. If he spoke now, he would be offering an explanation, a deflection, a lie.
But if he remained silent, Apollo would be forced to connect the dots. Apollo would remember the meals, the training sessions, the shared trauma, and the betrayal.
He would build the horror piece by piece, bone by bone, until the conclusion was inevitable.
Because a truth someone discovers for themselves can never be dismissed as a lie they were told.
Rex simply watched him through the blood dripping from his brow, his dark eyes steady and cold, waiting for the moment Apollo’s world finally shattered.

chapters.title: Chapter 1165. Turns Out ’It’s Complicated’ Doesn’t Cover Genocide, My Bad
paragraphs: Rex watched it happen in real time. He stood motionless, a statue of flesh and bone, as he witnessed the systematic dismantling of Apollo’s sanity.

He watched Apollo’s eyes, those bright, hopeful eyes, dart across the details that refused to be explained away. He watched them trace the familiar height, the specific muscular build, and the way his shoulders set when he braced for impact.

Apollo’s gaze lingered on the small, jagged scar just below Rex’s left ear. Apollo had asked about it once, months ago, in a sun-drenched training yard, receiving nothing but a dismissive joke in return.
Rex watched Apollo’s pupils dilate as his mind desperately spun through contingencies: ’Shapeshifting. An illusion. A mimicry spell.’

But Apollo’s own tactical training betrayed him; he knew the Lustful Villain’s abilities never included sophisticated illusion magic, and more damningly, Rex’s voice now unmasked, raw, and unguarded hadn’t shifted an octave.
"Rex," Apollo said again.
His voice had dropped to a whisper, a fragile sound that seemed to plead with the very fabric of reality to intervene. "Rex, please... tell me this isn’t you."
"Tell me it’s a trick... a complex illusion..."
"Or some kind of twisted magical feedback... Give me an explanation... Please."
"I could tell you that."
Rex’s tone had reverted to the easy, infuriating warmth and casual, fond cadence he used when they shared drinks in a tavern above ground.

The effect of hearing that familiar comfort come from this blood-streaked face, in this twisted violet domain, was worse than any demonic growl. It was more intimate than any attack; it was a violation of memory.
"It would be a lie, though," Rex continued, his voice steady, almost conversational. "And I think you’re old enough by now that you don’t need any more of those today."
The rejection hit Apollo with more force than any physical blow. His legs simply gave out.

There was no stumble, no collapse from exhaustion. Apollo’s divine constitution had been fully restored twenty minutes ago; the golden ichor of his power was still humming faintly beneath his skin, ready for war.
But his body had decided it could no longer support the weight of his soul. His knees hit the violet floor with a hollow thud.

One hand flew to his chest, fingers clawing desperately at the cracked armor plating over his sternum, as if something vital underneath his heart, his very essence, had come unmoored and he could hold it together through sheer physical pressure alone.
Tears began to carve pale, clean tracks through the dried blood and grime coating Apollo’s face.
"Why?" Apollo choked out.
The word broke in the middle, splintering into two separate agonies. "Why would you do this?"
He gasped for air, but each breath sounded like he was inhaling broken glass. "I trusted you..."
"I didn’t just trust you, Rex... I loved you like a brother!

"We bled together! We trained until our bones screamed!" His voice rose, cracking with a desperate need to remind Rex of the shared history that now felt like poison. "You pulled me out of that plaza when Tremor had my ribs caved in. I can still hear the sound of them snapping!"
"You sat with me in the dark after Calivara’s funeral when I couldn’t bear to see another human face!"
"You saved Elliot’s life during the Goblin King raid before we even truly knew each other!"
"You took an axe across your back for him, and I can still see you bleeding on the ground, dying for them—"
A violent sob caught in his throat, wracking his entire frame. He had to fight for air, struggling through the physical pain of a chest that felt like it was collapsing inward.
When he spoke again, it wasn’t a question; it was an accusation aimed at the heavens.
"Was all of it a lie...? Every single moment...?" Apollo looked up, his eyes bloodshot and drowning in grief. "Every time you said you cared?"
"Every time you helped me with Kaelira?"
"Every time you guided me through my harem, through my life... was that all just... reconnaissance?"

Rex listened to the entire confession without so much as a flinch. He stood there like a monument of indifference, letting Apollo’s grief spill across the violet floor like blood from an arterial wound.
His expression held nothing that could be mistaken for remorse. There was no flicker of guilt in those dark eyes, no downward cast of his head.
What he held instead was patience, the particular, unsettling patience of a predator who has no intention of hurrying a prey animal through its final, desperate confession.
"Some of it was a lie," Rex said when Apollo finally ran out of air.
His voice was terrifyingly calm, cutting through the sobbing silence. "Some of it wasn’t..."
"I actually did enjoy our time together, Apollo... not gonna lie."
"You’re not a boring person to be friends with, which is rarer than you’d think in our circles..."
"I’ve spent countless hours with people I found tedious—drones, sycophants, dullards—but you... were never one of them."
"But it didn’t stop you!" Apollo’s voice suddenly sharpened, the grief cracking like breaking glass to reveal a raw, bleeding vein of fury underneath.
The golden light around his fists flared erratically, casting jagged shadows across the domain. "It didn’t stop you from slaughtering my people in the streets!"
"From tearing Veylor away from Iris’s arms while she screamed for mercy!
"From killing Calivara... from butchering Eryndra... from turning Theo into—"
"No."
Rex cut him off, not with anger, but with a flat, factual finality that was infinitely more devastating. "Nothing stopped me."
"Because there was never a reason for me to stop."
Apollo raised his head, his face flushed with rage and tears, looking up at the man he thought he knew.

Rex was standing with his arms folded loosely across his chest, weight shifted onto one hip. He looked relaxed, almost casual, in the posture of a man leaning against a fence post while discussing the weather with a neighbor.
There was nothing performative about it; there was no theatrical villainy, no manic laughter, no grandiose posturing. That was the part Apollo’s mind simply could not process.
For months, Apollo had been constructing an image of the enemy, a monster fueled by hatred, a demon driven by some consuming vendetta. He expected a demon, nor did he expect a monster.
What he was looking at instead was a man who appeared to be mildly interested in the conversation and otherwise entirely comfortable in his own skin.

"I still believe," Apollo said, the words tumbling out of him with the desperate, suicidal momentum of someone who has decided to keep walking into a stone wall. "I still believe there is a part of you, the Rex I knew, that can still be saved."
"All of this... it has to have an explanation."
"Maybe you were coerced... Maybe there’s some ancient contract, some divine designation, some curse god, or whatever patron you serve has placed upon you that you can’t."
"You want an explanation," Rex interrupted. His tone remained conversational, almost empathetic, which made the words feel like poisoned honey. "I understand the impulse, Apollo."
"I truly do... People always crave an explanation because it makes a thing smaller."
"It makes it manageable."
Rex took a single step forward, the violet floor rippling beneath his boot like disturbed water.
"If I tell you I was coerced, then what happened to your people was done by circumstances, and you can direct your anger at the abstract concept of fate."

"If I tell you there’s a curse, you can hate the curse instead of me... Every version of the story where I had a reason is a version where you get to keep some part of the world you had this morning."
"You want to believe in a reason because without one, you have to face the truth."
Rex paused, letting the silence settle like ash.
"And the truth is much harder to live with than any lie."

chapters.title: Chapter 1166. The Parts That Helped You Grow Were the Parts Designed to Kill You
paragraphs: Rex didn’t stand over him like a conqueror. Instead, he crouched down, bringing himself level with Apollo’s kneeling form.

The movement was fluid, predatorily graceful, and utterly devoid of any reverence. Up close, the intimacy was nauseating; Rex looked like a friend sharing a secret, his breath steady despite the magical turbulence swirling around them.
"I’m not going to give you that luxury," Rex said, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial murmur. "You’ve earned the real thing, Apollo."
"And the real thing is that there is no grand design..."
"No cosmic accident. I looked at the situation, I saw what was available to be taken, and I took it."
’And I enjoyed taking it more than I have enjoyed anything else in either of the lives I’ve ever lived."
"Nothing controls me," Rex cut in again, and there was the first genuine edge of amusement in his voice, a dark, razor-sharp amusement.

Watching Apollo desperately construct elaborate excuses for him was genuinely entertaining. It was a game: Apollo was trying to build a cage of logic to contain a monster, and Rex was simply enjoying watching the bars bend.
"I did all of it because I chose to..."
"Because every drop of blood, every scream, every broken promise... I did it because I enjoyed it."
"How... long?" Apollo’s voice was hollow, the sound of a man whose internal compass had just been shattered.
"Be more specific."
"All of it... From the very beginning." Apollo’s hands had clenched into fists so tight against his thighs that his knuckles turned bone white, the tendons standing out like cables.
He couldn’t bear to look at Rex’s face anymore; he stared instead at a single spot on the violet floor between them, as if trying to anchor himself to reality. "When we met, at that academy..."
"When you helped my friends fight off those monsters and we shared that first drink... was it already decided then?"
"Was I already a target before I even learned your name?"
Rex let out a soft, almost thoughtful hum. "You weren’t a target then, Apollo..."
"Don’t flatter yourself. You were a resource I hadn’t finished evaluating."
"A variable in an equation I hadn’t finished writing..."
"The decision came later once I understood the true scale of what you actually were and what having you standing beside me as an ally would be worth to my objectives."
"That evaluation took a few months."
"So there was a point." Apollo’s voice cracked, a wet, splintering sound. "There was a moment where the path could have diverged.
"Where you could have chosen differently... Where we could have..."
"Probably not." Rex considered it for a heartbeat, tilting his head as if weighing a trivial question.

Then he shook his head with finality. "No. Being honest with you, which I have decided to be exactly once, and only today, there was never really a version of this where you and I ended up somewhere other than here."
"You were always going to be what you are: a shining beacon of naive heroism."
"And I was always going to be what I am..."
"The only real variable was how long the charade would take and how much entertainment I could extract from it along the way."
Rex’s eyes crinkled at the corners, a smile touching his lips that never reached his cold, dead eyes. "I got a great deal out of it, if that helps."
"It doesn’t," Apollo hissed, the word dripping with venomous agony. "It helps nothing..."
"It changes nothing."
"No," Rex agreed cheerfully, his tone as light as if they were discussing a pleasant afternoon stroll. "I didn’t think it would."
Apollo did not rise immediately. He remained collapsed on his knees, his forehead nearly touching the pulsing violet floor.

His hands were splayed flat against the ground as if trying to anchor his very soul to the earth, but his breathing betrayed him; it came in short, ragged, uneven gasps that sounded more like the death rattles of something broken than the breaths of a living man.
Rex watched him with the detached fascination of an entomologist observing a beetle struggling beneath glass. He made no move to comfort him nor to threaten him.

He simply let the silence stretch, thick and suffocating, allowing the weight of Rex’s confession to settle into Apollo’s bones. He knew that words were useless now; the real torture was letting Apollo sit inside the ruins of his own reality.
"Kaelira," Apollo finally whispered.
The name was a plea, a desperate attempt to find one single thread of goodness in the tapestry of betrayal. "What about her? Did you touch her?"
"Not hers... No." Rex shrugged one shoulder with casual indifference. "I never got to her..."
"She’s been too close to you too, perceptive, too suspicious by temperament..."
"And frankly, the tactical return on investment wasn’t worth the risk of her catching wind of my true nature too early."
"You still have her, Apollo... Consider it your one remaining victory."
"Congratulations."
A sound tore itself from Apollo’s throat. It was a laugh, but it was the most horrific sound heard in the domain thus far—wet, cracked, and utterly devoid of any human mirth.
It sounded like bones grinding together in a jar of blood.

"You want to know something truly interesting?" Rex continued, his voice dropping to a register that was almost gentle, almost tender. "The advice I gave you about her was the best advice I’ve ever given anyone."
"I meant every word of it... You did come back from that experience better than you went in, stronger, more self-aware."
"That’s the part that’s going to haunt you the most later if there even is a later."
"Not the lies, Apollo... Not the betrayal... It’s the fact that the parts of me that helped you grow were real."
With a guttural groan of exertion, Apollo began to force himself upright.
The process was agonizing to witness. He moved badly, his muscles twitching with suppressed tremors, using one unsteady hand against the throbbing floor to prevent himself from collapsing again.

When he finally stood fully upright, his face was a mask of something Rex found genuinely fascinating. The grief was still there, a crushing, tidal wave of sorrow, but layered over it was something else: a stubborn, pathological refusal to surrender.
He was clinging to the ghost of his friend with such ferocity that it seemed he might snap his own fingers trying to hold on.
"You helped me with Kaelira," Apollo said.

His voice was hoarse, and he sounded as though he were arguing with his own conscience as much as he was addressing Rex. "When she was recovering after the dungeon raid... when she couldn’t even stand without shaking... you were the one who told me to stop hovering."
"You told me to give her space to want to come back to me, instead of making her feel like her recovery was an obligation to my needs."
Apollo took a step forward, his boots squelching on the violet surface. "You gave me advice about my harem."
"You told me I was neglecting Nerith..."
"You told me I was being unfair, that I had to actually see each of them as individuals instead of treating them like a collection of assets."
"You taught me how to be a better partner, how to be a better man."
His eyes burned with a terrifying, confused light. "Why would you do that, Rex...?"
"Why would you invest that much effort into my happiness if your only goal was to destroy me?"
Rex’s smile didn’t falter. If anything, it sharpened.
"Because the advice was correct," Rex said simply, as if stating a mathematical truth. "And because the better your relationships became, the more deeply you trusted me."
"The more you believed I was your confidant, your brother, your guide, the more valuable you became."

"And the more deeply you trusted me, Apollo... the easier it was to reach in and tear each of them away from you, one by one, without you ever seeing the blade until it was already buried in your throat."

chapters.title: Chapter 1167. Your Goodness Was the Leash I Used to Drag You Here
paragraphs: Apollo’s pupils dilated until his irises were mere rings of gold around a void of black terror. He looked as though he had been struck physically, though Rex hadn’t moved an inch.
Rex watched with predatory satisfaction as the specific piece of the puzzle dropped into place. It was a masterpiece of psychological demolition.

He had waited for this exact moment, the moment where the past stops being a refuge and starts becoming a prison. Every conversation Apollo had cherished, every moment of vulnerability they had shared, was being retroactively weaponized, twisted into an instrument of torment.
"Talyra," Apollo whispered.
The name was a broken thing, barely audible over the low hum of the domain’s power. "Aisella... Nerith... Mireya... They—"
"All mine." Rex cut him off, the words landing with the wet thud of a guillotine blade. "For a while now."
"Talyra, Nerith, Mireya, and Aisella—they’ve all been in my bed... getting FUCKED while you were sleeping soundly in the next room..."
"You didn’t notice because they were good at it, Apollo..."
"They’re excellent performers..."
"They kept the charade up in front of you because they knew how much you needed to believe in it."
Apollo began to shake.
It wasn’t the tremor of exhaustion or the shiver of physical pain. This was something structural, the soundless shattering of a man’s foundational reality.

Rex had seen this expression before: once on Theo Nightwing’s face when his betrayal was laid bare, and once on Mordecai Vrael’s when he realized his kingdom had been hollowed out from within. It never got less satisfying to watch.
This was the precise moment a man discovers that his grief was incomplete. He had believed he was mourning three dead companions and one betrayed friend.

He was actually learning that the four women still standing beside him, the ones who still smiled at him, still touched his cheek, still spoke of love every single day, had been Rex’s playthings for months. They hadn’t just been complicit; they had been reporting on his every heartbeat.
The dead were only the part he had already counted. The living were the real wound.

Rex could see the gears grinding behind Apollo’s eyes. He could see that glassy, distant quality that overtakes a person when they begin to re-examine their entire history through a new, poisoned lens.
Apollo was running through the memories, applying Rex’s words as a corrosive acid to every precious moment.
’Nerith.’ Apollo remembered her laughing at the waterfall on the last night of the canyon expedition.
He remembered the way the moonlight caught the droplets on her skin as he finally found the courage to confess his feelings. She had cried then.
He had thought those were tears of joy, a breakthrough in their intimacy. He had spent weeks afterward basking in the glow of that moment.
Now, he wondered if she had been crying because she was thinking of the touch of Rex’s hands.
’Talyra.’ He remembered her returning from the island assessment with her hand still wrapped in blood-stained bandages.
She had insisted she was fine, but she had sat closer to him at dinner that night than she had in months, her thigh pressed against his in a gesture of comfort.
Now, the memory felt like a violation.
Had she been seeking comfort from him, or was she simply seeking a distraction before she returned to Rex?
’Mireya.’ Three days after the canyon expedition, she had come to his chambers in the dead of night.
She hadn’t asked for words; she had simply asked him to hold her and not ask why. He had held her for hours, feeling protective and like her anchor.
Now, he wondered whose arms she had truly been seeking when she asked for silence.
’Aisella.’ The memory of the plaza fight burned fresh.
She had knelt over his broken body, healing his wounds with desperate magic, her tears falling hot against his skin as she sobbed that she didn’t know what she would do if she lost him.
He had felt her love in that moment raw and terrifying.
Now, that memory felt like a mockery.
Was she crying for him, or was she crying because she was terrified of losing the protection Rex provided?
Every memory remained true. That was the cruelty of Rex’s design.
None of those moments had been faked. The laughter had been real, the tears had been real, and the touches had been real.
But they had all been performed within a context Apollo was never permitted to see—a context where every act of intimacy was merely another layer of the trap being set around his throat.
"Why," Apollo whispered.
The word was fractured, a broken thing that seemed to bleed out of his throat. "What is wrong with me?"
"What kind of monster am I?"

"What did I do to deserve this?" His voice rose slightly, cracking with a desperate, childlike need for a reason—any reason that would make sense of the carnage. "What could I have possibly done to make you want to destroy everything I love?"
Rex tilted his head to the side, studying Apollo with the clinical interest of a scholar examining a particularly fascinating specimen of decay.

For a moment, he actually considered the question honestly. He considered it because it deserved an honest answer and because the truth was far more devastating than any elaborate lie he could have woven.
Then he smiled. But it wasn’t the amused smirk from before, nor was it the predatory grin of a hunter.
This smile was something new, something hollow, empty, and utterly alien.
"Nothing," Rex said, his voice as calm as a still pond before a storm. "You didn’t do anything wrong at all, Apollo."

"You weren’t cruel... You weren’t selfish... You weren’t even weak..." He leaned forward slightly, his eyes locking onto Apollo’s with terrifying clarity. "You simply happened to be the protagonist of a story that was never supposed to be yours."
"You were playing a hero’s role in a world that was already written by someone else."
The silence that followed was absolute. It was a vacuum, sucking the air out of the domain, leaving Apollo gasping in the emptiness.
Then, Rex started laughing.
It began as a low chuckle in his chest but quickly spiraled into something far more primal. It was an unrestrained, genuine bark of laughter that tore through the quiet like a blade through silk.
The sound rolled across the impossible geometry of the domain, bouncing off surfaces that defied physics, returning distorted and echoing like the screams of something dying.
He laughed until his shoulders shook, until tears pricked the corners of his eyes, not from sadness, but from the sheer, overwhelming absurdity of it all.
He laughed at the question. He laughed at the pathetic, shattered expression on Apollo’s face.

He laughed at the cosmic irony of the entire situation: that this man, this paragon of virtue, had spent eighteen months being counseled on his own inevitable destruction by the very architect of that ruin and had thanked him for his wisdom every single time.
’How perfect,’ Rex thought, his mind racing with the dark euphoria of the moment. ’How deliciously grotesque.’
As the laughter subsided, the last vestiges of humanity vanished from Rex’s face. It didn’t fade slowly; it vanished instantaneously, like a candle being snuffed out by a cold wind.

What remained was something colder, sharper, and infinitely older than the man Apollo thought he knew. His features became angular, carved from something harder than stone, and his eyes, previously ordinary, began to pulse with a deep, malevolent violet-black light.
It was a glow that held no warmth, no recognition, no mercy, only a bottomless, ravenous appetite.
Rex’s grin widened, stretching unnaturally across his face as the magical pressure in the room began to spike, making the very air hum with lethal intent.

"You want to know what I find the funniest about all of this, Apollo?" Rex asked, his voice now carrying an unnatural resonance that seemed to vibrate in Apollo’s very bones. "You spent your entire existence trying to be a hero worth the title."
"You strove to protect every innocent, to uphold every principle, to be ’good’ at all costs."
Rex took a slow, deliberate step forward, the violet light from his eyes casting long, dancing shadows across the floor. "And that was your fatal flaw."
"Every noble choice you made, every sacrifice you offered, every ounce of compassion you showed... every single one of those choices was exactly what made you the perfect target."
"Your goodness wasn’t your shield, Apollo."
"It was the leash I used to drag you to this place."

chapters.title: Chapter 1168. Grief Is the Price of Having Loved Someone Properly...
paragraphs: Apollo stared up at him, his vision blurred by a hot flood of tears. His entire world, the moral compass he had relied upon to navigate the darkness, wasn’t just broken; it was being ground into powder beneath Rex’s boot.
Behind the tears, something deeper was happening. Something fundamental in his psyche was fracturing, a psychic collapse that made his hands shake with involuntary spasms.
"You’re not... you’re not the Rex I knew," Apollo whispered.
The words were pathetic, a weak attempt to cling to a ghost that had never existed.
"I was never the Rex you knew," Rex answered, the grin widening until it seemed to split his face unnaturally. "You just hadn’t met the real one until now."
"The one beneath the performance... The one who actually has the spine to do what needs to be done..."
Rex began to walk.
He didn’t charge; he didn’t threaten. He simply began to circle Apollo slowly, like a shark circling a wounded whale.

His hands hung loose at his sides, relaxed in a way that was more terrifying than any clenched fist. His boots made no sound whatsoever on the pulsing violet surface, as if he had become untethered from the physical laws of the world.
When he spoke again, his voice had shifted; it had lost its venom and gained something worse: the casual, measured cadence of a professor lecturing a student or a storyteller recounting a legend.
"Let me tell you something, Apollo..."
"Because I think you’ve earned the right to know... After everything I’ve taken from you, it would be almost cruel not to show you the full scale of my craftsmanship."
"You’re going to be the only person alive who ever gets to see the full picture, the complete architecture of this masterpiece."
"And really, it seems like such a waste not to share it with someone who appreciates the artistry."
Apollo lifted his head. His eyes were bloodshot, swollen from grief and exhaustion, but beneath the agony there was a terrible, hollow curiosity.
It was the morbid fascination of a man standing on the edge of an abyss, knowing that if he looked down, he would fall, but unable to tear his gaze away from the void.
"The Undead Bringer," Rex said, the name dropping like a guillotine blade into the silence. "That was me, Apollo..."

"Every apostate he slaughtered in those northern territories, every reincarnator who vanished without a trace during those six months of chaos, every bloodbath that kept your council awake at night... that was all my handiwork."
Rex paused, savoring the way Apollo’s breathing hitched.

"I wore Xavier Xenworth’s face to do it," Rex continued smoothly, stepping closer, his violet eyes casting jagged shadows across Apollo’s broken form. "Because the Goddess of Justice never formally withdrew his designation after his ’accidental’ death."
"His soul’s departure was ambiguous enough that the divine registry left his record in a transitional state—a ghost in the machine."
"So, when your investigators ran their signature scans, they didn’t see a new threat.
"They saw a corrupted Apostle of Justice... your entire network, your brilliant, tactical network, spent four months chasing a dead man, hunting a shadow that I had painted onto a corpse."

Apollo made a small, choked sound, a whimper that died in his throat. His mind flashed back to the war room, the maps spread across the table, the sleepless nights spent pouring over magical residue signatures.

He had personally led two of those investigations. He had stood before the council, confident and determined, promising that they would unmask the monster that was slaughtering their allies. He had staked his reputation, his authority, and his faith on the hunt.
And he had been hunting his best friend.
"Tremor," Rex continued, his voice relentless, steamrolling over Apollo’s attempts to breathe. "The catastrophic earthquake that leveled the northern district."
"The screams of thousands buried under tons of rubble..."
"All those civilians who died screaming for a god who never answered... That was me."
Rex took another step, his violet eyes pulsing like a dying star. "That stone meteor that tore through the Starlight Garden?"
"The one that took Lily and Diana out of the world before they could even scream?"
"That was my handiwork as well..."
"Do you remember the gauntlets of the Earth Sovereign’s Vessel? The ones I reported as stolen during that undead assault on Sable Island?"
"I had them fully integrated into my own circulatory system two days before the attack even began."

"I staged the theft, Apollo... I sent one of my own constructs running into the night with an empty artifact so your precious network would have a thief to chase, a convenient scapegoat to keep you from looking at me."
"The dragon..." Apollo whispered.

The words felt like glass shards in his throat. He knew where this was going; he could feel the shape of the horror forming in the air, but he couldn’t stop himself from asking, the way a condemned man might ask about the weather before the trapdoor drops.
"Ignivara." Rex nodded approvingly. "She was Legion once."
"Now she is mine... She has been mine since long before her public defection."
"Every scrap of intelligence she fed your network, every ’crucial’ warning that allowed you to reposition your forces? All of it was filtered through me first."
"I wrote her scripts... I dictated her lies..."
"She sat in a room with Valentina, your most trusted strategist, and delivered a briefing that I had personally authored.
"And Zane Mortavius?" Rex’s grin turned razor sharp. "I let him escape the purge specifically so he would act as my messenger, carrying my poison into your inner sanctum."
"Once he stopped being useful, I disposed of him."
Apollo was shaking violently now, his entire body convulsing with a primal terror. Every revelation landed like a war hammer against his skull, each one more devastating than the last.

The physical pain of their battle—the shattered ribs, the blood filling his lungs, the grinding pain in his limbs—was nothing compared to this. That fight had only broken his bones; this was breaking his soul.

He was watching the last year of his life be dismantled, piece by piece, revealing that every tragedy he had grieved, every investigation he had poured his heart into, every friend he had buried... they were all orchestrated performances.
He had been mourning corpses while the murderer stood at his shoulder, offering him a handkerchief.
’He was there,’ Apollo’s mind screamed. ’Every time I cried, he was there.’
’Every time I failed, he was there to help me pick up the pieces.’
"Wait," Apollo said, his voice thinning out until it was nothing more than a ghostly rasp. "The night of Veylor’s funeral."
"The city was in mourning... You... you stood next to Iris at the coffin."
"You put your hand on her shoulder..."
"You looked her in the eyes and told her that ’grief was the price of having loved someone properly. ’I remember it."
"Half the city remembers it... People called it the most noble thing anyone had done during the dark weeks."
Rex nodded slowly, completely unbothered, his expression one of mild academic interest. "I did say that."
"And I meant it, in its own twisted way."
"Grief is the price of having loved someone properly."
Rex leaned down until his face was inches from Apollo’s, the violet glow of his eyes casting a sickly light over Apollo’s tear-streaked features.
"The only problem, Apollo, is that I’d already killed him eleven hours earlier."
