chapters.title: Chapter 1186. There’s Never A Silent Death Other Than A Torturing Death
paragraphs: The silence that followed was not peaceful; it was a vacuum, heavy with the copper tang of blood and the acrid stench of burnt divine energy. Rex stood there, motionless, studying Apollo’s ruined, broken expression.
The man was a wreck of shattered bone and punctured organs, yet his eyes remained stubbornly fixed, refusing to cloud with the shame of defeat.

Rex felt something uncomfortable stirring beneath his own calculated detachment. It was an unspoken acknowledgment of the sheer, pathological stubbornness of a man who had lost every tangible thing—his power, his body, his future—and still refused to surrender the one thing. Rex couldn’t touch the core of his soul.
"That’s the part I’ll actually miss," Rex said quietly, almost to himself.
His voice lacked its usual mocking edge; it sounded almost hollow. "Not the friendship..."
"The conviction underneath it... It’s rare, Apollo."
"It’s the only thing about you I never managed to fake for myself."
But as Rex watched Apollo’s steady breathing, something twisted in his mind. That conviction, that quiet, dignified acceptance of death, irritated him.
It was a challenge. It was Apollo winning the only battle that mattered: the one for his own dignity.
Rex didn’t want a martyr. He didn’t want a saint to die with a smile on his bloodied face. He wanted to break the belief itself.
"But then again," Rex’s voice shifted, the warmth evaporating instantly, replaced by something glacial and cruel. "Dignity is such a fragile thing, isn’t it?"
Rex rose to his feet slowly, his shadow stretching over Apollo like a shroud. The violet-black aura around him flared, not in a burst of power, but in a slow, undulating wave of malice.
He didn’t raise his hand to deliver a killing blow. Instead, he reached down and grabbed Apollo by his matted hair, yanking his head back with a brutal JERK to force him to look up.
"Let’s see how long that faith lasts when your body stops belonging to you," Rex hissed.
He didn’t use magic yet. He wanted the tactile reality of it.
Rex drove his knee into Apollo’s sternum with precise, controlled force.
CRUNCH.
The sound of cartilage tearing echoed in the silent domain. Apollo’s mouth opened in a silent scream, blood frothing between his teeth.
"Still believing, Apollo?" Rex whispered, leaning close enough that Apollo could see his own dying reflection in the black visor of the mask. "Still thinking there’s goodness in the universe?"
Rex’s hand moved with terrifying speed. He didn’t strike; he dug.
His fingers, reinforced by Telekinesis, pressed into the open wounds of Apollo’s ribs, twisting with deliberate, agonizing slowness.
SQUELCH.

Apollo’s body convulsed, his back arching off the ground in an involuntary spasm of agony. A wet, choking sound tore from his throat—a sound that wasn’t quite a scream but something far more primal and broken.
’Break the spirit,’ Rex thought, his own inner monologue running cold and clinical as he watched the light in Apollo’s eyes flicker. ’Kill the conviction first. Then kill the man.’
Rex raised his other hand, and the air around Apollo’s legs began to hum with Gravity Manipulation. "I’m going to make you beg for the Goddess to take you, Apollo..."
"I’m going to make you curse her name."
The gravity intensified in localized pockets, twisting Apollo’s already shattered limbs in directions no human joint should move.
SNAP. POP. CRACK.
The sound of Apollo’s femur grinding against itself filled the space. Rex watched with predatory fascination, waiting for the moment when that steady gaze would finally shatter into pleading eyes.
Rex wasn’t satisfied with physical agony. Physical pain was finite; it could be endured through sheer willpower.
But psychological annihilation? That was eternal.
He wanted to reach into the very fabric of Apollo’s memory and tear it apart, strand by strand, until there was nothing left of the man but a hollowed-out shell of shame and grief.
"You think your martyrdom makes you special?" Rex’s voice was a venomous murmur. "You think your suffering sanctifies you?"
Rex’s free hand began to glow with a sickly, chronal gold light, the unmistakable hue of his Time Manipulation. But he wasn’t using it to slow his own movements or accelerate his strikes.
He was weaving something far more insidious. He began to tear at the air itself, ripping open microscopic fissures in reality.
SHHHHH TICK!
The sound of reality tearing was like glass breaking underwater. These weren’t random rifts; they were temporal wounds, bleeding fragments of Apollo’s most sacred memories.
But Rex was corrupting them as they emerged, forcing the past to bend to his sadistic will.
"Look at them, Apollo," Rex commanded, his voice echoing as if from multiple directions at once. "Look at what your ’goodness’ has failed to protect."
Around the kneeling, broken Apollo, the air began to fracture into a kaleidoscope of torment. One rift opened to his left: Talyra.

Apollo’s eyes widened in horror as he saw a memory of her but not as she was. In this temporal distortion, she was draped across a throne of shadow, her eyes glazed with ecstasy as Rex took her with a primal, unholy hunger.
The sound of her moans, distorted and amplified by the rift, tore through Apollo’s mind like a blade.
"NO—!" Apollo gasped, a wet cough spraying blood.
SHHH TICK!
Another rift tore open above them.
Aisella.

The memory played out in high definition the way her body arched, the way she begged for Rex to never stop, and her devotion twisted into a perverse, carnal worship that Apollo had never imagined possible.
"STOP IT!" Apollo shrieked, his voice cracking, his hands clawing weakly at the air as if he could physically push the images away.
Rex didn’t stop. He accelerated.

The rifts multiplied, forming a ring of psychic devastation around the dying Apostle. Nerith appeared in one, her regal composure shattered as she surrendered to Rex’s dominance with a ferocity that defied her nature.
Mireya appeared in another, her lips parted in a breathless surrender that made Apollo feel as if his own heart were being flayed alive.
But the killing blow came from the largest rift, one that opened directly in front of Apollo’s face.
It was Amelia. His mother.
The memory was vivid, cruel, and undeniable. The darkness was claiming the woman who had raised him with tales of light and virtue.
Rex’s hands were all over her, and she wasn’t fighting. She was enjoying it. Her face reflected a pleasure so profound it felt like a betrayal of everything Apollo believed in.
"AAAAAGH!!" Apollo’s scream was no longer human.

It was the sound of a soul being eviscerated. He began to thrash, his broken body convulsing as he tried to escape the visions, but Rex’s Gravity Manipulation kept him pinned, forcing his eyes to stay open, forcing him to witness every obscene detail.
Rex stepped into the center of the ring of rifts, the chronal energy swirling around him like a storm. "See how they respond to real power, Apollo?"
"Not your empty promises, not your platitudes... They crave the truth... They crave me."
Rex grabbed Apollo’s chin again, forcing him to look at the image of Amelia, whose eyes in the rift seemed to meet Apollo’s in a mocking smile.
"Your mother, your friends, your lovers... they didn’t want a savior, Apollo," Rex whispered, his breath hot against Apollo’s ear. "They wanted a master."
Rex’s fist connected with Apollo’s stomach, the blow amplified by a burst of temporal energy that made the impact feel as though it had happened a thousand times over in a single second.
WHAM THUD.

Apollo’s lungs seized; he couldn’t even draw air to scream. He could only gurgle, tears mixing with the blood streaming down his face, as the fractured images of his loved ones being taken by Rex circled him like vultures.
"Does it hurt more than the broken bones, Apollo?" Rex asked, his voice dripping with sadistic satisfaction. "Does the truth hurt worse than the pain?"

"Let the shame consume you... That’s where the truth lives..."

He raised both hands, fingertips crackling with a volatile cocktail of Gravity Manipulation and Time Manipulation. The air between them became hypercompressed, screaming as it was squeezed into impossible densities.
VROOOOOOM
"You want to be an Apostle of Life?" Rex asked, his eyes glowing with a malevolent gold and violet light. "Then let’s see how much life you can actually endure."
Rex slammed his palms together.
BOOM.
A shockwave of gravitational force exploded outward, but instead of pushing Apollo away, it imploded inward, wrapping around Apollo’s broken body like a vise made of neutron star matter.
Apollo’s bones didn’t just crack this time; they ground against each other, the sound like wet gravel being crushed in a fist.
CRUNCH SQUELCH.
"This is the weight of your failure," Rex hissed.
As Apollo gasped for air that wouldn’t come, Rex activated the temporal rifts again, but this time he did something worse. He synchronized them.

The rifts began to spin, creating a chronal vortex that blurred the images of Talyra, Aisella, Nerith, Mireya, and Amelia. Their moans and screams of ecstasy merged into a single, haunting chorus that echoed through the chamber.
"MAKE IT STOP! PLEASE!" Apollo’s voice finally broke.
The plea was pathetic, stripped of all dignity, a raw wound of sound that made Rex’s grin widen.
"Make what stop, Apollo? The truth? Or the pleasure they’re feeling?" Rex leaned in, his free hand weaving through the air, plucking at the strands of time itself.
With each pluck, a new sensory detail flooded Apollo’s mind: the smell of Amelia’s perfume as she surrendered, the heat of Talyra’s skin, and the specific way Nerith’s eyes rolled back.
Rex then began a ritual of exquisite cruelty. He used Telekinesis to lift Apollo’s shattered fingers off the ground, holding them suspended in midair.
Then, with precise, microscopic applications of Gravity, he began to increase the pressure on each individual joint.
POP. SNAP. CRACKLE.
"One finger for every lie you told yourself about being a hero," Rex counted, each word punctuated by the wet sound of breaking cartilage. "One for every promise you couldn’t keep."
Apollo’s body convulsed violently. His eyes were blown wide, pupils dilated to the point of blackness, staring at nothing but the kaleidoscopic nightmare surrounding him.
"I... I loved them..." he wheezed, blood bubbling between his teeth like crimson foam.
"Love is just a word mortals use to justify their weakness," Rex countered.
He grabbed Apollo’s throat, not to strangle him, but to hold him steady while he unleashed a concentrated burst of Temporal Decay directly into Apollo’s chest.
SZZZZZT
It wasn’t fire; it was time. Apollo felt his cellular structure aging and reversing in rapid, agonizing succession.
His skin blistered and healed, then withered and peeled, then tore open again. It was a sensory overload that bypassed pain and went straight to existential terror.
"You’re not even a man anymore, Apollo," Rex whispered, his face inches from Apollo’s convulsing features. "You’re just a collection of broken memories and failed ideals."
Rex then increased the gravitational pressure to its absolute limit. The ground beneath Apollo shattered completely, sending him plummeting into a crater of his own blood and debris.
Rex descended slowly, hovering above the pit like a dark god, his cape billowing in the chronal wind.
"I’m going to leave you here, Apollo," Rex said, his voice echoing with finality. "Not dead... Death would be too merciful..."
"You will live in this moment forever..."
"Every second, the rifts will reopen..."
"Every second, you will watch them choose me over you..."
"Every second, you will feel your bones break again and again."
Rex raised his hand one last time, gathering a sphere of pure, compressed void energy. "Welcome to eternity."

Rex descended into the crater like a predator circling a wounded animal that refused to stop twitching. The air in the pit was thick enough to choke on, saturated with the metallic tang of Apollo’s blood, the sulfurous stench of burnt divine essence, and the nauseating sweetness of the chronal distortions bleeding from the rifts.
"You’re still breathing, Apollo," Rex observed, his voice dripping with a perverse fascination. "Even after everything..."
"Your body is clinging to life like a parasite..."
"Tell me... does that make you feel righteous? Does your heart beating against those shattered ribs feel like victory?"
Rex didn’t wait for an answer. He wanted to see the exact moment the light died in Apollo’s eyes, but he wasn’t ready to let it happen yet.
He wanted to prolong the sunset.

Rex raised both hands, fingers splayed, and began to weave a complex web of Gravity Manipulation and Temporal Distortion. He wasn’t just crushing Apollo anymore; he was beginning to manipulate the very concept of Apollo’s physical presence in space time.
VROOOOOO THUMMM
The sound was low, subsonic, vibrating through the marrow of Apollo’s bones. Rex began to twist the gravity around Apollo’s limbs into spiraling funnels.
"Let’s try something different... Let’s see what happens when your body exists in two different moments at once."
With a flick of his wrists, Rex forced a temporal overlap. Apollo’s left arm was suddenly thrust five seconds into the future, while his right arm remained in the present.
The biological dissonance was catastrophic. The nervous system screamed as it tried to process signals from two different points simultaneously.
"AAAAAAGGHHHH... GAAAAH!" Apollo’s scream was torn from his throat as his muscles tore themselves apart from the inside out, trying to move toward a future that his present self hadn’t reached yet.
His tendons snapped like overextended rubber bands.
SNAP. TWANG.
Rex watched, utterly unconcerned with the horror, his mind analyzing the magical feedback. ’Interesting...’
’The cellular regeneration is trying to compensate for the temporal lag, but it’s creating a feedback loop of agony.’
"Look at them again, Apollo," Rex commanded, his voice cutting through the wet gurgling of Apollo’s breathing. "Don’t look away now..."
"The best part is coming..."
The rifts around them pulsed brighter, turning from sickly gold to a deep, bruised purple. The images of Talyra, Aisella, Nerith, Mireya, and Amelia became more vivid and more interactive.

Through the temporal manipulation, Rex made the images bleed into the real world. Pale, ghostly hands from the rifts reached out, stroking Apollo’s bloodied face while the images of the women continued their obscene, ecstatic surrender to Rex’s shadow.
"Feel them, Apollo," Rex whispered, leaning down until his mask nearly touched Apollo’s forehead. "Feel their touch..."
"Feel how they crave the darkness you tried to protect them from."
Rex then activated his Telekinesis to its full, horrifying potential. He didn’t just lift Apollo; he began to pull Apollo’s body apart at a molecular level.
He used telekinetic micro forces to pry open the wounds Rex had already made, widening them with excruciating precision.
SQUELCH. SLICE.
"Every nerve ending is a string on a harp, Apollo," Rex murmured, his hands moving like a conductor’s. "And I am going to play a masterpiece."

Rex began to ’play’ the harp. With precise telekinetic pokes, he would stimulate Apollo’s pain receptors to their absolute maximum capacity, then instantly freeze the nerve signals with Time Manipulation so the pain never faded; it only accumulated.
"This is called ’Stasis Pain,’" Rex explained conversationally as he drove a fist into Apollo’s already collapsed lung.
THUD CRUNCH.
"The pain doesn’t pass... It doesn’t dull."
"It simply stacks... One second of agony becomes two, then four, then eight..."
Apollo’s eyes rolled back in his head. His body was no longer responding to conscious commands; it was merely a vessel for pure, unadulterated torment.

His jaw hung slack, blood dripping in steady rhythm onto the debris. He was trapped in a prison of his own flesh, where every heartbeat felt like a hammer blow and every breath felt like swallowing broken glass.
Rex suddenly stood upright, his aura flaring in a massive, violet-black supernova that pushed back the edges of the rifts. "But you’re still too conscious, Apollo... Too present."
Rex raised his palm toward the sky. "Let’s deepen the hole."
He unleashed a concentrated Gravity Well directly beneath Apollo. The ground didn’t just break; it collapsed into a localized singularity.

Apollo was dragged down into a crushing vortex of stone and blood. As he fell, Rex unleashed a barrage of Temporal Bolts—streaks of chronal energy that struck Apollo repeatedly, each one aging a different part of his body by decades in a millisecond.
ZAP CRACKLE BOOM.
One leg withered into bone and desiccated flesh; another remained young and bleeding; his torso became a patchwork of aged skin and fresh lacerations.
The sensory overload was so intense that Apollo’s brain began to misfire, causing him to hallucinate that he was being flayed alive while simultaneously being frozen in ice.
Rex hovered above the swirling vortex of destruction, his cape snapping in the supernatural wind, watching the spectacle with the detached curiosity of a scientist watching a chemical reaction.
"Don’t die yet, Apollo," Rex called down into the chaos, his voice carrying easily over the howling winds. "We haven’t even begun to explore the limits of your suffering."

chapters.title: Chapter 1188. A Toy That No Longer Produced an Interesting Sound
paragraphs: The transition through the failing temporal spiral left Rex suspended in a pocket of absolute, ringing silence. For several precious seconds, he was alone with his own thoughts, a luxury he rarely afforded himself.
His mind flickered back to the anomaly. The figure at the far edge of the domain had not reappeared.

Divine Perception, still humming as a passive subroutine in his consciousness, continued its relentless scan of the surrounding space. It returned nothing: no signature, no residual energy, and no indication that anyone god or demon had been watching.
Rex filed the anomaly away with cold, surgical precision. It would be a problem to solve later, a thread to pull once the war concluded.

But right now, there was a more immediate audience waiting. Beyond the doorway of this collapsing reality lay a corridor lined with ten thousand witnesses, and they would not wait patiently for their entertainment.
As he prepared to reemerge, Rex considered his next move with the same ruthless practicality he applied to every tactical decision. He weighed two futures.
In one, he would simply execute Apollo the instant they breached the corridor—a quick, clean death that denied the spectators any theater.
In the other, he would drag this broken, humiliated husk before them as a living monument to the futility of resistance.
Both had merit. But only one of them would allow him to watch Elizabeth’s face as she witnessed the true depth of his depravity.
Only one would allow him to gauge, in real time, exactly how much terror a single demonstration could sow through the hearts of an entire army.
He had already decided. In the wreckage of this dying domain, he had chosen his path.
He would not make it quick.
Rex stepped forward, his boots crunching on bone fragments and dried blood. He loomed over Apollo’s ruined form like a monument to inevitability.
The Apostle’s breathing was a wet, stuttering thing, the sound of air struggling through lungs that refused to stop functioning despite their collapse.
Rex brought his boot down onto Apollo’s already shattered right leg. He didn’t stomp; he pressed... Slowly... Deliberately...

He applied pressure with the measured force of a man testing the ripeness of fruit. The sound that followed was sickeningly distinct: the wet, splintering CRUNCH of bone fragments grinding against one another as the femur gave way for the second time.
Because Apollo had no strength left to tense his muscles, there was no resistance to soften the impact. The injury didn’t just break; it disintegrated.
Apollo’s body jerked once, a reflexive spasm of agony that found no outlet. His mouth opened, but no scream emerged, only a single, ragged exhale that sounded like wind through dead leaves.
Rex wasn’t done. His hands reached down, gloved fingers wrapping around Apollo’s left arm.
He gripped the shoulder joint, feeling the heat of the infection and the blood beneath the skin. With careful, unhurried precision, Rex began to twist.
He moved with the patience of a craftsman, rotating the limb millimeter by millimeter, feeling the tendons stretch to their breaking point before they finally surrendered.
SQUELCH. GRIND. POP.

The shoulder joint separated from the socket with a wet, grinding sound that echoed off the walls of the crumbling chamber. The arm hung at an impossible angle, held on only by ravaged muscle and torn skin.
Apollo made no sound at all now. His eyes had lost their focus, staring blankly at some distant point beyond reality, his pupils blown wide as his consciousness retreated further into the dark.
With each new injury Rex inflicted, the man seemed to sink deeper into the cracked floor, his body collapsing further into itself, a hollowed-out shell that had nothing left to resist the inevitable.

There was a particular, nauseating quality to the silence that followed each new injury, a stillness that felt less like unconsciousness and more like the profound resignation of a man who had simply stopped believing that any response he could produce would alter the inevitable.

Apollo wasn’t just broken; he was hollowed out. The spark that had made him a threat, the divine fire that had once burned with such righteous conviction, had been systematically extinguished by Rex’s relentless cruelty.

Rex watched this collapse with the detached precision of an entomologist observing a beetle pinned to a board. He noted the specific way Apollo’s pupils refused to track movement, the way his breathing had shifted from labored gasps to a shallow, rattling wheeze.

He filed this under Psychological Attrition, a data point to be analyzed later. Even this, even the specific, visceral texture of a person’s complete spiritual surrender, held its own small, perverse measure of interest.
"I’ve enjoyed this quite thoroughly," Rex said, his voice cutting through the stagnant air like a scalpel.

He stood over the barely moving wreck of the man he had once called a friend, his expression settling into the flat, faintly bored look of a child who had finished with a toy that no longer produced an interesting sound. "But I find myself growing impatient...
"The audience is waiting, Apollo... And I hate to keep them waiting for the finale."
Rex raised one hand toward the dying sky of the domain.
Violet black energy began to hemorrhage from his fingertips, drawn from the Mark of Lust Authority that had never truly left him. The energy didn’t just glow; it writhed like a living shadow.

Simultaneously, the fragments of his shattered mask—pieces of obsidian slick material—scattered across the blood-soaked floor since Apollo’s earlier desperate strike began to stir. They levitated in slow, unnatural spirals, caught in a localized gravitational well.
SHHHHH VROOOOOM
The fragments drifted upward, humming with malevolent intent, converging across the upper half of Rex’s face in a seamless dance of reconstruction.
The reformation took only seconds: the violet surface knitted itself back together, sealing away the human features Apollo had exposed with such devastating effort.
The mask didn’t just repair itself; it reasserted itself, restoring the terrifying visage of Lord Xerollion completely, as though the damage had never occurred.

Rex rolled his shoulders once beneath the renewed armor, testing the fit like a man adjusting a well-worn coat, feeling the familiar, comfortable weight of his godhood settling back into place around whatever remained of his humanity.
The domain itself was dying around them. The slow, violet pulse that had once sustained this pocket dimension was now reduced to a stuttering, sickly flicker.
Whole sections of the floor beneath them simply ceased to exist, plunging into an absolute, hungry darkness that seemed to lap at the edges of the remaining light.

Rex glanced at the temporal readings flickering across his inner vision. He had perhaps another sixty seconds before the structural integrity of this reality failed completely, depositing them both somewhere considerably less controlled than his own doorway.
In any other circumstance, that would be a tactical disadvantage. But Rex was not any other circumstance.
A minute was more than sufficient to deliver a killing blow.
"One last lesson before we depart, Apostle," Rex whispered, the mask’s voice carrying an unnatural, layered resonance. "In the end, light doesn’t defeat darkness..."
"It just provides the contrast necessary for darkness to be seen."

chapters.title: Chapter 1189. A Sack of Broken Meat Before Ten Thousand Witnesses
paragraphs: Xerollion reached down, his movements fluid and utterly devoid of exertion. His gloved fingers closed around what remained of Apollo’s collarbone, the fabric now fused with congealed blood and torn flesh.

With a casual jerk that made Apollo’s shattered vertebrae protest with a wet CRUNCH, Rex hauled the ruined body off the floor. Apollo’s head lolled backward, his neck limp, his mouth agape in a silent, unconscious plea for an end that would not come.
With his free hand, Rex reached into the very fabric of the failing reality. He didn’t just move through space; he tore it.
His claws raked across the air, leaving glowing violet gashes that bled raw chronal energy.
SHHHHH VROOOOOM
The spiral tore open with the sound of rending metal. The violet-black vortex spun into existence, a hungry mouth of swirling void that demanded to be fed.

Rex stepped into the abyss, dragging Apollo’s broken corpse behind him like a trophy of war. As they crossed the threshold, the portal snapped shut behind them with the force of a collapsing star, swallowing the last gasps of the dying domain.
Behind them, unseen by any living eye, the final remnants of that reality imploded into absolute nothingness, an experiment concluded, its purpose served, its existence erased.
BOOM.
The return to the northern corridor was not a gentle landing. They materialized in a violent burst of dark energy that cracked the stone floor beneath them.
Rex and Apollo dropped onto the solid granite in the exact coordinates where they had vanished, appearing to the assembled soldiers as if they had never left, only worse.
What had felt like hours of agony in the void passed in what seemed to the witnesses like mere seconds of supernatural displacement.
The effect was instantaneous. The cacophony of war, the clash of steel, the screams of dying men, and the thunder of magic died in an instant.

Every fighter engaged in that stretch of the corridor froze mid-swing. The news of their reappearance rippled through the ranks like a physical shockwave, a wave of turning heads and dropped weapons that spread from the center outward.

Ten thousand soldiers, both divine and demonic, stood in a terrifying, unnatural silence. It was the kind of silence that precedes a catastrophe, the held breath of an army about to witness something that would sear itself into their collective memory forever.
Then, they saw him.

Apollo Brightsoul, the Apostle of Life, the golden beacon of Aethelgard, the hero whose name had been whispered in prayers for generations, hung from Xerollion’s grip like something discarded, something broken beyond recognition.
He was no longer a man; he was a crime scene.

His body was a visceral ruin from head to foot. Blood, thick and arterial crimson, soaked every visible inch of his tan skin, dripping steadily onto the pristine stone floor with a rhythmic DRIP... DRIP... DRIP.
One arm hung useless at his side, severed at the shoulder by the grinding force of Rex’s earlier torment, the muscle tissue frayed like old rope.
His legs were bent at grotesque, impossible angles, with shattered femurs and twisted tibias that made it clear neither would ever carry the weight of a hero again.
Most devastating of all was the absence of light. There was no golden aura.
No defiant spark of divine essence flickered in his eyes.
No last stand.
There was nothing left but the raw, wet, bleeding evidence of complete and total annihilation. The hero was dead; only the meat remained.
The silence that swallowed the northern corridor in that first heartbeat had a texture—something visceral and suffocating—that no survivor would ever be able to articulate.
It was not the silence of exhaustion, though thousands of battle-worn soldiers stood within it. It was the silence of a collective reality fracturing.

It was the quiet, hollow interval between the moment humanity believes its strongest champion is invincible and the moment they understand, with bone-deep certainty, exactly how wrong that belief had been.
Valentina Von Starlight stood frozen at the precipice of her crumbling formation. Her face, usually a mask of regal composure, had drained of every drop of color, leaving her skin as pale as marble.
Her hands, which had commanded armies through fifty years of relentless crisis, now trembled visibly at her sides, a betrayal of her body that she couldn’t suppress.
The unshakable confidence she had carried into this corridor—the belief that she stood among the apex of Aethelgard’s power—had been pulverized before ten thousand witnesses.
She was watching the second most powerful being in the entire city reduced to a sack of broken meat and arterial spray.
She had personally taught Apollo advanced ward theory when he was seventeen.
She had mentored him.
She had seen his potential bloom into the finest Apostle of Life this generation had produced.

Now, staring at the twisted, mangled ruin of his limbs and the hollow emptiness in his eyes, she was confronted with a truth that defied her entire life’s work: all that divine training had meant nothing against the monster standing before them.
Beside her, Morwenna Nightwing had gone rigid with a primal horror. One hand rose unconsciously to cover her mouth as her breath came in shallow, ragged hitches.
The complex magical calculations that had been racing through her mind and the theories she had been testing since her private conversation with Rex days earlier simply stopped.

They were incinerated, replaced by a single, overwhelming animal recognition: she had been studying a predator whose scale she had catastrophically underestimated. This wasn’t a rival power; this was an apex catastrophe.
"APOLLO!"

The scream tore through the silence as Elliot Von Starlight lunged forward, his face a contorted mask of grief and fury. He didn’t even make it two steps before three armored soldiers threw themselves across his path, catching him bodily.
They dragged him back, their boots skidding on the stone as he thrashed with inhuman strength.
"Let me go!" Elliot shrieked, his voice cracking and breaking into raw sobs. "That’s my friend!"
"Let me go; I have to get to him. I have to help him—!"
"You’ll die!" one of the soldiers barked, his voice low, urgent, and terrified.
He dug his fingers into Elliot’s armor to anchor him. "Look at him, kid!"
"Look at what’s holding him!"
"You won’t even take five steps before you’re gutted like the rest of us!"

Evelyn Astralight stood locked in place beside the struggling Elliot, her earlier suspicions burned away by the cold fire of raw terror. The realization hit her with the force of a physical blow: whatever power had been moving beneath Aethelgard’s foundations for the past year existed on a scale that made every previous war look like a child’s skirmish.
For the last hour, she had been trying to place a familiar cadence in a masked stranger’s movements, a pattern she couldn’t quite name.
Now, staring at the man holding Apollo aloft like a discarded, blood-soaked doll, that familiarity no longer mattered.
Whatever she had suspected, the reality had already outgrown her comprehension. Her theories could not contain the truth, which was too big, too cruel, and too violent.
And further up the corridor, among the front ranks of the Aethelgard soldiers still struggling to maintain formation, the final blow to their morale landed.
"APOLLO! NO! APOLLO—"

Rex Rexilion screamed Apollo’s name with a raw, cracking desperation that vibrated through the stone floor. He threw himself forward with such ferocity that two soldiers had to brace themselves against each other to hold him back, their faces strained with the effort of restraining his agonized grief.

His face was a perfect, devastating mask of helpless loss, a performance of such exquisite pain that not a single witness in that corridor, not one of the ten thousand souls watching, thought to question the sincerity of his tears.

chapters.title: Chapter 1190. Your Numbers Won’t Accomplish What a God-Touched Hero Could Not
paragraphs: On the opposite side of the corridor, among the ranks of the Underlayer, the atmosphere was starkly different. There was no horror here, no paralyzed disbelief.
Instead, there was something far more unsettling: satisfaction.
Cassandra Vexmoor stood with her arms crossed, her pale features illuminated by the intermittent violet flickers of the dying corridor.
Beside her, Gorvasha Bloodtusk let out a low, rumbling sound that might have been a chuckle if the situation weren’t so grim. Their expressions were open, undisguised displays of triumph.
They watched the culmination of months of infiltration, manipulation, and bloodshed unfold exactly as their architect had promised. Neither spoke.

Words would have only cheapened the moment. The silence between them carried the quiet, predatory pride of soldiers watching a grand campaign reach the precise, bloody conclusion their master had designed.
DRIP. DRIP. DRIP.
The corridor was filled with a silence so absolute it felt physical, a weight pressing down on the lungs of every living being present.

The only sounds that dared to puncture it were the scattered, broken sobs of the wounded and the low, ragged breathing of thousands of soldiers who no longer knew whether they were witnessing a battle or a public execution.

Somewhere in the shattered wreckage of the Aethelgard formation, a young soldier began to weep openly, a high, keening sound of pure terror, and no one moved to comfort him. No one even dared to ask him to stop.

Xerollion, sensing the moment had reached its peak of psychological torment, moved with terrifying deliberation. His free hand reached up, fingers tangling roughly into Apollo’s matted, blood-soaked hair.

With a brutal jerk that forced Apollo’s neck to crack audibly, CRACK, he lifted the hero’s head. He forced the ruined, barely conscious face upward, positioning it like a grotesque offering so that both armies could see the extent of the devastation.
When Xerollion spoke, he didn’t shout. He didn’t need to.
His voice carried across the entire length of the corridor with a cold, commanding clarity that seemed to vibrate through the very marrow of every soul present.
"Look at him," Xerollion commanded, the words dripping with venomous contempt. "Look closely at your hero."
"Look at the golden paragon of your faith... The one you trusted to shield you from the dark..."
"The one you believed would carry Aethelgard to salvation this day...
He paused, letting the silence stretch like a tightening noose. His violet black eyes, cold and unblinking behind the mask, swept slowly across the frozen ranks of Aethelgard’s soldiers.

He drank in their reaction: the way their eyes flinched away from Apollo’s mangled features, the way their knuckles whitened on their sword hilts, and the visible tremors of terror that rippled through the formation like wind through dead grass.
He fed on their despair.

"You came down here believing you carried justice in your hands," Xerollion continued, his voice growing harder, each syllable cutting deeper than any blade. "You believed you could descend into our domain and punish the Underlayer for sins you imagined we committed."
"You came with the bloated, rotting arrogance of conquerors, never once stopping to ask yourselves the only question that mattered..."
He leaned forward slightly, the shadow of his mask falling over Apollo’s unconscious face.
"...whether you were actually prepared for what truly waits for you beneath the foundations of your own city."

Xerollion raised Apollo’s shattered frame higher, muscles in his arm coiling with effortless strength as he displayed the full, gruesome extent of the devastation to every witness gathered in that corridor.

He turned slowly in place, performing a methodical and deliberate rotation to ensure that no section of the assembled armies, on either side, could later claim they had not witnessed the truth with their own eyes.
The light from the dying corridor glinted off the wet blood coating Apollo’s exposed ribs and the twisted metal of his broken armor.
"This is the result of your arrogance," Xerollion declared.

His voice began to climb, gaining volume and power, echoing off the ancient stone walls with such force that the corridor itself seemed to shrink, the ceiling pressing down under the psychological weight of his words. "Your Apostle of Life, Aethelgard’s last hope, the beacon of your salvation is nothing more than a broken toy to me."
A wet SQUELCH sounded as Apollo’s head lolled to the side, his jaw hanging at an unnatural angle.

"I did not need my army to do this," Xerollion continued, his gloved hand tightening around Apollo’s hair until the scalp audibly stretched. "I did not need the corridor, or the trap, or any of the thousand advantages this ground has given me today."

"I did this alone, with my own two hands, while your finest soldiers stood four hundred meters away, watching the light in the sky and praying, praying that it meant something other than what it truly meant."

He leaned forward, his masked visage casting a shadow that seemed to swallow the light. "And if this is what your strongest can suffer, if this is the limit of your divine protection, then I want every one of you to imagine to truly feel in your bones exactly what waits for the rest of you."
The effect was catastrophic. A wave of raw, unadulterated terror rippled through the Aethelgard ranks like a plague.

The formation didn’t just waver; it began to dissolve. Soldiers began edging backward instinctively, their boots scuffing against the stone in a desperate attempt to create distance between themselves and the monster.

Field commanders, men who had survived countless siege battles, exchanged panicked, hollow glances, their hands frozen on their sword hilts, their minds screaming that there was no tactical solution for what they were seeing.
In the third rank, the sharp CLATTER of a young soldier’s spear hitting the floor rang out like a death knell. Nobody moved to retrieve it. Nobody dared to breathe.
"This isn’t finished!"
A captain near the front, one of the few officers who had maintained his composure through the entire duel, his armor still relatively intact, stepped forward on legs that visibly shook.
He raised his voice in a desperate attempt to reclaim authority, though it cracked halfway through the sentence, betraying his terror. "We still outnumber you three to one!"
"We still have our formation! We can still—"
"Can you?"

Xerollion turned his masked face toward the man with unhurried, terrifying interest. He didn’t move to attack; he simply observed, as though genuinely curious about the captain’s delusions rather than threatened by the interruption.
The silence that followed was heavier than before, more intimate, more deadly.

"Your Apostle of Life just spent the better part of an hour trying to erase me from existence," Xerollion said, his voice dropping to a conversational whisper that somehow reached every ear in the corridor. "He fought with a portion of his goddess flowing directly through his veins, a power that should have incinerated anything in its path."
"And he failed... He fucking broke."
Xerollion took a single step toward the captain, the violet energy at his feet pulsing like a heartbeat.
VROOOOM.

"Tell me honestly, Captain," Xerollion asked, tilting his head with a predator’s curiosity. "With all that righteous fury and those three to one odds... what exactly do you believe your numbers are going to accomplish that a god-touched hero could not?"

chapters.title: Chapter 1191. The Predator Wasn’t Waiting in the Dark... He Was Already at Your Table
paragraphs: The captain had no answer. The question hung in the air like a guillotine blade suspended by a single fraying thread.
Around him, the silence was absolutely not a supportive silence but a hollow, shameful one. No lieutenant stepped forward to bolster his courage; no sergeant offered a tactical counterargument.
The authority he had spent decades cultivating evaporated in an instant, leaving behind only a frightened man in expensive armor.
After a long, humiliating silence that seemed to stretch into eternity, the captain lowered his head, his shoulders slumping, and retreated into the ranks.
He did not speak again. He simply became another frightened ghost in a corridor full of them.
Standing on the periphery of Valentina’s crumbling forces, Elizabeth Von Starlight watched the carnage unfold with an expression carefully sculpted into one of shock and visceral horror.
To any observer, she was another victim of the moment’s terror. But beneath the mask, her mind was a storm of cold calculation and nauseating guilt.

She was the only person in that entire corridor who knew with absolute, terrifying certainty exactly whose voice was speaking and exactly how every syllable of this psychological slaughter had been rehearsed in the dark.

She had known for weeks in the abstract exactly what Rex was capable of. She had seen the blueprints of his ambition, understood the terrifying scope of his power, and grasped exactly how far he intended to push this war until Aethelgard snapped like dry kindling.

But knowing it in theory was nothing like watching it performed. Watching him dismantle the city’s faith in front of ten thousand souls who trusted her, who had marched into this trap believing her own Key had opened a path to justice, felt like swallowing molten lead.
The betrayal sat like a stone in her chest, crushing her lungs.
Her hand moved instinctively to the hilt of a dagger at her belt. Her knuckles turned white as she gripped the weapon, but there was no plan behind the gesture.

No strike to deliver, no assassination to attempt. It was merely the reflexive spasm of a body that demanded action even when the mind attached to it understood that resistance was not just futile; it was suicidal.
’God help us,’ she thought, her inner voice a faint whisper against the roaring terror of the crowd. ’He isn’t just killing our heroes... He’s killing our reality.’
Xerollion sensed the shift in the air. He could feel the last vestiges of hope bleeding out of the Aethelgard formation.

He turned his attention back to the masses, his presence expanding until he seemed to fill every inch of the stone corridor. When he spoke again, his voice dropped into a cold, quiet register—a register so intimate and controlled that it somehow carried more menace than any scream.
It reached the furthest edges of the corridor like a poisonous vapor.

"Aethelgard will never win against the Underlayer," Xerollion said, each word measured, each syllable a nail in a coffin. "Because you never truly understood the nature of the enemy you were fighting."

"You built your entire campaign on the comforting delusion that the worst thing beneath your city was some ancient demon king with delusions of grandeur, a monster you could identify, name, and eventually slay."
He paused, tilting his head as if listening to the heartbeat of the city above them.
"You never considered that something far worse than any demon might simply be wearing a kind face and standing at your dinner table."
"You never considered that the predator wasn’t waiting in the dark but was already walking among you."
The violet energy pulsing from his boots flared brighter, casting jagged, dancing shadows that looked like grasping claws against the walls.
"Today," Xerollion promised, his voice dropping to a deadly, final whisper, "I am going to give you a lesson you will never forget."
"I am going to show you what happens when your world finally meets its true master."

Xerollion shifted his attention with the slow, deliberate grace of an executioner. His free hand rose, fingers splayed like claws, and positioned itself inches from Apollo’s exposed, blood-slicked throat.
Almost immediately, the air around his fingertips began to warp. Violet black energy thick as tar and crackling with malevolent static began to coil and spiral around his digits.
BZZZZT CRACKLE.
The sound was wrong; it wasn’t the clean hum of holy magic but something hungry, something that sounded like teeth grinding against bone.
The entire corridor seemed to contract. Ten thousand lungs drew one single, collective breath and held it, trapped in the throat of a thousand terrified souls.

Every eye in the chamber—soldier, commander, spy, and monster alike—was fixed on that gathering orb of annihilation. The certainty of the coming atrocity was so absolute that the air itself felt pressurized, as if the world were bracing for an impact that would shatter reality.
"NO! STOP IT! STOP!"
Elliot’s scream tore through the suffocating silence. It wasn’t the battle cry of a prince or the roar of a warrior; it was the raw, guttural shriek of a child witnessing his world burn.
He thrashed against the grip of the three soldiers holding him, his boots scraping uselessly against the stone.
"DON’T DO THIS!" he howled, his voice breaking into wet, desperate sobs. "Please, whatever you are, whatever you want, just stop!"
"He hasn’t done anything to deserve this!"
"Take me instead!"
"Kill me, kill all of us, just don’t...! PLEASE—"
His pleas bounced off the stone walls, hollow and pathetic, swallowed whole by the predatory silence that followed.

Valentina Von Starlight took one involuntary step forward, her hand outstretched as if she could somehow bridge the impossible chasm separating her from the center of the carnage. But she stopped mid-motion, her boot freezing on the stone.
The distance—the sheer, yawning gulf of space between her position and the two figures rendered her authority, her experience, and her very existence utterly meaningless.
For fifty years, she had been the immovable object, the strategist who could solve any crisis with preparation and steel.

Now, standing at the edge of this abyss, she understood for the first time in her long life the true, terrifying meaning of powerlessness. She wasn’t a commander anymore; she was merely a spectator to her own extinction.
Xerollion ignored the chaos. He ignored the screams. His focus was singular, honed to the point of lethal perfection.
He looked down at Apollo not with hatred, which would have required effort, but with the detached curiosity of a man observing an insect before crushing it.
"Goodbye, Apollo Brightsoul," Xerollion said.
His voice had dropped to something final, something hollow, utterly devoid of mercy or hesitation. It was the sound of a door closing forever.
"The hero who failed to protect anything that ever mattered to him..."
"The light that burned out before the dawn."
The violet black energy at his fingertips reached its critical mass. It began to pulse with a rhythmic, deadly intensity—THUM THUM... THUM THUM—matching the terrified heartbeat of everyone present.
The light grew so bright it cast harsh, jagged shadows that danced wildly across Apollo’s broken features, making his death throes look like a grotesque puppet show.

The entire corridor held its breath in an absolute, suffocating silence. Time itself seemed to stretch, thinning out until there was nothing left but the glow at Xerollion’s fingertips and the terrifying expectation of the final second, the moment that would decide whether the Apostle of Life would die as a martyr or be erased as a failure.

The question hung in the air like a guillotine blade suspended by a single fraying thread.
Around him, the silence was absolutely not a supportive silence but a hollow, shameful one.
No lieutenant stepped forward to bolster his courage; no sergeant offered a tactical counterargument.
The authority he had spent decades cultivating evaporated in an instant, leaving behind only a frightened man in expensive armor.
After a long, humiliating silence that seemed to stretch into eternity, the captain lowered his head, his shoulders slumping, and retreated into the ranks.
He did not speak again.
He simply became another frightened ghost in a corridor full of them.
Standing on the periphery of Valentina’s crumbling forces, Elizabeth Von Starlight watched the carnage unfold with an expression carefully sculpted into one of shock and visceral horror.
To any observer, she was another victim of the moment’s terror.

She was the only person in that entire corridor who knew with absolute, terrifying certainty exactly whose voice was speaking and exactly how every syllable of this psychological slaughter had been rehearsed in the dark.
She had known for weeks in the abstract exactly what Rex was capable of.
She had seen the blueprints of his ambition, understood the terrifying scope of his power, and grasped exactly how far he intended to push this war until Aethelgard snapped like dry kindling.

The betrayal sat like a stone in her chest, crushing her lungs.

No strike to deliver, no assassination to attempt.

chapters.title: Chapter 1192. The Fall of the Golden Apostle
paragraphs: The violet-black energy at Xerollion’s fingertips reached its breaking point. It didn’t explode; it didn’t roar.
Instead, it condensed into a single, impossibly thin needle of absolute annihilation.
SHIIIIIIIIIIING.

The energy left his fingertips in one clean, surgical line. It crossed the final few inches between them faster than any human eye could register, slicing through the air with a sound like silk tearing.

It passed through Apollo Brightsoul’s throat with a precision that was more terrifying than any messy slaughter. There was no spray, no arterial fountain, just a small, cauterized dark mark where the violet black light had passed through his vertebrae, severing his spine and his life in the same microsecond.
But Xerollion was not done with his prize.
As the blade of energy severed the flesh, Xerollion’s other hand shot forward, palm open. "Mine."
VROOOOOM WHIRRRRR.

A different kind of magic ignited something deeper, more ancient, and infinitely more cruel. His palm pressed against Apollo’s chest, and suddenly, the golden fire that had defined the Apostle’s entire existence began to leak out.

It wasn’t blood; it was a shimmering, ethereal essence that screamed without making a sound. Through the sheer force of Soul Manipulation, Xerollion reached past the physical armor and the broken bones, grasping the very core of Apollo’s being.

Apollo’s eyes flew open one last time, not with pain, but with the recognition of his own soul being forcibly evicted from his body. The golden light flickered violently, fighting against the encroaching violet darkness.
With a wet, spiritual THWIP, the essence was wrenched free, coiling around Xerollion’s arm like a captured star, pulsing with the fading rhythm of a dying god.
Then came the final, brutal punctuation.

With a casual flick of his wrist, Xerollion’s free hand moved in a horizontal arc. A blade of compressed shadow manifested for a heartbeat, and with a sickening CRUNCH SLICE, Apollo’s head was severed completely from his shoulders.

The corridor around them had already been reduced to something barely recognizable as a passage. Sections of the ceiling hung in loose, cracked slabs, and the torchlight from the natural crystal veins flickered unevenly where the stone itself had been fractured by the accumulated violence.
Into that wrecked, half-lit space, the single sound of Apollo’s body meeting the floor arrived with an outsized, terrible clarity.
Xerollion released his grip.
The headless corpse of Apollo Brightsoul, the Apostle of Life, the hero of Aethelgard, fell the short distance to the corridor floor.

His body landed without ceremony, one arm folding beneath him at an angle that no longer mattered to a body that could no longer feel. The severed head rolled a few feet away, its eyes still glassy with the shock of its own departure.
THUD.
The sound was quiet, almost apologetic, entirely wrong for the weight of what it represented. It carried further through that dead silence than any scream could have.
The golden light was gone.
The hero was dead.
And the soul, the only part of him that could still feel agony, was now trapped in the fist of the monster who intended to make eternity a torment.
For a fraction of a second, nobody moved. The world seemed to have stopped spinning, held captive by the horrific image of the fallen light.
Then the corridor broke apart into chaos.

It didn’t begin with a roar or a charge. It started as a single, inhuman wail from somewhere deep in the third rank of Aethelgard’s formation, a sound stripped of language, a raw vocalization of pure psychological collapse.
That sound acted like a spark in a powder keg. Within seconds, the sound spread outward in every direction at once.
The disciplined ranks of Aethelgard dissolved into a writhing mass of broken men. Soldiers dropped to their knees with wet THUDs, their weapons clattering to the stone like discarded toys.
Men who had stormed battlefields and survived sieges simply folded, their minds snapping under the impossible weight of seeing their god-touched champion reduced to meat and bone.
Valentina’s voice rose above the cacophony a heartbeat later.
"Apollo... no... Apollo." Her voice cracked violently in the middle of his name.

The iron-willed matriarch, the pillar of the city, finally shattered. Her rigid composure gave way entirely as her knees buckled; she stumbled forward, catching herself against the shoulder of a nearby soldier who was too numb to even notice her weight.

Morwenna pressed both hands over her mouth, her knuckles white, her eyes wide and glassy with a thousand-yard stare. She had survived thirty years of political assassination attempts and shadow wars, but she found that none of it had prepared her for this kind of visceral, spiritual annihilation.
In the second rank, a seasoned captain who had held his position through the entire duel simply sat down where he stood. He didn’t retreat; he didn’t flee.

He simply ceased to function, his sword still clutched in a white-knuckled grip as he stared at nothingness. Near him, a young soldier began reciting something under her breath, a rapid, frantic litany of prayers or fragments of scripture.
Her lips moved in a desperate rhythm, but no sound came out, only the visible tremor of her jaw.
On the Underlayer’s side, the reaction carried a different, more unsettling texture. There was no cheering yet.
Even the hardened demons and bloodthirsty orcs who had trained for months for this exact moment found themselves momentarily stunned.
They stood in a state of quiet, predatory awe, like wolves watching a lion demonstrate the true meaning of slaughter.
Cassandra’s arms, folded with practiced indifference throughout the fighting, dropped slowly to her sides.
Gorvasha’s grip on his hammer tightened until the leather wrap creaked audibly under his palm, his eyes fixed on the corpse with a grim fascination.
And then, there was Rex.
Farther back in the formation, Rex, the architect of this nightmare, tore free of the two soldiers restraining him.
He did it with a burst of strength that looked, to every horrified eye watching, like pure, desperate grief overriding physical limitation.
He threw himself forward, screaming Apollo’s name with a raw, ragged horror painted across his features. It was a masterpiece of deception, the finest piece of theater he had performed all day.

He ran toward the carnage with the desperation of a man losing his soul, and the performance landed perfectly on an audience too shattered to notice anything except the shape of their own shared devastation.
In the center of this storm of grief, Elliot Von Starlight stood frozen.
His eyes were locked on the crumpled, headless shape of his friend’s body. Something behind his pupils was changing visible, terrifying degrees.

His irises seemed to contract into pinpricks of molten fire while his jaw set into a hard, unnatural line. Whatever was breaking inside him went deeper than grief; it was the sound of something ancient and terrible cracking open.
It was the specific, total detonation of a man who had never touched the outer edges of his own capacity for rage, suddenly being handed the entire ocean of it at once.
"APOLLO!!!"
The scream tore out of him like a physical blade. It didn’t just echo; it tore through the air, vibrating the very stones of the corridor.
And then, the light came.
BOOOOOOOM.
White light exploded outward from every inch of his body. This wasn’t the controlled, disciplined glow of his usual heroic strikes; this was an uncontrolled supernova of raw, unmitigated fury.
The pressure wave hit like a physical hammer. Evelyn, who had been standing close enough to reach for his arm, was thrown backward off her feet as if struck by a battering ram.
She scrambled up, gasping for air, her eyes wide with terror as she watched her closest friend transform into something she no longer recognized.
The boy was gone. In his place stood something primal, something incandescent, something that looked ready to burn the entire world down just to spite the darkness.

chapters.title: Chapter 1193. Like a Child Throwing Stones at a Mountain
paragraphs: The corridor still reeked of scorched stone, ionized air, and the iron-sweet tang of blood, a smell that clung to the back of the throat like poison.

For a long moment after Apollo’s body finally settled into its grotesque stillness, the world seemed to have ceased to exist. Even the demons, creatures born of violence who had spent the last hour fighting for their very lives, stood frozen at the edges of the wreckage.

They were predators who had suddenly found themselves in the presence of something they didn’t understand: a silence that wasn’t peaceful but predatory, as if the very air were gathering itself for a second, a more devastating act.

Evelyn’s scream had already come and gone, a hoarse, broken sound that had drained the last of her strength. What remained was a silence so absolute it felt heavy, the kind of quiet that only follows something that has been irrevocably broken.
Then, Elliot moved.
He didn’t run; he ignited. He tore through the Underlayer’s stunned front ranks at a speed that defied physics, outstripping every display of agility he had shown during the earlier engagement.
Demon soldiers who would normally have intercepted any threat stood paralyzed, their instincts failing them as the white light wrapped around Elliot burned through the air.
FSHHHHHHH.
The heat was so intense that the stone beneath his boots cracked and spiderwebbed with every stride, scorching a path of molten glass through the center of the corridor.
He came to a halt directly in front of Xerollion. The proximity was suicidal.
The heat radiating off Elliot’s body was a physical wall, shimmering in waves that should have been unbearable even to the masked monster standing across from him.
Elliot’s face—the face that had always carried a spark of hope, a gentle smile, and a kindness—was gone. In its place was a mask of pure, undiluted hatred.
Tears cut hot, stinging tracks down cheeks flushed crimson with fury, his chest heaving as if his lungs were filled with liquid fire.
"YOU KILLED HIM!" Elliot screamed, his voice cracking like a whip. "YOU KILLED APOLLO!"
"YOU MONSTER...!"
"YOU FUCKING BASTARD!"
"HE WAS EVERYTHING TO US!"
His hands were shaking, not from terror, but from the sheer voltage of the power coursing through his veins. "MY FRIEND! MY BROTHER! HE GAVE EVERYTHING FOR AETHELGARD, AND YOU JUST TOOK IT!"
"YOU FUCKING TOOK IT LIKE IT MEANT NOTHING!"
Xerollion didn’t flinch. He didn’t even shift his stance.
His masked visage remained impassive, reflecting the white inferno of Elliot’s rage without being consumed by it.
"Yes," Xerollion answered.
His voice was terrifyingly calm, carrying not one trace of regret. It was the same level, almost conversational tone he had used when discussing tactics or weather.
"And now I imagine you intend to try avenging him."
The casual cruelty of the response was the final spark in the powder keg.
"AVENGING HIM...? I’M NOT JUST GOING TO AVENGE HIM!" Elliot’s roar was deafening, a sound that seemed to shake the very foundations of Aethelgard and Underlayer itself.

The white light around him surged upward in jagged, violent pillars, climbing brighter and brighter until it was blinding. Soldiers thirty meters back had to shield their eyes, their boots scraping backward in instinctive retreat from the supernova forming in the corridor.
"I AM GOING TO ERASE YOU FROM EXISTENCE!" Elliot screamed, his voice ascending into something inhuman, something primal. "I AM GOING TO TEAR YOUR SOUL APART PIECE BY PIECE!"
"I AM GOING TO BURN EVERY SHRED OF YOUR BEING UNTIL THERE IS ABSOLUTELY NOTHING LEFT BUT ASH AND MEMORY!"
"I WILL DESTROY YOU, XEROLLION! I WILL DESTROY EVERYTHING YOU ARE! "

The light became a solid wall of radiance, the air screaming as it was superheated. Elliot’s eyes were no longer human; they were twin suns of incandescent rage, focused entirely on the man who had stolen the light from their world.
Elliot exploded forward. This wasn’t a duel; it was an assassination attempt born of pure, unadulterated hatred.

He channeled every ounce of his grief, every fragment of his shattered hope, into the fundamental mechanics of his power. The white light didn’t just coat his skin anymore; it screamed, vibrating with such high frequency that the air itself began to superheat and hiss around him.
FSHHHHHHH.
He unleashed the full devastating output of Heroic Strike. It was, without question, the most violent display of raw power witnessed during the entire siege.
His fist, encased in a corona of incandescent white flame, tore through the air. The sheer displacement of oxygen created a sonic crack BOOM as he closed the distance.

The strike was aimed square at Xerollion’s sternum, carrying enough compressed kinetic energy to shatter a fortress gate. The launch was so violent that the stone floor beneath Elliot’s rear foot didn’t just crack; it exploded in a spray of granite shrapnel.
Xerollion didn’t move with panic. He moved with the terrifying economy of a god.
With a micro adjustment that seemed almost lazy, he tilted his torso mere inches to the left. The fist whizzed past his ribs, close enough that the heat singed the fabric of his clothes.
Unable to check its momentum, the punch continued its devastating trajectory, burying itself into a massive support column fifty feet down the corridor.
CRUNCH SHATTER.
The column didn’t just break; it disintegrated. The impact shook the foundation, causing half the ceiling to buckle and rain down in a deadly cascade of broken rock and choking dust.
Inside the cold, analytical void of Xerollion’s mind, a flicker of data passed.
[Heroic Strike: catalogued.]
[Light-based physical amplification. No divine signature detected. No further analysis required.]
"An impressive amount of force for anger in a being so freshly born," Xerollion said.
His voice emerged from behind the mask as calm as a scholar discussing a weather pattern. He didn’t even seem winded by the displaced air.
"Unfortunately, little Starlight... raw emotion is a poor substitute for precision.
"It isn’t going to be enough."
Elliot didn’t answer. He couldn’t.
His lungs were burning; his mind was a white-hot furnace of vengeance. He wasn’t concerned about precision.
He wasn’t concerned about technique.
He cared about the sound of Xerollion’s bones breaking.
He attacked again immediately.
Then again.
And again.

It became a relentless, terrifying sequence of violence. Punches, elbows, and knees—each strike driven by a primal rage that bypassed every shred of discipline his instructors had spent years drilling into his bones.
Every time a blow missed or connected with the stone floor, the entire corridor shuddered as if an earthquake were passing through.
THUD. CRACK. WHAM.

But to Xerollion, it was like watching a child throw stones at a mountain. Through the combined haze of his Foresight and absolute Martial Arts Mastery, he saw the attacks before they were even conceived in Elliot’s desperate mind.

He saw the electrical impulses in Elliot’s muscles; he saw the trajectory of the fury. He moved through the storm of white light like a ghost, turning aside strikes with casual deflections that felt deeply, personally insulting.
A wild, desperate overhand swing left Elliot’s ribs exposed for a heartbeat, a fatal opening. Xerollion could have driven a blade through his chest.
Instead, he simply stepped back, letting the sheer momentum of Elliot’s own rage carry the boy two full steps past him.

Elliot spun around, his boots skidding on the debris, and threw a rapid-fire combination of three strikes that possessed genuine technical merit buried somewhere beneath the screaming emotion, but they met nothing but empty air.
Xerollion was already gone, repositioning with fluid grace before each fist could find purchase.
"You were trained well," Xerollion observed, his voice cutting through the sounds of grinding stone.
He ducked beneath a roundhouse kick that would have decapitated any other living being in existence. "I can see the Academy’s foundation underneath all of this."
"The footwork is solid, the weight distribution is correct, but it’s a shame that you’re overshadowing it with so much noise."
The implication stung worse than any physical blow: that Elliot’s grief was making him weak. That his love for Apollo was a flaw in his combat equation.
"SHUT UP!" Elliot spat.
The words were punctuated by a spray of crimson. His lip had split during the last failed impact, and blood ran down his chin, hot and metallic.
"SHUT UP AND FIGHT ME, YOU COWARDLY BASTARD!"
His eyes burned with a light that was no longer heroic. It was the light of a dying star, desperate to take everything down with it.

For a long moment after Apollo’s body finally settled into its grotesque stillness, the world seemed to have ceased to exist.
Even the demons, creatures born of violence who had spent the last hour fighting for their very lives, stood frozen at the edges of the wreckage.

They were predators who had suddenly found themselves in the presence of something they didn’t understand: a silence that wasn’t peaceful but predatory, as if the very air were gathering itself for a second, a more devastating act.
Evelyn’s scream had already come and gone, a hoarse, broken sound that had drained the last of her strength.
What remained was a silence so absolute it felt heavy, the kind of quiet that only follows something that has been irrevocably broken.
Then, Elliot moved.
He didn’t run; he ignited.
He tore through the Underlayer’s stunned front ranks at a speed that defied physics, outstripping every display of agility he had shown during the earlier engagement.
Demon soldiers who would normally have intercepted any threat stood paralyzed, their instincts failing them as the white light wrapped around Elliot burned through the air.
FSHHHHHHH.
The heat was so intense that the stone beneath his boots cracked and spiderwebbed with every stride, scorching a path of molten glass through the center of the corridor.
He came to a halt directly in front of Xerollion.
The proximity was suicidal.
The heat radiating off Elliot’s body was a physical wall, shimmering in waves that should have been unbearable even to the masked monster standing across from him.
Elliot’s face—the face that had always carried a spark of hope, a gentle smile, and a kindness—was gone.
In its place was a mask of pure, undiluted hatred.
Tears cut hot, stinging tracks down cheeks flushed crimson with fury, his chest heaving as if his lungs were filled with liquid fire.
"YOU KILLED HIM!" Elliot screamed, his voice cracking like a whip.
"YOU KILLED APOLLO!"
"YOU MONSTER...!"
"YOU FUCKING BASTARD!"
"HE WAS EVERYTHING TO US!"
His hands were shaking, not from terror, but from the sheer voltage of the power coursing through his veins.
"MY FRIEND!
MY BROTHER!
HE GAVE EVERYTHING FOR AETHELGARD, AND YOU JUST TOOK IT!"
"YOU FUCKING TOOK IT LIKE IT MEANT NOTHING!"
Xerollion didn’t flinch.
He didn’t even shift his stance.
His masked visage remained impassive, reflecting the white inferno of Elliot’s rage without being consumed by it.

It was the same level, almost conversational tone he had used when discussing tactics or weather.
"And now I imagine you intend to try avenging him."
The casual cruelty of the response was the final spark in the powder keg.
"AVENGING HIM...?
I’M NOT JUST GOING TO AVENGE HIM!" Elliot’s roar was deafening, a sound that seemed to shake the very foundations of Aethelgard and Underlayer itself.
The white light around him surged upward in jagged, violent pillars, climbing brighter and brighter until it was blinding.
Soldiers thirty meters back had to shield their eyes, their boots scraping backward in instinctive retreat from the supernova forming in the corridor.
"I AM GOING TO ERASE YOU FROM EXISTENCE!" Elliot screamed, his voice ascending into something inhuman, something primal.
"I AM GOING TO TEAR YOUR SOUL APART PIECE BY PIECE!"
"I AM GOING TO BURN EVERY SHRED OF YOUR BEING UNTIL THERE IS ABSOLUTELY NOTHING LEFT BUT ASH AND MEMORY!"
"I WILL DESTROY YOU, XEROLLION!
I WILL DESTROY EVERYTHING YOU ARE!
The light became a solid wall of radiance, the air screaming as it was superheated.
Elliot’s eyes were no longer human; they were twin suns of incandescent rage, focused entirely on the man who had stolen the light from their world.
Elliot exploded forward.
This wasn’t a duel; it was an assassination attempt born of pure, unadulterated hatred.
He channeled every ounce of his grief, every fragment of his shattered hope, into the fundamental mechanics of his power.
The white light didn’t just coat his skin anymore; it screamed, vibrating with such high frequency that the air itself began to superheat and hiss around him.
FSHHHHHHH.
He unleashed the full devastating output of Heroic Strike.
It was, without question, the most violent display of raw power witnessed during the entire siege.
His fist, encased in a corona of incandescent white flame, tore through the air.
The sheer displacement of oxygen created a sonic crack BOOM as he closed the distance.
The strike was aimed square at Xerollion’s sternum, carrying enough compressed kinetic energy to shatter a fortress gate.
The launch was so violent that the stone floor beneath Elliot’s rear foot didn’t just crack; it exploded in a spray of granite shrapnel.
Xerollion didn’t move with panic.
He moved with the terrifying economy of a god.
With a micro adjustment that seemed almost lazy, he tilted his torso mere inches to the left.
The fist whizzed past his ribs, close enough that the heat singed the fabric of his clothes.

No divine signature detected.
No further analysis required.]
