chapters.title: Chapter 1194. You Almost Became More Than a Disappointment
paragraphs: Something in that exchange—the clinical, detached insult to his training—struck a nerve deeper than his grief. It pierced through the static of his rage and touched something colder: his pride.
Elliot didn’t scream this time. He didn’t roar.
Instead, he did something far more terrifying. He stopped.
He planted his feet with a deliberate, bone-deep solidity. He drew a ragged breath that whistled painfully through his split lip and bloodied teeth.

In that moment of stillness, the wild, supernova-like bloom of white light around his body began to collapse inward. It stopped flickering erratically and started to compress, spinning tighter and tighter around his limbs until it looked like molten diamond rather than fire.
The air around him stopped hissing and began to hum with a deadly, focused frequency.
HUMMMMMMMMM.
When he moved again, it wasn’t the desperate lunge of a grieving boy; it was the calculated strike of a predator.

He moved with the precise, lethal rhythm his instructors had spent years carving into his muscle memory. Weight shifted seamlessly from heel to ball of foot. His hips rotated with mechanical perfection.
He threw a low, testing jab not to kill, but to measure the distance, and the strike snapped out like a whip.
Xerollion noticed the shift immediately. The small, almost imperceptible tilt of his masked head was the only outward sign that the game had changed.
For the first time since the slaughter began, Xerollion actually engaged his feet, sliding half a step to the left with liquid grace as Elliot’s jab hissed past his jaw.
But the follow-up was already there. A cross came faster than the jab, aimed to catch Xerollion while his center of gravity was still adjusting.

Xerollion didn’t dodge this time; he braced, catching the blow against his forearm with a wet THWACK. The force was so concentrated that the impact drove a faint, smoking groove into the stone beneath Xerollion’s boots.
"There it is," Xerollion said.

His voice remained calm, but there was something almost approving buried beneath the surface—the interest of a scientist seeing a specimen finally show its true nature. "That is the fighter your family paid good coin to build."
"Hold on to that discipline for just a moment longer, and this conversation might last a few minutes more."
Elliot didn’t grant him the satisfaction of an answer. He became a storm of controlled violence.

He pressed the advantage with terrifying fluidity. He chained a vicious low kick aimed at Xerollion’s knee into a rising elbow that aimed for the mask, followed immediately by a compressed palm strike aimed directly at the sternum.
Each motion flowed into the next with zero telegraphing, no wasted energy, and no screams of rage, just pure, lethal execution.
WHAM. CRACK. THUD.
For three full, heart-stopping exchanges, the dynamic shifted. Xerollion was no longer simply watching a performance; he was actively defending against a threat.
A palm strike that he had to redirect with force rather than ignore; a knee that he actually had to block with his forearm rather than simply sidestep; a feint that forced him to commit his weight.
By any honest measure of combat, it was the finest sequence Elliot had ever produced, the culmination of years of sweat, blood, and discipline, weaponized by the desperate need to kill.
’I can do this,’ Elliot thought, his mind racing with cold calculation. ’I can find the opening...’
’I can break him... For Apollo... For everything...’
But it lasted for exactly as long as his composure could hold.

The discipline was a dam, and the grief was the ocean pressing against it. The moment Apollo’s blood-soaked face surfaced behind his eyes again, the image of that severed head rolling across the stone, the dam didn’t just leak; it shattered.

The cold calculation evaporated, replaced instantly by the screaming, white-hot agony of loss. The discipline cracked straight down the middle, and the rage came flooding back in to fill the void like molten lead.
His next strike, a powerful hook that should have been devastating, was thrown with too much shoulder and too much emotion.
It was sloppy, and it was telegraphed like it was exactly the kind of predictable, emotional attack Xerollion had been reading since the first second of the fight.
Xerollion didn’t even need to use Foresight this time. He simply stepped inside the arc of the swing, his movement so economical it seemed to defy the chaos surrounding them.
"Unfortunate," Xerollion said.
The approval was gone.
The interest had vanished.
His voice returned to that flat, soul-crushing assessment that made Elliot feel smaller than the dust beneath their feet. "You almost had something there..."
"You almost became more than a disappointment."
Xerollion didn’t escalate. He didn’t need to.

He simply began to answer with measured, surgical strikes of his own. These weren’t the city-leveling blows he had unleashed against Apollo; these were the precise applications of force required to dismantle a human body.
He was beginning the slow, methodical work of grinding down a young man who had never once, in his entire life, faced anything that did not eventually yield to enough determination.
The first strike came like a lightning bolt. A straight punch caught Elliot across the jaw with a wet CRACK.

Elliot’s head snapped sideways with such violence that his neck vertebrae groaned under the strain, sending a crimson spray of saliva and blood across the scorched stone floor. Before Elliot could even register the pain, Xerollion was already in motion.
A follow-up roundhouse kick buried itself deep into Elliot’s solar plexus.
THUD.
The air exploded out of Elliot’s lungs in a pained wheeze. He doubled over, his body convulsing as he staggered backward several steps.

He came up coughing thick, metallic ropes of blood spattering his chin, but his eyes remained twin suns of hatred. Without a single second of hesitation, without even pausing to catch his breath, he threw himself back into the inferno.
Elliot’s desperation manifested as a wild, haymaker swing. It was pure fury, uncalculated and raw.

It caught nothing but empty air. Xerollion didn’t hesitate; he exploited the opening instantly. He stepped inside the arc of the swing and drove a short, brutal elbow directly into Elliot’s left shoulder.
POP CRUNCH.
The sound was the unmistakable noise of a joint being forced from its socket. Elliot screamed through clenched teeth, a sound that was half agony, half defiance.
He staggered sideways, his left arm suddenly hanging useless at his side, the limb twitching involuntarily. Yet, he kept his footing.
He stayed upright purely through a stubbornness so profound it bordered on insanity. His right arm kept rising anyway.
A moment later, he threw another punch using that same ruined left arm. He either forgot or simply refused to acknowledge that the shoulder was shattered.
The strike arrived half a second slower and considerably weaker than it should have been.
Xerollion didn’t even move his feet. He simply reached out and caught the fist in his open palm.
The impact was pathetic compared to the earlier exchanges.
"That arm doesn’t function anymore," Xerollion said.
His voice was intimate, almost conversational, as he held the fist still without any visible effort. "You felt it separate..."
"I watched you feel it. The nerves screamed, didn’t they?"
"I DON’T CARE!" Elliot roared, his voice cracking. "I DON’T CARE ABOUT THE PAIN! JUST DIE!"

Xerollion released the fist rather than breaking it further, stepping back with fluid grace to let Elliot collapse into a defensive stance that was now fundamentally broken, a stance that no longer had two working arms to hold it.
Desperation drove Elliot to one final, suicidal gambit. A spinning hook kick came next, thrown from his good leg with every remaining shred of strength in his body.

Xerollion ducked under it entirely, the wind of the kick rustling his hair as it passed overhead. As Elliot overextended, Xerollion drove a palm strike into Elliot’s exposed chest with the force of a battering ram.
CRACK SHATTER.
Elliot was launched backward, skidding across the debris-strewn floor until he slammed into a collapsed section of a support column. The impact was catastrophic.
His ribs cracked audibly, splintering against the stone. His breath left him in one long, involuntary gasp that sounded more like a death rattle.
For several agonizing seconds, he simply lay there in the dust, staring up at the cracked, uncaring ceiling, blood pooling beneath his head.
’Move,’ his mind screamed. ’Move or you’re dead.’
’Move or Apollo dies for nothing.’
With a wet, grinding sound of bone against bone, he forced himself back onto unsteady, shaking legs.
"You cannot beat me with rage alone," Xerollion said.

He moved with terrifying calm, sliding beneath a white-hot slash that Elliot had launched from his bare knuckles—a desperate, improvised technique born of pure instinct that Elliot would likely never be able to replicate.
"Anger makes the attack stronger, yes."
"But it also makes the mind loud... And a loud mind is a predictable one."

chapters.title: Chapter 1195. How Does the Meat Continue to Move When the Spirit Has Been Incinerated
paragraphs: Elliot kept coming. He was no longer a soldier; he was a walking wound, a creature of pure, stubborn refusal.
But the arithmetic of the fight was cruel, and the damage was accumulating on his side of the exchange with devastating speed.
When he tried to throw a desperate jab, Xerollion parried at an unnatural angle, twisting Elliot’s wrist mid-strike.
CRACK.
The joint twisted wrong, the tendons straining to their breaking point before the wrist visibly swelled into a purple, throbbing mass.
When Xerollion followed with a sweeping kick that caught Elliot’s support leg, Elliot’s knee slammed into the unforgiving stone floor with a wet THUD CRUNCH.
The impact should have shattered the patella, sending lightning bolts of agony up his thigh that would have paralyzed any normal man.
Yet, he got up. Every single time.

Each time he rose, he looked less human and more like a vengeful specter, driven by the phantom image of Apollo’s face that burned behind his eyelids, a memory so vivid it acted as both a fuel and a curse.
’I can’t fall,’ Elliot’s mind screamed through the haze of pain. ’If I fall, he’s gone forever.’
’If I stop, Apollo dies twice...’
’Breathe... Just fucking breathe...’

Somewhere in the middle of that relentless punishment, amidst the taste of copper and the grinding of bone, Elliot found something else. A final, desperate reservoir of spirit that didn’t come from training or discipline but from the raw, bleeding core of his soul.
He staggered back several paces, putting distance between himself and Xerollion for the first time since the slaughter began. His breathing was ragged, each inhale a wet rattle in his chest.
He planted his feet wide, ignoring the way his left shoulder screamed in protest.
Slowly, deliberately, he began to gather every scrap of Heroic Strike’s remaining output. The white light around his fists didn’t just glow; it condensed.
It became a dense, terrifying corona of pressurized energy, so bright it cast sharp, jagged shadows across the wrecked corridor.
HUMMMMMMMMM.
The soldiers in the distance instinctively recoiled. They didn’t need orders; they could feel the atmospheric pressure shifting, sensing a cataclysm gathering in the hands of a dying boy.
"Absolute Blow," Elliot rasped.

His voice was thick, muffled by a mouth full of blood and broken teeth. The technique was a legend among his class, something he had trained for two years and had failed to execute during a sparring match that had left him humiliated.
But this wasn’t a sparring match.
"This one..." he growled, his eyes igniting with a suicidal brilliance, "...is not going to miss.
Instead of aiming at Xerollion’s torso, Elliot drove both fists downward with everything he had left. He slammed his fists into the stone floor like twin meteors.
BOOOOOOOMMMMMMM!!!

The corridor didn’t just shake; it screamed. A catastrophic shockwave erupted from the point of impact, tearing the floor open in a jagged, volcanic fissure that raced down the corridor’s full length.

Stone shattered upward in chunks the size of human torsos, spinning through the air like deadly shrapnel. The force was so violent that the soldiers thirty meters back were lifted off their feet and thrown backward by the displaced air.
For the first time in the entire engagement, Xerollion’s composure wavered. He didn’t simply lean or step aside.
Recognizing the raw destructive potential of the technique, he crossed both forearms in front of his face in a rigid guard and braced his entire body.
The wave of kinetic energy and debris slammed into him like a physical wall.
CRASHHHHH.

Xerollion was forced backward, his boots skidding across the stone as he fought to maintain his center of gravity. Cracks spiderwebbed outward from beneath his feet as he dug in, holding his ground against the inferno of light and stone.
For several seconds, the world was nothing but chaos—dust, smoke, and the grinding sound of crumbling masonry hung suspended in the air.
Then, slowly, the debris settled.
Xerollion lowered his arms. His mask was streaked with grey dust, and his cloak was tattered at the edges, but he remained otherwise untouched.
He stood in the center of the newly formed crater, looking at the boy who had nearly leveled the corridor.
"That one had some weight to it," Xerollion admitted.
His voice was no longer dismissive; there was a genuine note of recognition in it. "The first attack today that required an actual answer... instead of merely deciding not to bother."
Elliot didn’t have the luxury of feeling pride. He didn’t have the strength to savor the fact that he had finally forced Xerollion to brace.
His vision was tunneling, the edges of his sight fraying into black static as his body screamed a singular, desperate command: ’Die... Make him die.’

Staggering forward on legs that felt less like bone and muscle and more like shattered glass, Elliot threw himself at Xerollion one last time. It was a pathetic, clumsy double strike, a desperate lunge with whatever strength remained in his one functional arm.
He was a wounded animal throwing its last gambit at a predator.
Xerollion didn’t wait for the attack to land. He closed the remaining distance himself, moving with a speed that bypassed human perception.
To Elliot’s failing eyes, Xerollion didn’t run; he simply existed in a new position closer to him.
WHIP.
A single open palm strike caught Elliot square in the sternum. The impact wasn’t a punch; it was a concentrated explosion of force.
THOOM.
Elliot was launched backward, his boots skidding uselessly over the jagged debris of the crater. He slid across the broken stone until his spine collided with the far wall with a bone-jarring CRACK.
The stone behind him spiderwebbed from the impact.

For a terrifying second, his legs simply gave out, and he began to slide down the wall toward the blood-soaked floor, but his fingernails clawed at the masonry, catching grooves in the stone, refusing to let his body collapse completely.
He hung there, suspended between standing and falling, a broken marionette held up by sheer spite.
By the fifth or sixth exchange, any pretense of combat remained. Elliot’s technique had degraded entirely into something primal, a flailing, desperate struggle for survival.
Every strike was thrown with maximum, soul-crushing effort and zero tactical thought. He was swinging at shadows, swinging at ghosts, swinging at the air itself.

Xerollion found himself, briefly, almost bored by the predictable rhythm of the boy’s agony, though something in the sheer, unnatural stubbornness of the human spirit kept a sliver of his analytical attention engaged.
’How?’ Xerollion wondered, watching the boy struggle to lift a bleeding fist. ’How does the meat continue to move when the spirit has already been incinerated?’

There was a specific, haunting quality to fighting someone whose every motion was dictated by grief rather than training. It was a rawness that Xerollion recognized from the deep, buried archives of his own memory from his own earliest days in this world, before the System had granted him the tools to make emotion irrelevant to outcome.
He remembered, distantly, what it had felt like to want something so badly that wanting became the entire strategy. To feel the world burn because it had taken what was yours.
It had been centuries since he had needed to recall that feeling for any reason other than recognizing it in a dying child.
"Why..." Elliot gasped.
Each word was a struggle, punctuated by a wet cough that brought up fresh flecks of crimson. He forced himself upright, his vertebrae popping audibly as he fought gravity.
His one good arm shook violently, while the ruined left arm hung like dead weight at his side. "Why... why did you do this to him?"
"To all of us? What did any of us... ever do to you?"
The question hung in the air, thick with the smell of blood and burnt stone.
Xerollion didn’t answer immediately. He stood motionless in the center of the devastation, the picture of absolute calm amidst the wreckage.
When he finally spoke, there was something almost gentle in his tone, a soft, terrifying compassion that was more insulting than any blade.
"Nothing at all," Xerollion answered. "You were simply convenient."
He stepped forward, the hem of his cloak brushing against the blood-slicked stone. "Both things can be true at once, Elliot."
"You can have done nothing wrong, lived a life of virtue and honor, and still have been exactly what I needed to achieve my objective."

chapters.title: Chapter 1196. She Didn’t Know Who I Was, But She Knew What I Represent
paragraphs: Elliot spat a thick glob of crimson onto the stone, the blood frothing between his lips. He said nothing further.
There was nothing left—no anger to fuel his lungs, no words to bridge the chasm between his grief and Xerollion’s indifference.
The silence that followed was worse than any scream; it was the sound of a soul finally breaking under the weight of inevitable defeat.
But the body has a stubbornness that the mind cannot control.

With a primal, guttural sound that was more animal than human, Elliot gathered every remaining spark of his life force. He focused on the core of his being, drawing on the last reserves of the Heroic Strike.

The white light didn’t just glow; it screamed. It condensed around his fist into a sphere of pure, pressurized radiance so dense it began to distort the air around it like heat rising from asphalt. VROOOOOOOOM.

With a final, desperate roar that tore his vocal cords, he threw it forward. It was everything he was: every memory of Apollo, every drop of blood spilled, and every ounce of his broken pride condensed into a single point of annihilation.
Xerollion didn’t flinch, and he didn’t dodge. He simply reached out.
THWACK.
The impact stopped dead against Xerollion’s open palm. The momentum didn’t dissipate; it was simply arrested, as if the laws of physics had been forcibly suspended.
For one suspended, horrifying moment, the entire corridor held its breath. The dust motes froze midair.
The distant soldiers stopped breathing. Elliot’s eyes widened, pupils contracting as disbelief washed over his face.
The strongest thing he had ever produced was the culmination of his life’s training, and his deepest agony had failed to even push the man’s hand back an inch.
Then, Xerollion pushed back.
It wasn’t a punch; it was a dismissal. A simple flick of force.
BOOM.
The reversal was catastrophic. Elliot was launched backward like a ragdoll caught in a hurricane.

He flew several meters through the air before slamming into the far corridor wall with a wet CRUNCH of ribs against masonry. He slid down the stone, leaving a crimson streak behind him, before collapsing into a heap at the base of the wall.
His body finally gave out, the fire in his eyes flickering into dim embers. He lay there, a broken marionette with its strings severed, unable to even twitch a finger.
Evelyn was there within a heartbeat. Her speed was a blur of desperation, closing the distance before the settling dust had even begun to clear.
She collapsed to her knees beside him, gathering his battered frame into her arms. "Elliot!
"Elliot, look at me!" she sobbed, the sound raw and ragged, echoing off the shattered walls.
Her fingers trembled as she pressed them frantically against his neck, searching for the pulse.
There. A shallow, stuttering rhythm.
Thump... thump...

It was weak, like the wings of a dying bird, but it was there. A fragile sliver of relief broke through the horror etched into her features, though her tears continued to fall freely onto his bloodied face.
Xerollion stepped forward, his boots crunching on the fragments of the corridor. He stood over them like a monument to inevitability, studying the scene with an analytical detachment.
Behind the impassive stillness of his mask, his mind was already moving past this moment, already calculating the next variable.

What he said next contained an element that, to a sentimental observer, might resemble mercy, as, to a sentimental observer, resemble mercy if mercy could be engineered with the cold precision of a mathematical equation.
"I’ll let you live," Xerollion announced.
His voice didn’t need to be loud; it carried with unnatural clarity across the wreckage, reaching every soldier still frozen in terror further down the hall. "Not out of compassion..."
"Your death would provide no tactical advantage... It would be a waste of resources."
He looked down at the broken boy, then up at the terrified survivors, his gaze making them feel exposed, as if he were reading their very heartbeats.
"Let him live," Xerollion commanded, his voice dropping to a cold, echoing timbre. "Let him live to remember today."
"Let him remember the day Aethelgard learned exactly how far its arrogance could carry it before it finally meets the ground."

Evelyn looked up at him, her gaze a volatile cocktail of raw hatred and paralyzing fear. She pulled Elliot’s unconscious, broken form tighter against her chest, cradling his head as if she could physically shield him from the reality of their defeat.

Around them, the corridor settled back into a suffocating, tomb-like silence. The only sound was the distant drip of blood from a cracked pillar and the ragged, wet breathing of the dying boy in her arms.

Both armies, the proud defenders of Aethelgard and the inexorable force that had dismantled them, stood frozen, watching the last threads of hope unravel. No one could guess what would come next in a war that had already, unmistakably, tipped entirely to one side.
Slowly, with hands that refused to shake despite the adrenaline coursing through her veins, Evelyn lowered Elliot to the ground.

She positioned him carefully against the wall, her fingers lingering one last time on his pulse point to confirm the shallow rise and fall of his chest. When she finally straightened, something fundamental had shifted within her.
The tears that had streaked her face had dried, leaving salt tracks in the dust. Her grief hadn’t vanished; it had simply crystallized.
In its place was a stillness so absolute it was unnerving the kind of calm that precedes a lightning strike.
She rose to her feet, turning to face Xerollion directly. The suspicion she had carried like a quiet ember for the better part of an hour suddenly roared into a cold, deliberate flame.
"I suspected it from the beginning," Evelyn said.
Her voice was eerily steady, cutting through the stale air as she stepped past Elliot’s fallen body. "The way you move that economy of motion..."
"The way you speak that detached, almost bored cadence..."
"All of it felt familiar... Every instinct I have has been screaming at me, and I kept lying to myself, telling myself it was only coincidence."
Xerollion regarded her, tilting his head slightly. His interest was genuine now.
Of everyone he had systematically dismantled during this engagement, she was the only one who had arrived at this conclusion without a single shred of concrete evidence.
She hadn’t read his technique or heard his name; she had simply felt him. It was an instinctive wariness, a primal recognition that he found rare enough to warrant genuine respect.
"You’re perceptive," Xerollion answered, his voice carrying effortlessly across the debris. "More than the others..."
"Unfortunately, perception is a luxury of the living, Evelyn..."
"Suspicion alone won’t save you from what happens next."
He watched her closely.
She didn’t posture. She didn’t scream or weep.

Her weight was balanced evenly on the balls of her feet, her hands loose rather than clenched in fists. This wasn’t the flailing desperation of Elliot’s grief-driven assault; this was something far more dangerous.

She had already accepted the likelihood of her own death, and she had chosen to face it not out of madness, but out of a cold, analytical need to prove her theory before she became another casualty of history.
’She knows,’ Xerollion thought, a flicker of something almost like amusement stirring behind his mask. ’She doesn’t know who I am, but she knows what I represent.’
Evelyn didn’t offer a rebuttal. She didn’t waste breath on accusations or pleas.

She simply shifted her stance, the air around her beginning to ripple and distort as her mana reserves surged toward the surface. The temperature in the corridor seemed to drop as she drew everything inward.
Without another word, she activated her full superhuman speed.
FWOOOOOM.
The sound barrier didn’t just break; it shattered. In an instant, she vanished from her position, leaving nothing behind but a shockwave that kicked up a cloud of stone dust and blood.

chapters.title: Chapter 1197. Burning Through Your Life Force to Chase a Shadow
paragraphs: Evelyn didn’t just move; she tore through the fabric of reality. Her body blurred out of ordinary perception in an instant, leaving behind only a faint, haunting afterimage of pale blue light that streaked across the debris like a comet’s tail.

In less than a tenth of a second, she reappeared directly behind Xerollion. There was no wind-up, no warning, just a fist driven toward his exposed spine with enough kinetic force to pulverize solid granite.
BOOOM.
Xerollion spun on his heel with preternatural grace, his body reacting before his mind even registered the threat. He caught the strike on his forearm.
The collision was cataclysmic. A visible shockwave rippled outward from the point of contact, sending loose masonry cascading from the ceiling like deadly rain.
CRACK THUD.
The ground beneath their feet spiderwebbed from the sheer pressure of the halted momentum.
Evelyn did not pause to assess the exchange. She couldn’t afford to.

She vanished again immediately, her speed pushing the limits of her own cardiovascular system. She reappeared from four different angles in less than two seconds—a whirlwind of blue light and lethal intent.
Left hook, high roundhouse, gut thrust, and spinning elbow, each strike aimed to exploit the split-second openings created by her own velocity.
She was trying to use her raw speed to compensate for the terrifying chasm in physical power between them.
’Too fast,’ Xerollion thought, his mind racing to match her rhythm. ’She’s not just running; she’s vibrating through the air.’
His Foresight read the pattern of her movement with increasing difficulty. Her velocity made her predictions slippery, like trying to catch smoke with bare hands.
Every time he locked onto a trajectory, she shifted mid-stride, forcing him to sharpen his precision to a razor’s edge.

Beneath the surface, his Full Potential Adaptation began to hum, working like a furnace to process her unique acceleration patterns, converting her raw mechanism of speed into data he could reliably anticipate.
She wasn’t done. She wasn’t even close.
Mid-stride, Evelyn reached down and tore a massive chunk of a broken column off the floor. With a grunt of exertion, she hurled it directly at Xerollion’s head.
As the stone flew, she vanished, closing the gap behind the projectile.

Xerollion’s instincts flared; he swatted the stone aside with a casual open palm strike. CLANG, but it was exactly what she wanted. His attention flicked toward the debris for a fraction of a heartbeat.
In that heartbeat, she struck.
She drove a knee upward toward his ribs from below, a low, vicious strike aimed at his solar plexus. The strike was so fast that it nearly slipped beneath his guard entirely.
THUD.
Xerollion caught the knee against his forearm instead of his ribs, but the impact was so violent it sent a visible tremor through the corded muscle beneath his sleeve.
"Too slow," Xerollion muttered.
He answered with a short, brutal counter—a piston-like jab. Evelyn’s eyes widened; she barely managed to weave around it, but the edge of his fist clipped her shoulder.
SHLUCK.
The force spun her half a step off balance, her boots skidding across the blood-slicked stone.
But Evelyn didn’t fight the spin; she weaponized it.
Leveraging the centrifugal force from her stumble, she whipped back around, her body coiled like a spring. Her elbow shot upward, but she wasn’t aiming for his chest or his throat.

She aimed directly at the center of the mask covering his face. This was the first attack that carried something more deliberate than simple damage; it was a surgical strike, a probe designed to pierce his mystery.
Xerollion noticed the intent instantly. The moment his tactical mind registered her target, he tilted his head back by a hair’s breadth.
WHOOSH.
Her elbow whistled past the edge of the mask, missing by millimeters. The displaced air pressure from her strike was so intense she could feel the phantom wind of it against her own knuckles.
Xerollion straightened his posture, his breathing still unnervingly controlled.
For the first time since the slaughter began, something sharper and colder entered his voice.
"Interesting," Xerollion said.
The detached boredom was gone, replaced by a predatory focus. "You’re not trying to hurt me anymore..."
"You’re not trying to kill me... You’re trying to see something."
Evelyn didn’t stop. She couldn’t stop.
Her heart was hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird, and her muscles screamed with the buildup of lactic acid, but she pushed through.
She was already moving again before the last sentence had fully left her lips, her form blurring once more as she refused to give him a single second to settle into his new rhythm.
"I want to know who you really are," Evelyn spat, her voice raw with defiance. "Everyone else in this corridor is too broken to ask..."
"Too terrified to look... But I’m not."

Evelyn became a creature of pure motion, a blue streak of vengeance that refused to acknowledge the impossible gulf between them. She came at the mask twice more in rapid succession, her movements becoming more complex, more deceptive.
The first strike appeared to be a vicious palm thrust aimed at his throat, but mid-flight, her fingers splayed into a grasping claw, a feint designed to tear the mask free.
The second was a desperate, full-body lunge that abandoned all defensive caution in favor of raw, unadulterated velocity.
WHOOSH.
WHOOSH.
Both times, she struck air. Xerollion simply wasn’t where her hands expected him to be.

He didn’t dodge with theatrical flair; he shifted those last few crucial inches through nothing more dramatic than flawless, economical footwork and a read on her intent that arrived a fraction of a second before her muscles even fully contracted.
To Evelyn, it felt like fighting a ghost made of iron.
On the third attempt, she committed everything. Her fist screamed toward the mask, the displaced air whistling like a blade.
SNAP.
Xerollion’s hand shot out. He didn’t block; he intercepted.
His fingers clamped around her wrist an inch from the mask’s edge. The sudden halt sent a shockwave up her arm that made her teeth rattle.
He held her there, motionless, not with crushing force, but with a terrifying firmness that signaled the absolute end of her gambit.
"Not today," Xerollion said.

His voice was almost gentle, a soft murmur that sounded obscene amidst the wreckage and the blood. Before she could even process the humiliation of being caught, he released her wrist and stepped back, effortlessly gliding out of her reach.
"You’ll have to settle for suspicion a while longer."
Evelyn gasped for air, her lungs burning like she had swallowed molten glass. Her heart hammered against her ribs THUD THUD, THUD THUD, and her vision swam.
She felt exposed, raw, and utterly powerless.

Xerollion watched her, and for the first time, a spark of genuine interest flickered behind the mask. She was the fastest thing he had personally exchanged blows with since that cataclysmic fight in Kaeleth’s domain.
There was a specific, cold pleasure in this—a small pocket of genuine challenge buried inside an engagement that had otherwise felt like nothing more than clearing debris from a path.
"Your speed is impressive," Xerollion said.

He ducked beneath another strike, a spinning back fist that came from an angle so improbable it should have been impossible to predict. He moved like water, flowing around her attack without breaking his stride.
"But speed without sufficient power behind it only tires you out faster than it tires me..."
"You are burning through your life force to chase a shadow."
Evelyn said nothing. She couldn’t afford words.
The time for talking had died with Apollo.

Instead, she answered with a roar of pure magical output. She began to weave considerably stronger strikes into her combinations, each blow carrying a crackling aura of azure energy that shattered the stone floor where they landed.
CRACK BOOM.
The air around her began to hum with lethal static.
The soldiers watching from the shadows gasped. They had fought alongside her for years, but they had never seen this.
They had never seen this monster.
For two years, Evelyn had lived behind a self-imposed prison. She had deliberately capped her own output at forty percent, a discipline born of a deep, paranoid caution.

She knew what she carried; she knew that to unleash her full strength was to invite attention she wasn’t ready to handle. But watching Apollo fall, watching Elliot be broken like a child’s toy, that caution hadn’t just evaporated; it had been incinerated.
’No more holding back,’ she thought, her inner voice screaming over the roar of her own blood. ’No more hiding...’
’If I die, I die as what I truly am.’
She pushed past the seventy percent mark.
FWOOOOOOOM.
The transformation was instantaneous. The corridor’s remaining torchlight didn’t just flicker; it stretched and blurred into long, agonizing streaks of amber wherever she passed.
Her movements were no longer just fast; they were violent distortions in space. Each step she took left a cratered imprint in the stone.
The blue light trailing her wasn’t a faint afterimage anymore; it was a blazing comet of azure mana that threatened to ignite the very oxygen in the room.
The pressure in the corridor spiked so sharply that the ears of the nearby soldiers began to bleed.

chapters.title: Chapter 1198. There Is a Difference Between Submission and Revelation
paragraphs: The shift was not merely visible; it was seismic. The ground beneath Evelyn didn’t just crack; it detonated.
CRUNCH BOOM.

Spiderweb fractures spidered outward from her boots as she ignited her mana, sending shockwaves through the ancient masonry. The pale blue aura that had been a soft trail now hardened into a searing, brilliant white, so intense that its edges became razor sharp.
Where her afterimages grazed the corridor walls, the stone didn’t just chip; it scorched, leaving glowing, molten scars in the wake of her passage.
She entered a state of hyperaccelerated violence. The space between one heartbeat and the next was no longer a continuous flow; it was fractured into six, seven, eight distinct positions.
Each position was a deadly proposition.
WHAM. WHAM. WHAM.

She was a hurricane of azure lightning. Her strikes became a coordinated assault on his entire anatomy: a lightning-fast jab at his wrist to break his guard, a devastating roundhouse aimed at his ribs to crack bone, and a vicious kick to the back of his knee to destabilize his stance.
She was hunting for a weakness, testing every possible angle, every infinitesimal gap her earlier, more cautious attempts had failed to exploit.
The exchange stretched on, a brutal ballet of destruction that lasted far longer than any confrontation Xerollion had faced that day.
The already ruined corridor became a slaughterhouse of debris. Dust clouds choked the air, mixed with the copper tang of blood and the acrid stench of burned mana.

For the first time, Evelyn wasn’t just bouncing off him; she was connecting. Two solid strikes landed, one to his sternum and another to his temple, sending a visible shudder through Xerollion’s frame that actually rocked him back on his heels.
’I’m hitting him,’ she thought, her mind screaming over the roar of her own power. ’I’m actually making him move!’
But the triumph was hollow.
Every time her fist connected with a wet THUD, every time her magic tore flesh, his Infinite Regeneration responded with terrifying immediacy.
The wounds would bubble and hiss, the flesh knitting together with unnatural speed. The cycle was maddening.
She was pouring her very soul into every strike, burning through her life force like a candle in a hurricane, while he remained an immovable object.
The frustration began to seep into her bones, a cold, corrosive despair that whispered: ’You are fighting God with a blade of glass.’
Then, it happened.
Evelyn pivoted on one foot, channeling seventy percent of her power into a vicious cross. Her knuckles screamed as they connected with the exposed flesh just beneath the edge of his mask.
SHLICK.
A thin, crimson line opened along Xerollion’s cheekbone. Blood—real, warm blood—sprayed across her knuckles.
For half a second, Evelyn allowed herself to breathe. A spark of hope, fragile and dangerous, ignited in her chest.
’He bleeds... He’s real... He can be broken. ’

It lasted exactly as long as it took for the wound to vanish. Before she could even follow up with the next strike in her combo, she watched in horror as the skin crawled and fused, and the blood reabsorbed into the newly formed flesh.
The wound closed before it had even finished bleeding. The spark of hope died instantly, replaced by a crushing weight of futility.
Xerollion didn’t even flinch. He simply raised the back of his hand, wiping the last crimson smear from his jaw with a casual motion that felt like a deliberate insult to her effort.
"You’re making a tactical error, Evelyn," Xerollion said.
His voice wasn’t mocking; it was worse. It was sympathetic. "You cannot win this by wearing me down..."
"You are fighting an ocean with a spoon."
He stepped forward, forcing her to retreat as his presence seemed to expand, filling the corridor. "There is nothing here to wear down..."
"Every wound closes... Every strike I take only teaches me your rhythm faster..."
"Every second you fight me, you become more predictable."
Evelyn’s teeth were bared in a snarl, blood dripping from her own split lips. Her muscles were twitching with exhaustion, her vision tunneling, but something deeper than strategy was driving her now.
It was the raw, stubborn refusal of a cornered animal. She wasn’t fighting for Aethelgard anymore.
She wasn’t fighting for Apollo. She was fighting because stopping meant admitting that everything they had built was meaningless.
"Then I’ll just have to hit you somewhere that matters," Evelyn hissed through clenched teeth. "I’ll hit you until there’s nothing left to regenerate."
With a scream of pure, unadulterated defiance, she threw herself back into the fray, her body dissolving into a white-hot blur of suicidal intensity.
Evelyn reached for something she had never dared to attempt before, a technique that pushed her mana system to its absolute breaking point.

Desperate to shatter his perfect composure, she didn’t just accelerate; she fractured her own presence. With a wet, tearing sound of displaced air, she split her speed into a cascade of simultaneous afterimages.
FSHHH FSHHH FSHHH!
Suddenly, the corridor was flooded with six, eight, ten versions of Evelyn, each one a perfect, terrifying replica of the other.
They weren’t mere optical illusions; they carried independent, convincing motion, each one weaving through the debris with its own lethal trajectory.
Her goal was simple: overload his processing power, confuse his senses, and find the one microsecond where his godlike perception would falter.
For a heartbeat, the impossible happened. Xerollion hesitated. His head tilted, eyes scanning the chaos as his brain struggled to process the sudden multiplication of threats.
The armies watching from the shadows held their collective breath; a single woman had momentarily stalled the unstoppable force.
But the victory was a mirage.
Beneath the surface of the illusion, Divine Perception and Foresight roared to life in perfect synchronization. They didn’t look at the motion; they looked at the soul of the attack.

They traced the infinitesimal thread of genuine energy signature, the unique, white-hot mana frequency that only the real Evelyn possessed, threading through the web of decoys. With surgical precision, his mind isolated the true body from the ghostly shells.
"A clever trick," Xerollion said, his voice cutting through the chaos like a blade.
Before the real Evelyn could even register that her gambit had failed, his hand shot out. He didn’t grab an afterimage; he seized her actual wrist mid-strike.
CLANK.
The contact was absolute. The surprise that flooded her features was raw and naked—the horror of a predator realizing it has walked straight into a trap.
"But you forget," Xerollion continued, his grip tightening just enough to make her bones creak, "that I read considerably more than physical movement..."
"I read the intent behind the spark."
Without warning, he twisted, using her own momentum against her.
CRACK.

He threw her down onto the unforgiving stone floor with controlled but devastating force. Her back slammed against the debris with a bone-jarring THUD, driving the air from her lungs in a pained wheeze.

Before she could even attempt to roll away, he pressed down, pinning her with a passive layer of telekinetic pressure. It felt like an invisible mountain had been placed on her chest, crushing her into the stone and rendering her limbs useless despite her weakening, desperate struggles.

The adrenaline that had sustained her began to hemorrhage away, leaving only the cold, crushing reality of exhaustion. Her muscles spasmed involuntarily, her breathing coming in ragged, desperate gasps.
Xerollion crouched close, his mask mere inches from her face. The proximity was suffocating.
"You’re stronger than I expected," he murmured, studying her with a detached, clinical curiosity that felt more violating than any blow. "What system do you carry, Evelyn?"
"What manner of power allows you to fracture yourself like that? I’m curious."
Evelyn’s face was pressed against the blood-stained stone, but her eyes remained fixed on his. Even as her strength ebbed, the hatred in them burned brighter than her mana ever had.
"I won’t tell you... anything," she spat, each word a battle against the telekinetic weight crushing her ribs. "Kill me if you want..."
"Break every bone in my body... But I will never bow to you."
Xerollion didn’t need her words. His Emotional Insight began to peel back the layers of her psyche like rotting parchment.
He didn’t need her consent to read her. Beneath the screaming fury and the paralyzing terror, he found something profound, something almost alien in its purity.
It was a loyalty so fierce, so absolute, that it transcended self-preservation. She wasn’t fighting for her life; she was fighting as a bulwark for the broken souls bleeding out around her.
’How fascinating,’ he thought. ’Elliot’s loyalty was a wildfire—chaotic, consuming, and predictable.’
’But hers... hers is a fortress. It is disciplined and even calculated in surrender.’
"I never asked you to bow," Xerollion said, tilting his head.
His tone held something that might have been mistaken for admiration if he weren’t a monster. "I asked what you carry..."
"There is a fundamental difference between submission and revelation, though I understand why the distinction would be meaningless to someone who believes they have already lost everything."
Evelyn’s lips curled into a blood-flecked snarl.
"It doesn’t matter to me at all," she whispered, her voice cracking but her resolve unshaken. "Nothing you ask matters..."
"You could ask me the color of the sky, the name of God, or the secrets of the stars... and I would still give you nothing."

She wasn’t fighting for her life; she was fighting as a bulwark for the broken souls bleeding out around her.
’How fascinating,’ he thought. ’Elliot’s loyalty was a wildfire—chaotic, consuming, and predictable.’
’But hers... hers is a fortress.
It is disciplined and even calculated in surrender.’
"I never asked you to bow," Xerollion said, tilting his head.
His tone held something that might have been mistaken for admiration if he weren’t a monster.
"I asked what you carry..."
"There is a fundamental difference between submission and revelation, though I understand why the distinction would be meaningless to someone who believes they have already lost everything."
Evelyn’s lips curled into a blood-flecked snarl.
"It doesn’t matter to me at all," she whispered, her voice cracking but her resolve unshaken.
"Nothing you ask matters..."
"You could ask me the color of the sky, the name of God, or the secrets of the stars... and I would still give you nothing."

chapters.title: Chapter 1199. A Private Terror Tied to a Night She Never Spoke Of
paragraphs: Xerollion considered her defiance for a long moment. The silence that followed was more oppressive than the sounds of battle, a heavy, ringing void that seemed to suck the oxygen from the corridor.
His head tilted with the mechanical curiosity of an apex predator examining a specimen that had proven more durable than expected.
Then, with a slow, deliberate motion, he rose to his feet.
WHOOSH.
The telekinetic pressure vanished instantly. Without the invisible force holding her up, Evelyn collapsed completely.

Her body hit the stone with a wet THUD, her lungs seizing as she gasped for air that felt like poison. Her ribs screamed in protest, each breath sending sharp, stabbing pain through her chest where the pressure had nearly crushed them.
Blood pooled beneath her cheek, mixing with the dust and debris to form a dark, viscous paste.
"I have no intention of killing you," Xerollion said, his voice echoing off the shattered walls with terrifying calm. "You’re far too interesting to end so simply, Evelyn..."
"Your death would give me nothing beyond a fleeting moment of satisfaction, and I’ve already had enough satisfaction for one day."
Evelyn didn’t move. She couldn’t.
Her fingers twitched against the stone, scraping weakly through the rubble as she tried to find purchase, tried to find the strength to rise again, to throw one last desperate strike.
But her mana system was fried; her circuits burned out from the seventy percent exertion. Her body felt like it was made of lead and broken glass.
’Is this it?’ Her mind screamed. ’After everything?’
’After Apollo? After all that power I hid?’
’I die on a filthy floor, staring at a monster who doesn’t even think I’m worth the effort of killing?’
She watched through blurred vision as Xerollion turned his back on her. The casualness of the gesture was the ultimate insult.
He wasn’t retreating; he was simply moving on to something more worthy of his time.
But before he could walk away, the remaining soldiers, driven by a desperate, suicidal courage born of seeing their comrades slaughtered, attempted one final, coordinated gambit.
"For Aethelgard!" one screamed, his voice cracking.
Three soldiers charged from the shadows, their weapons enchanted with residual light magic.
SHING! CLANG!
Xerollion didn’t even turn around. With a flick of his wrist, a wave of telekinetic force exploded outward.
BOOM.
The soldiers weren’t just knocked back; they were pulverized. One soldier’s arm snapped with an audible CRACK as he hit a pillar, his bone piercing through the skin in a spray of crimson.
Another was hurled against the ceiling with such velocity that his body crumpled like wet paper upon impact. The corridor was filled with the sounds of breaking bone and the wet gurgle of dying men.
Xerollion stepped through the carnage as if walking through a garden, his boots clicking softly on the blood-slicked stone. He didn’t spare them a glance.
He didn’t care. They were insects, and he had already finished swiping them away.

Evelyn lay there, battered and broken, but breathing, her eyes tracking his every movement with a volatile cocktail of relief and deepening hatred. The relief was involuntary, a biological response to not being dead; the hatred was conscious, a cold fire that refused to be extinguished.

The understanding settled over her like a shroud: she had been left alive not out of mercy, not out of compassion, but through the cold, detached calculation of a man who had already dismantled nearly everyone who mattered to Aethelgard that day.
Mercy required emotion.
He had none.
He had only interest.

Further down the corridor, the few remaining soldiers who still stood watched in horrified silence. They watched defeat after defeat unfold without end, each new casualty a hammer blow to their crumbling resolve.
Whatever hope they had carried into this corridor, whatever belief they had that they could win, that they could survive, was thinning, evaporating like mist in a furnace with every passing second.
The light of the corridor was fading, the torches guttering out, leaving only the glow of burning mana and the spreading darkness of inevitable defeat.
But then... somewhere...
Valentina moved first.
The motion was not sudden or panicked; it was the measured, inevitable movement of a tectonic plate shifting.
She stepped away from the position she had been holding since the moment Apollo fell, a frozen statue of grief, and replaced it with something far more dangerous: a hard, glacial resolve.
The pallor that had drained her face moments ago was gone, replaced by a terrifying clarity. The weight of Aethelgard’s survival now rested entirely on her shoulders.
As Headmaster and the strongest mage remaining in their crumbling ranks, she knew that if she did not act now, the last ember of hope would be snuffed out forever.
For one suspended heartbeat, time itself seemed to clot. Neither she nor Morwenna moved.
They stood like twin pillars of defiance amidst a landscape of absolute carnage.
Valentina’s eyes swept over the wreckage of their failure. Her gaze landed on Apollo, motionless and broken, a fallen god sprawled against the far wall.

Then to Elliot slumped against the jagged stone, his breathing shallow and wet, while Evelyn’s shaking, blood-slicked hands pressed futilely against his chest as if she could push the life back into him by sheer force of will.
The corridor was a tomb: shattered tiles, severed limbs, cracked pillars dripping with fresh blood, and the acrid smoke of spent enchantments.
FZZT... CRACKLE...

The magical residue in the air hummed with the death throes of their spells. Valentina catalogued every detail—the trajectory of the debris, the positioning of the enemy, and the exact magical signature of the devastation—with the cold efficiency of a scholar analyzing a hostile spell pattern.
Then, she forcibly shoved it away. She buried the horror in a dark corner of her mind.
There would be time to grieve later. If there was a later.
Beside her, Morwenna’s jaw tightened. The steel in the warrior’s expression mirrored Valentina’s own.
Morwenna had buried enough soldiers to fill a cathedral; she knew that to dwell on the dead mid-battle was to invite the grave to claim you next.
Valentina turned her head slightly toward Morwenna. No words were needed.
They exchanged a single, sharp nod, a silent pact forged in the blood of their comrades. They were the last two standing.

Two of the most seasoned veterans left on this godforsaken battlefield, both acutely aware of the terrifying truth: they had just watched Apollo, Elliot, and Evelyn be dismantled one by one like clockwork toys.
"The two of us," Valentina said, her voice cutting through the ringing silence like a honed blade.

Her grimoire snapped open in her left hand, its ancient pages fluttering violently as headmaster-tier magical energy began to manifest. A corona of brilliant, unstable violet light erupted around her, casting long, dancing shadows that made her appear larger than life.
VROOOOM.
The air began to vibrate with the sheer pressure of her gathering mana. "Together, we might actually have a chance."
Morwenna didn’t hesitate. Her hand went to the hilt of her combat blade, drawing it with a lethal SHING.

Her expression remained composed, a mask of military discipline, but beneath that surface, a cold unease writhed like a serpent. It was a private terror, a secret tied to a night she had never spoken of, a truth that made this entire confrontation infinitely more complicated than any battlefield strategy could account for.
If she failed here, she wasn’t just losing a war; she was failing the one thing she had sworn to protect in the dark.

The two women squared their shoulders, their eyes locking onto the silhouette of the enemy. The air between them and the approaching threat began to crackle with static, the tension so thick it felt as though the very atmosphere might shatter.

chapters.title: Chapter 1200. Decades of Experience Against Eternity
paragraphs: They moved as one.

It was not the desperate scramble of survivors but the synchronized execution of two masters. They launched their assault from opposite flanks, creating a pincer movement designed to shatter any single point of focus.
Valentina became the storm; Morwenna became the blade that guided it.
FWOOOOOM SHHHHIIIIII!

Valentina’s grimoire didn’t just hover; it screamed. The ancient tome levitated beside her shoulder, its pages flipping with supernatural fury. FLAP FLAP FLAP FLAP, each page flaring with luminous, burning sigils.
Her fingers danced through the air like a conductor leading a symphony of destruction. Through her dual simultaneous grimoire technique, she unleashed a torrent of opposing elements.
Waves of infernal crimson fire and jagged, cerulean ice twisted around each other in a lethal, coiling vortex.
This wasn’t standard elemental casting. In most mages, fire melts ice; ice smothers flame.

But Valentina’s mana was different; it was disciplined, pressurized, and absolute. The flames licked along the frozen surfaces without melting them, while the ice hardened along the edges of the fire without being consumed.
It was a braided current of elemental paradox, a technique that would take a prodigy a decade to grasp, which she had forced into submission in six years through sheer, unadulterated stubbornness.
WHIRRRRR CRACKLE!
Beneath the leading edge of that elemental hurricane, Morwenna struck. She moved with the terrifying economy of motion that only thirty years of combat instruction could produce.
She was low to the ground, her boots finding purchase on the blood-slicked debris without hesitation. Her blade caught the dying torchlight in short, lethal arcs.
SHING. SHING. SHING.

She wasn’t swinging wildly; she was herding. Each feint, each precise cut aimed at his tendons or his guard, was designed to force Xerollion to shift his weight, to open a millimeter of space, to react.
She was a predator corralling prey into the path of a blizzard.
Xerollion met the onslaught with something he hadn’t shown all day: genuine alertness. The casual cruelty in his stance vanished, replaced by a coiled, predatory stillness.
BOOM. CLANG. CRACK.
His Full Potential Adaptation roared to life, his mind becoming a supercomputer processing two distinct, high-level threat vectors simultaneously.
’Dual source engagement detected, his mind catalogued with cold precision.’
’Elemental grimoire casting layered against hyper-efficient close-quarters blade work.’
’Two independent threat vectors running in parallel.’
’Adaptation protocols engaged: adjusting for thermal variance and kinetic trajectory simultaneously.’
For the first time, something akin to satisfaction flickered in his thoughts. Apollo had been convicted without craft, all heart, and no technique.
Elliot had been raw power without discipline, a blunt instrument. Evelyn had been speed without the substance to back it up.
But Valentina and Morwenna?
They brought something terrifyingly beautiful: decades of accumulated experience layered over flawless skill. They were not just fighters; they were living weapons.

A small, distant part of him felt something approaching regret the way a collector might regret crushing a priceless work of art because he knew that even this masterpiece would not be enough to stop him.
Morwenna lunged, her blade whistling toward his throat.
SST!
Xerollion didn’t retreat; he simply tilted his head by an inch, the steel grazing his mask with a shower of sparks.
TCHHH!
In the same heartbeat, Valentina sent a concentrated lance of braided frost fire screaming toward his chest.
KRA KOOOOM!
Xerollion’s telekinetic barrier flared. The fireball struck his barrier and detonated against the corridor wall instead, sending chunks of stone raining down like shrapnel.
CRUNCH.
One shard embedded itself in the wall beside Morwenna’s head as she twisted mid-lunge, her reflexes saving her from being decapitated by her own debris.

He caught Morwenna’s next strike on his bare forearm, the enchanted steel sparking against his skin while his free hand swept outward, catching one of Valentina’s secondary ice spikes and redirecting its momentum into the ground.
CRACK SHATTER.
The floor exploded beneath them as the redirected magic tore through the masonry.
"A reasonably good partnership," Xerollion said, his voice calm despite the chaos of ice shards and flames whipping around him.
His eyes remained fixed on them through the smoke, cold and unblinking. "The coordination is impressive..."
"The discipline is... admirable."
He stepped into Morwenna’s guard, forcing her to abort a killing thrust, then pivoted to face Valentina’s next incantation. "But you both already know this isn’t going to be sufficient..."
"You are bringing decades of experience to a fight against eternity."
Morwenna said nothing. Silence was her weapon, a controlled void that allowed her to focus entirely on the mechanics of slaughter.
Her blade swept in a viciously low arc toward his ankles, a strike not meant to kill but to sever his connection to the ground.
Simultaneously, Valentina answered his taunt not with words, but with a devastating compound spell.
KRA KOOOOOM!
A spinning lance of jagged ice, wrapped in a writhing cocoon of contained lightning, shrieked through the air.
ZZZZT SHHHH!
The spell was launched at a precise, lethal angle, engineered to arrive at the exact millisecond Morwenna’s blade forced Xerollion to commit his weight to a defensive pivot.
It was a trap built of physics and timing, an extremely well-coordinated gambit for two women who had never trained together in their entire lives.
Xerollion’s eyes narrowed. ’Synchronized tactical execution... high-level coordination...’
Even as he twisted his body with supernatural fluidity to clear the strike, his mind was already calculating. He met the ice lance with a short, violent burst of telekinetic pressure.
CRACK SHATTER!
The lance detonated several feet short of its target, sending fragments of frozen lightning scattering across the stone like deadly glass confetti.
WHOOSH.
He didn’t wait for the debris to settle. He used the half-second of distraction to close the distance on Morwenna.
He moved like a shadow given mass, testing her guard with two lightning-fast strikes of his own.
CLANG! CLANG!

The sound of steel meeting telekinetic force rang through the corridor like a funeral bell. Morwenna caught the first strike on the flat of her blade and rolled her wrist with practiced grace, redirecting the second past her shoulder.
She gave ground exactly as far as necessary, not an inch more, maintaining the perfect distance between her life and his wrath.
The moment she regained her footing, she launched a brutal low sweep aimed at his ankles.
WHIP!
It was a strike meant to upend a giant. Xerollion was forced to leave the ground entirely for a fraction of a second, his boots losing contact with the blood-slicked tile.
’Now.’
Valentina’s next casting arrived in that same stolen heartbeat. A compressed sphere of raw, violet arcane force screamed across the corridor.
VROOOOM!
It clipped Xerollion’s side while he was still airborne, the impact sending him skidding several feet across the broken tiles.
SKREEEEE.
The sound of his boots dragging against stone echoed as he fought to maintain his balance.
For several exchanges, the two women tested him like wolves testing the hide of a dragon. They fought separately, probing his defenses, before finally finding their combined rhythm.

Morwenna feinted high with a diagonal slash that forced his guard upward, then abruptly dropped into what her soldiers called the Nightwing Guard, a low, coiled defensive stance built to absorb a devastating counter blow while keeping the blade positioned for an immediate, lethal riposte.
Behind her, Valentina layered the trap: a rolling wall of frost materialized, thick and opaque, cutting off his escape routes.
FROOOOOSH.
Xerollion was forced into a binary choice: burn through the frost wall or maneuver around it. Both options would cost him the one thing he couldn’t afford to lose time.
He chose to dominate both.
BOOM!
With a primal burst of telekinetic force, he shattered the frost wall. Shards of ice exploded outward like shrapnel.
SHING!
He stepped directly into Morwenna’s waiting riposte, a strike he anticipated a half second later than she expected.

Instead of letting the blade pierce his ribs, he caught the steel against his forearm. The impact was so violent it sent a shockwave through Morwenna’s arm, the force hard enough to numb her fingers around the hilt.
’Damn it,’ Morwenna thought, her pulse hammering against her ribs. ’He’s reading the timing...’
’He’s not just reacting; he’s predicting.’

But twenty years of blood-soaked muscle memory refused to let a numbed hand become a fatal opening. Without breaking her stance, she adjusted her grip with a grunt of exertion and answered immediately.
She twisted her wrist in a desperate, reversed cut. The enchanted steel bit deep.
SQUELCH.
A shallow but clean line opened across Xerollion’s forearm, crimson blood welling up instantly and trickling down his skin.
It was a small victory, a single drop of blood in an ocean of slaughter, but it was proof: he could bleed.

It clipped Xerollion’s side while he was still airborne, the impact sending him skidding several feet across the broken tiles.
SKREEEEE.
The sound of his boots dragging against stone echoed as he fought to maintain his balance.
For several exchanges, the two women tested him like wolves testing the hide of a dragon.
They fought separately, probing his defenses, before finally finding their combined rhythm.

Morwenna feinted high with a diagonal slash that forced his guard upward, then abruptly dropped into what her soldiers called the Nightwing Guard, a low, coiled defensive stance built to absorb a devastating counter blow while keeping the blade positioned for an immediate, lethal riposte.
Behind her, Valentina layered the trap: a rolling wall of frost materialized, thick and opaque, cutting off his escape routes.
FROOOOOSH.
Xerollion was forced into a binary choice: burn through the frost wall or maneuver around it.
Both options would cost him the one thing he couldn’t afford to lose time.
He chose to dominate both.
BOOM!
With a primal burst of telekinetic force, he shattered the frost wall.
Shards of ice exploded outward like shrapnel.
SHING!
He stepped directly into Morwenna’s waiting riposte, a strike he anticipated a half second later than she expected.
Instead of letting the blade pierce his ribs, he caught the steel against his forearm.
The impact was so violent it sent a shockwave through Morwenna’s arm, the force hard enough to numb her fingers around the hilt.
’Damn it,’ Morwenna thought, her pulse hammering against her ribs. ’He’s reading the timing...’
’He’s not just reacting; he’s predicting.’
But twenty years of blood-soaked muscle memory refused to let a numbed hand become a fatal opening.
Without breaking her stance, she adjusted her grip with a grunt of exertion and answered immediately.
She twisted her wrist in a desperate, reversed cut.
The enchanted steel bit deep.
SQUELCH.
A shallow but clean line opened across Xerollion’s forearm, crimson blood welling up instantly and trickling down his skin.
It was a small victory, a single drop of blood in an ocean of slaughter, but it was proof: he could bleed.
